description: "Jesus defined the symbol Himself: the lost coin is the repenting sinner. Both original languages name the tribute penny a census coin — and a kingdom is a beast, so Caesar's coin bears the beast's image and name. God mints His own coinage: dug from the field, refined in fire, stamped with His Name — and collected, a half-shekel ransom a head, whenever His people are counted. The mark of the beast resolves as the counterfeit census: its name for the Name, its number for the count, buy-and-sell where the atonement money stood."
og_title: "The Coin — MEAT The Bible's Symbolic Language"
epigraphs:
  - quote: "Render therefore unto Caesar the things which are Caesar's; and unto God the things that are God's."
    ref: "Matthew 22:21"
---
Jesus defined this chapter's symbol Himself, in a parable built for the purpose:

[quote.scripture, Luke 15:8-10, NKJV]
____
Or what woman, having ten silver *coins*, if she loses one coin, does not light a sym:sym-lamp[lamp], sweep the house, and search carefully until she finds it?
And when she has found it, she calls her friends and neighbors together, saying, “Rejoice with me, for I have found the piece which I lost!”
Likewise, I say to you, there is joy in the presence of the angels of God over *one sinner who repents*.
____

The equation is stated in the last line: the found coin *is* the repenting sinner — the same celebration that met the prodigal son (Luke 15:23-24, 32), told with silver instead of a son.
Identify this symbol correctly, and it unlocks a mystery woven through half a dozen parables — and, at the far end, the wisdom Revelation calls for: the mark of the sym:sym-beast[beast], its *image*, its sym:sym-name[name], the *number of its name*, and why no man may buy or sell without them.

Decode the parable's own symbols first.
The woman sweeps *the house* — and in the paired lost-sheep parable, the sheep are __“the lost sheep of the *house of Israel*”__ (Matthew 10:6); her ten coins are the house's ten tribes.
She searches by a lit sym:sym-lamp[lamp] — and the lamp is the commandment (Proverbs 6:23); its sym:sym-light[light] is the commandment lived, as the link:/books/symbolic-language/light-and-darkness/[Light and Darkness] chapter proves.
By that obedience the coin is found: the lost are sought by the light of the law.

[discrete]
=== The Coin of the Census

One coin in the Gospels is named, examined face-up, and ruled on — and the scene opens as a trap:

[quote.scripture, Matthew 22:15-21, NKJV]
____
Then the Pharisees went and plotted how they might entangle Him in His talk.
And they sent to Him their disciples with the Herodians, saying, “Teacher, we know that You are true, and teach the sym:sym-way[way] of God in sym:sym-truth[truth]; nor do You care about anyone, for You do not regard the *person* of men.
Tell us, therefore, what do You think? Is it lawful to pay *taxes* to Caesar, or not?”
But Jesus perceived their wickedness, and said, “Why do you test Me, you hypocrites?
Show Me the coin of the *census*.”footnote:fn10census[“Tax money” in the Greek is _nomisma tou kēnsou_ — literally “the coin of the census,” Rome's registration of persons for the head-tax.] So they brought Him a *denarius*.
And He said to them, “Whose *image* and *inscription* is this?”
They said to Him, “Caesar's.” And He said to them, “*Render* therefore to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and to God the things that are God's.”
____

Look at what the coin carries: an image and a name.
A sym:sym-beast[beast] is a kingdom — __“the fourth beast shall be the fourth *kingdom* upon earth”__ (Daniel 7:23) — and a kingdom stamps its money.
Caesar's census coin therefore bears, on its face, the *image* of the beast and the *name* of the beast — the very two things Revelation says the world will be made to carry.
Jesus held the whole question of the mark in His hand, and His ruling was already complete: give the beast back its coin.

Read without the symbols, __“render unto Caesar”__ is a mirror — the tax-lover sees a command to pay, the tax-hater hears that everything is God's — and the scene shrinks to a clever escape from a trap.
Read with them, the sentence divides the world's whole estate by image and inscription: everything stamped by the beast returns to the beast, and everything stamped by God returns to God.
Whose image do *you* bear?
__“God created man in his own *image*”__ (Genesis 1:27), and the sym:sym-seal[seal] writes His inscription on the forehead — so what is rendered unto God is the image-bearer himself: __“present your *bodies* a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable unto God, which is your *reasonable service*”__ (Romans 12:1).

So the pivot of the chapter is a question the tribute scene forces: if Caesar has a coin bearing his image, his inscription, struck for his census — what coin bears the *image* of God, the *seal* of God, the *name* of God, and the *number of His name*?
The parable of the woman already answered: we are His coinage.
What follows traces His coin through Scripture — minted, spent, carried in a fish's mouth, counted, and counterfeited.

[discrete]
=== The Mint

A coin is the seal made money, and His coin is minted the way all coin is: dug from a field, refined in fire, stamped with the name.
The sym:sym-field[field] is the world (Matthew 13:38), and the treasure hid in it was worth selling everything to buy (Matthew 13:44).
A coin lying loose is simply picked up; what the buyer found was *ore* — gold scattered through the clay of the field — and ore is not spent; it is refined.
The refining is the trial — __“he *knoweth* the way that I take: when he hath tried me, I shall come forth as *gold*”__ (Job 23:10) — and Zechariah hears what comes out of the furnace when the sym:sym-remnant[refined third] is brought through:

[quote.scripture, Zechariah 13:9]
____
…I will *refine* them as silver is refined, and will try them as *gold* is tried: they shall *call on my name*, and I will hear them: I will say, It is *my people*: and they shall say, The LORD is *my God*.
____

Refined, then stamped: those who come through the fire call on the Name, and God claims them as His own.
The stamp is the seal the link:/books/symbolic-language/the-seal/[Seal] chapter defined — the Name written on the forehead and the hand, the law sealed in the man.

[discrete]
=== What His Coin Buys

Caesar's coin moves in Caesar's market.
God's coin has a market of its own, and Scripture posts its prices: __“*Buy* the truth, and *sell it not*; also wisdom, and instruction, and understanding”__ (Proverbs 23:23).
Solomon wrote the whole exchange out — and notice what the money is, and where the goods come from:

[quote.scripture, Proverbs 2:3-6]
____
Yea, if thou criest after *knowledge*, and liftest up thy voice for *understanding*; If thou seekest her as *silver*, and searchest for her as for *hid treasures*; Then shalt thou understand the fear of the LORD, and find the knowledge of God.
For the LORD giveth *wisdom*: out of his *mouth* cometh knowledge and understanding.
____

Here is the treasure-hid-in-a-field parable in proverb form, centuries early: the seeking is priced *as silver*, the goods are *hid treasures*, and they issue __“out of his *mouth*.”__
The risen Lord still runs the counter: __“I counsel thee to *buy of me* gold *tried in the fire*, that thou mayest be rich”__ (Revelation 3:18) — He sells exactly what His mint produces.
The vocabulary of this market — silver, treasure, and a *mouth* — carries us to the strangest coin-scene in the Gospels.

[discrete]
=== The Fish That Carries It

At Capernaum the collectors come asking after a very particular coin:

[quote.scripture, Matthew 17:24-27, ASV]
____
And when they were come to Capernaum, they that received the *half-shekel* came to Peter, and said, Doth not your teacher pay the half-shekel? He saith, Yea.
And when he came into the house, Jesus spake first to him, saying, What thinkest thou, Simon? the kings of the earth, from whom do they receive toll or tribute? from their sons, or from strangers?
And when he said, From strangers, Jesus said unto him, Therefore the *sons are free*.
But, lest we cause them to stumble, go thou to the sym:sym-sea[sea], and cast a hook, and take up the sym:sym-fish[fish] that *first cometh up*; and when thou hast opened his *mouth*, thou shalt find a *shekel*: that take, and give unto them *for me and thee*.
____

The sym:sym-fish[fish] is the one symbol even the world still reads: people put fish on their cars as a sign of their faith — the fish is a believer.
Read the rest of the scene the same way: Peter, the fisher *of men* (Matthew 4:19), goes to the sym:sym-sea[sea] — the peoples and nations — and the *first* fish that comes up out of it carries silver in its *mouth*.
The Son owes no ransom in His Father's house — __“then are the sons free”__ — yet He pays, and the payment is a parable in miniature.
Why a fish, why *first*, and why the *mouth*?
The answers are all in the law the coin was minted under — for the half-shekel the collectors asked for is not a market price; it is a statute.

[discrete]
=== The Census and Its Ransom

The law prices persons in silver — not as a figure of speech, but as statute: a man vowed to God is redeemed __“by thy estimation”__, in sanctuary shekels (Leviticus 27:2-8).
Whenever Israel is counted, every counted head owes a coin:

[quote.scripture, Exodus 30:12, 15]
____
When thou takest the sum of the children of Israel after their number, then shall they give every man *a ransom for his soul* unto the LORD, when thou numberest them; that there be *no plague* among them, when thou numberest them… The *rich* shall not give *more*, and the *poor* shall not give *less* than half a shekel… to make an *atonement* for your souls.
____

Every clause carries doctrine.
The ransom is owed *at the counting* — to stand in God's census is to stand ransomed.
The old spiritual asks for exactly this: __“Lord, how I want to be *in that number*, when the saints go marching in”__ — *that number* is the census of the ransomed.
The price is flat — no man's soul outbids another's at that window.
The tribute trap opened with this very clause, spoken as flattery — __“You do not regard the *person* of men”__ — and Scripture testifies it of God in the census's own pair:

[quote.scripture, Job 34:19]
____
…that accepteth not the persons of princes, nor regardeth the *rich* more than the *poor*? for they all are the *work of his hands*.
____

What was offered as bait was the census price, stated back to its Author — every soul His work, every soul the same half shekel.

The money is called __“a *memorial*”__ (Exodus 30:16) — the same word the law uses for the sign bound between the eyes (on the forehead) — and it is not banked but appointed __“for the service of the tabernacle.”__
Exodus records the appointment to the shekel: __“of the hundred talents of silver were *cast the sockets of the sanctuary*, and the sockets of the vail; … a talent for a socket”__ (Exodus 38:25-27) — a half-shekel a head for 603,550 counted men, melted into the foundations.
*God's house stood on the ransom-money of His counted people.* The house has never changed its engineering: __“ye also, as *lively stones*, are built up a *spiritual house*”__ (1 Peter 2:5), and the sym:sym-stone[stone] is covenant sym:sym-rock[rock] — a temple of covenant-people, socketed in redemption silver.

The census began at the door in Egypt.
The first ransom of the firstborn was the Passover lamb — the firstborn under the marked doors were *bought* with its blood — and Israel marched out __“on the *fifteenth* day of the first month”__ (Numbers 33:3).
On the morrow — the *sixteenth*, the day of firstfruits, the very day of the year the Firstborn would rise as __“the *firstfruits* of them that slept”__ (1 Corinthians 15:20) — God stated His claim:

[quote.scripture, Exodus 13:2]
____
Sanctify unto me all the firstborn, whatsoever *openeth the womb* among the children of Israel, both of man and of beast: it is *mine*.
____

The womb the law watched opens again in Revelation, where the travailing woman __“brought forth a *man child*… and her child was *caught up unto God*, and to his throne”__ (Revelation 12:5).
The dragon stands before her to devour him as Egypt's king stood before the firstborn — every redeemed firstborn a rehearsal of __“the *firstborn* of every creature”__ (Colossians 1:15).
Under the claim, every firstborn thereafter __“shalt thou *redeem*”__ (Exodus 13:13), and the redemption travels under a sign with three locations:

[quote.scripture, Exodus 13:9]
____
And it shall be for a *sign* unto thee upon thine *hand*, and for a *memorial* between thine *eyes*, that the LORD'S law may be in thy *mouth*: for with a strong hand hath the LORD brought thee out of Egypt.
____

Hand, eyes, mouth.
When the claimed were redeemed by silver, the count was a census of names: __“Number all the firstborn… take the *number of their names*”__ (Numbers 3:40) — 22,273 of them, exact to the man where the army musters are round, and the overage above the Levites' count was ransomed at five shekels a head (Numbers 3:43-50).
God counts what He redeems by name — and the price attaches to the name counted.

Now the fish gives up its riddle.
The redemption sign's third location is the *mouth* — __“that the LORD's law may be in thy mouth”__ — and the seal-texts keep the word there: __“the word is very nigh unto thee, *in thy mouth*, and in thy heart”__ (Deuteronomy 30:14); __“*confess with thy mouth* the Lord Jesus”__ (Romans 10:9).
A man wears the seal on his forehead; a fish carries it in its mouth — on a fish they are the same place.
The first man drawn up out of the sea of nations comes up with the ransom-witness in his mouth: the caught man carries his confession, and the confession is his redemption.
The coin itself is exact: a stater — one full shekel, precisely *two* half-shekel ransoms — __“for me and thee.”__
The Hebrew Gospel seals the grammar: the coin is given _be'ad_ us — “on behalf of” — the very preposition of the atonement, __“and Aaron shall make atonement *for* himself, and *for* his house”__ (Leviticus 16:6).
The substitution is in the preposition: one pays, another is covered.

[discrete]
=== The Mark of the Beast

Now the piece this symbol unlocks.
Revelation holds two enrollments, and nearly every reader studies the beast's *mark* in isolation — never suspecting that the mark is an enrollment at all.
Set the two side by side instead.
In chapter seven, God counts:

[quote.scripture, Revelation 7:4]
____
And I heard the *number* of them which were *sealed*: and there were sealed *144,000* of all the tribes of the children of Israel.
____

This is a census, taken tribe by tribe like Sinai's, of servants sealed in their foreheads before the link:/books/symbolic-language/the-four-winds/[four winds] blow.
The Hebrew of the count carries the firstborn census inside it: 144 _alaphim_ — and the consonants of *thousands* are the consonants of _alluphim_, *chiefs*, *firsts* — and Revelation names the sealed exactly that: __“the *firstfruits* unto God and to the Lamb”__ (Revelation 14:4).
God's last census, like His first, is a census of firstborn.
In chapter thirteen, the beast counts:

[quote.scripture, Revelation 13:16-18]
____
And he causeth *all*, both small and great, *rich and poor*, free and bond, to receive a *mark* in their right hand, or in their foreheads: And that no man might *buy or sell*, save he that had the mark, or the *name* of the beast, or the *number of his name*… Let him that hath understanding *count the number* of the beast: for it is the number of a man…
____

The mark of the beast is the counterfeit of the temple census, member for member.
Its *name* sits where the sym:sym-name[NAME] goes; its *number* answers the number of the sealed; its enrollment is universal where God's is __“of all the tribes”__; and where God's census collects a ransom-coin for the sanctuary, the beast's census issues its coin-mark for the market — __“no man might buy or sell”__ without it.

Even the word is mint vocabulary: the *mark* is _charagma_ — an impression struck or engraved, the die-strike — and its only other use in the New Testament is coin-and-idol language, the Godhead falsely imaged in __“gold, or silver… *graven* by art and man's device”__ (Acts 17:29).
The man who takes the mark is *minted*: the beast's image and inscription struck on flesh — the census coin, paid in persons.

The counterfeit even keeps the ransom's equality clause: where the census took the same half shekel of __“the *rich*”__ and __“the *poor*”__ (Exodus 30:15), the mark falls on __“rich and poor”__ — with __“small and great, free and bond”__ stacked beside them, and the Hebrew Revelation reads __“the wealthy and the poor”__ outright.
The beast's census, like God's, is no respecter of persons: the counterfeit keeps even that clause.
Even the registers face each other in the same chapter — the beast's rolls against __“the *book of life* of the Lamb”__ (Revelation 13:8), the register of which the psalm says, __“The LORD shall *count*, when he *writeth up* the people”__ (Psalm 87:6).

The plague-clause inverts with the rest.
The ransom was paid __“that there be *no plague* among them, when thou numberest them”__ — and the tormentors of the trumpets touch __“only those men which have *not* the seal of God in their foreheads”__ (Revelation 9:4), while the first vial falls __“upon the men which had the *mark of the beast*”__ (Revelation 16:2).
God's counted take no plague; Babylon's counted are the plague's named address.
Nor can Babylon's market starve the sealed, for the other market never closed:

[quote.scripture, Isaiah 55:1]
____
Ho, every one that thirsteth, come ye to the waters, and he that hath *no money*; come ye, *buy*, and eat; yea, come, buy wine and milk *without money* and without price.
____

The beast's enrollment is older than Rome.
Its founding charter was spoken on the plain of Shinar:

[quote.scripture, Genesis 11:4]
____
Go to, let us build us a city and a tower, whose top may reach unto heaven; and let us *make us a name*, lest we be scattered abroad upon the face of the whole earth.
____

Babel opened a counter-covenant: a name of man's own minting for every man to be enrolled under.
The reason the marked cannot be saved is now plain grammar: they are counted under the wrong name, and __“there is none other *name* under heaven given among men, whereby we *must be saved*”__ (Acts 4:12).
Two names, two censuses, two coinages — no man is enrolled in both.

[discrete]
=== The Number of One Man

__“Let him that hath understanding *count* the number of the beast: for it is the number of a man”__ (Revelation 13:18) — and the Hebrew Revelation reads *one man*, _adam echad_.
Most reach for gematria here, as though Revelation were asking for another candidate whose letters add to 666.
This chapter's claim is different: Revelation 13 is not first a gematria problem but a covenant census problem.

The words themselves vote that way.
The Greek verb is _psēphizō_ — to tally with a _psēphos_, the pebble used for ancient counting and voting — and its only other use in Scripture is a cost-tally: __“which of you, intending to build a tower, sitteth not down first, and *counteth the cost*?”__ (Luke 14:28).
John hands the overcomer the very object four chapters earlier: __“I will give him a *white stone*, and in the stone a *new name written*, which no man knoweth saving he that receiveth it”__ (Revelation 2:17) — and his word is not _lithos_, a rock, but _psēphos_, the counting-pebble.
A psēphos is a vote and an enrollment-token: Paul casts one against the saints — __“I gave my *voice* against them”__ (Acts 26:10) — and Matthias is __“*numbered* with the eleven”__ by one (Acts 1:26).

The Hebrew Revelation names what the white stone holds: the overcomer receives __“a *good testimony*, and in this testimony a *new name* written”__ — God's vote cast *for* a man, his sealed entry in the census of the sealed; the mark is the vote against, carried on the flesh.
The Hebrew's counting verb agrees: _chashav_ — the ledger-reckoning of __“counted it to him for *righteousness*”__ (Genesis 15:6) and of the law's redemption-price arithmetic (Leviticus 25:50-52) — and its text finishes the instruction as a tally: __“you shall find the *sum*.”__

Scripture uses the number itself twice: once as money, once as a census — the two things the beast's enrollment controls.
The number 666 is a *money* figure:

[quote.scripture, 1 Kings 10:14]
____
Now the weight of gold that came to Solomon in *one year* was *666 talents* of gold…
____

The revenue lands at the very turn where the king began multiplying gold against the law of the king (Deuteronomy 17:17).
It is also a *census* figure, and the roll shows the format of a number-of-a-name exactly:

[quote.scripture, Ezra 2:13]
____
The children of *Adonikam*, *666*.
____

It is a count filed under the name that owns it, in the register of those *coming out of Babylon*.
A number of a name is a census entry; Revelation keeps both ledgers in that grammar — __“I heard the *number* of them which were sealed”__ (Revelation 7:4) stands against the number of *its* name, and the victors of the sea of glass overcome __“the beast… his mark, and the *number of his name*”__ (Revelation 15:2) — the enrollment itself, refused.

So the instruction __“count the number”__ asks for arithmetic, not alphabet-magic: a census is a thing you *count* — the redeemed against the enrolled.
The link:/books/symbolic-language/the-remnant/[Remnant] chapter runs that count down 15 converging lines of evidence, and they settle near 2 persons in 1,000 — beside 1 in 666, which is 1.5 in 1,000.
The wisdom the verse calls for is the verdict the count returns: __“*few* there be that find it”__ (Matthew 7:14) — how few are ransomed, and how broad the way of the enrolled.
Every man ends in one census or the other: counted and ransomed, or counted and marked.

Hosea acted the ransomed side out in one verse: commanded to love an adulteress __“according to the love of the LORD toward the children of Israel,”__ he went to market for his own wife — __“So I *bought her* to me for fifteen pieces of silver, and for an homer of barley”__ (Hosea 3:2) — the Husband paying coin to redeem the wife who left him.
The sym:sym-marriage[marriage] itself — what joins it, what can break it, and how far the Husband went to keep it — is the next chapter.

title: "Marriage and Divorce"
slug: marriage-and-divorce
order: 12
permalink: /books/meat-bibles-symbolic-language/marriage-and-divorce/
description: "The common reading says Jesus permits divorce for sexual immorality (porneia). But under the law, adultery carries death, not divorce — a dead spouse needs no bill — and Jesus uses two different Greek words in the same sentence. Scripture's own usage points elsewhere: the union that is itself fornication — the out-of-covenant marriage — where putting away is not permitted but commanded (Ezra). And God keeps His own statute: He gave adulterous Israel the bill of divorce, faced His own no-return rule, and answered it at the cross — the Husband took the wife's death penalty and rose to marry her renewed. The Bible ends with a burning and a wedding."
og_title: "Marriage and Divorce — MEAT The Bible's Symbolic Language"
epigraphs:
  - quote: "…which my covenant they brake, although I was an husband unto them, saith the LORD."
    ref: "Jeremiah 31:32"
---
The common reading says Jesus permits divorce for sexual immorality, taking _porneia_ broadly as illicit sexual activity outside monogamous marriage.
Other readers confine the exception to sin discovered during betrothal, like Joseph’s dilemma, or tie it to the forbidden unions of Leviticus 18.

Every camp shares the same assumption.
All three read the exception as a _permission_ about _literal_ sex, and not one of them opens the Torah to ask what the law itself does with each case.
This chapter will run that test — the law first, then the words, then the Bible’s symbolic language — and the common interpretation will not survive it.

[discrete]
=== The Collision with the Law

Here is the problem the common view never faces.
Under the law, adultery is not a divorce ground; it is a capital crime:

[quote.scripture, Leviticus 20:10]
____
And the man that committeth *adultery* with another man’s wife, even he that committeth adultery with his neighbour’s wife, the adulterer and the adulteress shall surely be *put to death*.
____

Deuteronomy repeats it for the married and the betrothed alike — __“they shall *both* of them die… so shalt thou put away evil from Israel”__ (Deuteronomy 22:22-24) — and the scribes could still quote it to Jesus’ face: __“Moses in the law commanded us, that such should be *stoned*: but what sayest thou?”__
(John 8:5).
A dead spouse needs no bill of divorcement.

If the exception clause means __“divorce is permitted for adultery,”__ then Jesus quietly commuted a death penalty — amended the law — a dozen verses after declaring that __“one jot or one tittle shall in no wise pass from the law”__ (Matthew 5:18), in the same sermon.
The reading that everyone holds makes Jesus break the rule He had just laid down.
Either He contradicted Himself in a single chapter, or the exception is not about adultery at all.

[discrete]
=== Two Words in One Sentence

The Greek settles which, because Jesus used two different words — in the same breath:

[quote.scripture, Matthew 5:32]
____
But I say unto you, That whosoever shall put away his wife, saving for the cause of *fornication*, causeth her to commit *adultery*: and whosoever shall marry her that is divorced committeth adultery.
____

The exception is _porneia_ — fornication; the consequence is _moicheia_ — adultery.
He had the adultery-word in His mouth and did not use it for the exception; and when He lists the sins of the heart, He lists them separately: __“*adulteries*, *fornications*”__ (Matthew 15:19) — two words, two things.

Mark and Luke record the saying with no exception at all — __“Whosoever shall put away his wife, and marry another, committeth adultery”__ (Mark 10:11; Luke 16:18) — the absolute form.footnote:hebnt[The Hebrew text of Mark and Luke (the Cochin manuscript tradition, _Ele Ha-Sodot_, c. 1700) carries the same absolute form, with no exception clause, using the very verb of Leviticus 20:10; the manuscripts are presented at https://TimeTested.Bible[TimeTested.Bible].]
Only Matthew carries the clause — and Matthew has already shown his readers the case it covers.

In his first chapter: Mary, __“espoused to Joseph,”__ is found with child, and Joseph — called __“her *husband*”__ and __“a *just* man”__ in the same verse — is __“minded to *put her away* privily”__ (Matthew 1:18-19).
A betrothed man in Israel is a husband; ending a betrothal takes a putting-away; and the text calls Joseph _just_ — law-keeping — in the very act of resolving suspected fornication by a quiet bill rather than a public stoning.
The exception clause covers Joseph; it does not commute Leviticus.

[discrete]
=== What God Hath Joined

Before the divorce question can be answered, marriage itself must be defined — and Scripture defines it as one would expect:

[quote.scripture, Matthew 19:4-6]
____
And he answered and said unto them, Have ye not read, that he which made them *at the beginning* made them male and female,
And said, For this cause shall a man leave father and mother, and shall cleave to his wife: and they twain shall be *one flesh*?
Wherefore they are no more twain, but one flesh.
What therefore *God hath joined together*, let not man put asunder.
____

He answers from the beginning, quoting Genesis 2:24.
What kind of joining?
The last chapter watched it enacted: the husband spreads his wing over the bride — __“I spread my skirt over thee… yea, I sware unto thee, and *entered into a covenant* with thee… and thou becamest mine”__ (Ezekiel 16:8) — and she is called by his name.
Malachi names the wife by the bond: __“she is thy companion, and *the wife of thy covenant*”__ (Malachi 2:14).
And Proverbs names the bond by its Owner — the adulterous woman is one __“which forsaketh the guide of her youth, and forgetteth *the covenant of her God*”__ (Proverbs 2:17).

sym:sym-marriage[Marriage] is the covenant in miniature: a one-flesh union that God Himself joins, sworn, witnessed, and worn like a sym:sym-name[name].
The joining is real whichever way it runs — __“he which is *joined to an* sym:sym-harlot[harlot] is one body… but he that is *joined unto the Lord* is one spirit”__ (1 Corinthians 6:16-17) — which is why the question _of who joined this union_ will turn out to be the whole divorce question.

[discrete]
=== The Nakedness of a Thing

Now open the statute the Pharisees waved at Jesus:

[quote.scripture, Deuteronomy 24:1]
____
When a man hath taken a wife, and married her, and it come to pass that she find no favour in his eyes, because he hath found *some uncleanness* in her: then let him write her a *bill of divorcement*, and give it in her hand, and send her *out of his house*.
____

__“Some uncleanness”__ is, in the Hebrew, _the nakedness of a thing_ — and __“nakedness”__ here is the exact word of the forbidden-union chapter: __“None of you shall approach to any that is near of kin to him, to uncover their sym:sym-naked[nakedness]”__ (Leviticus 18:6), the catalog of unions that were never lawful to make.
The statute’s own vocabulary points away from adultery — which Deuteronomy has already sentenced to death two chapters earlier — and toward the union with something unlawful at its root: the sym:sym-naked[nakedness] uncovered, the covenant covering absent.

Read the rest of the statute’s shape.
Divorce is regulated, never celebrated: the bill in her hand protects the woman (a hard-hearted man could otherwise simply cast her out and leave her bound); she is free to remarry (Deuteronomy 24:2); and one door is bolted — her first husband __“may not take her again… after that she is defiled: for that is *abomination*”__ (Deuteronomy 24:4).
The no-return rule matters because the whole gospel will hang on it before this chapter ends.
The law also forbids divorce outright in two cases (Deuteronomy 22:19, 29), and guards the wife’s provision — __“her food, her raiment, and her duty of marriage, shall he not diminish”__ (Exodus 21:10), the very rights the seven women of the last chapter offered to waive.

When the Pharisees asked Jesus, __“Is it lawful for a man to put away his wife *for every cause*?”__footnote:everycause[Their phrase quotes a standing rabbinic dispute: the school of Hillel allowed divorce “for any cause” — a spoiled dish would do — while the school of Shammai confined it to unchastity (Mishnah, Gittin 9:10).
Jesus’ answer sides with neither school; it goes back to the joining.] — He answered past the whole debate: Moses __“*suffered*”__ divorce __“because of the hardness of your hearts”__ — but __“*from the beginning it was not so*”__ (Matthew 19:8).
The statute manages the wreckage of hard hearts; it does not bless it.
__“The LORD… hateth putting away”__ (Malachi 2:16) — when what is put away is __“the wife of thy covenant.”__

[discrete]
=== The Commanded Divorce

There is a union the law refuses to bless — and there, Scripture does not permit divorce; it commands it.
Watch how the law describes marrying outside the covenant:

[quote.scripture, Exodus 34:15-16]
____
Lest thou make a covenant with the inhabitants of the land, and they *go a whoring after their gods*… And thou take of their daughters unto thy sons, and their daughters go a whoring after their gods, and *make thy sons go a whoring* after their gods.
____

The out-of-covenant marriage is not at risk of leading to fornication; the law calls the union itself a going-a-whoring — sym:sym-fornication[fornication] in the Bible’s symbolic language is covenant-unfaithfulness, and Israel commits it __“with *stones* and with *stocks*”__ (Jeremiah 3:9), with high places (2 Chronicles 21:11), with kingdoms (Revelation 17:2), and with the daughters of strange gods (Deuteronomy 7:3-4).
Now read Ezra with that definition in hand.
The returned exiles had __“taken of their daughters… so that the *holy seed* have mingled themselves with the people of those lands”__ (Ezra 9:2), and the remedy was a covenant:

[quote.scripture, Ezra 10:3]
____
Now therefore let us make a covenant with our God to *put away all the wives*, and such as are born of them… of those that *tremble at the commandment* of our God; and let it be done *according to the law*.
____

__“Put away… according to the law”__ — divorce, not as concession but as obedience, demanded by the men who trembled at the commandment; and Nehemiah enforces the same, holding up Solomon as the proof of where the strange wives lead: __“even him did outlandish women cause to sin”__ (Nehemiah 13:26).

Here Malachi’s oracle shows its two edges, for the same prophet who thundered __“the LORD… hateth putting away”__ thunders first against the marriage Ezra dissolved: __“Judah… hath *married the daughter of a strange god*.
The LORD will *cut off* the man that doeth this”__ (Malachi 2:11-12).
Putting away the wife of the covenant is treachery; keeping the daughter of the strange god is treachery.
Divorce in Scripture is evil or obedience depending entirely on _which union it severs_ — because __“what God hath joined together”__ is a covenant clause, and the union God never joined is the one He commands undone.

Paul keeps both edges for the assemblies — and marks whose voice is whose.
To the married he gives the absolute rule and names its source: __“I command, yet *not I, but the Lord*, Let not the wife depart from her husband”__ (1 Corinthians 7:10).
Then, turning to the man called while already married to an unbeliever, he changes the attribution: __“But to the rest speak *I, not the Lord*”__ (1 Corinthians 7:12) — the absolute belongs to the Lord; the mixed-marriage counsel is the apostle’s own judgment, for a case Ezra’s courts never faced: a man converted mid-marriage, his household half in and half out.

Paul’s judgment runs the opposite direction from Ezra’s: __“if she be pleased to dwell with him, let him *not* put her away… and the unbelieving wife is *sanctified* by the husband”__ (1 Corinthians 7:12, 14).
Paul writes the rule in both directions — the believing wife likewise does not leave her unbelieving husband, who is sanctified by her (1 Corinthians 7:13-14) — for a reason Ezra’s generation did not have.
The covenant door now stands open to every nation, and the out-of-covenant spouse is no longer a pull toward strange gods but a soul within reach of the salvation the sym:sym-gospel[gospel] now publishes to all peoples: __“For what knowest thou, O wife, whether thou shalt *save* thy husband?”__
(1 Corinthians 7:16).
In Ezra’s day the strange wives drew the holy seed out; in Paul’s day the believing spouse may draw the sym:sym-stranger[stranger] in.
New marriages are still made __“*only in the Lord*”__ (1 Corinthians 7:39), and if the unbeliever departs, the believer __“is not under bondage”__ (1 Corinthians 7:15).

[discrete]
=== The Deposed Queen

Scripture also stages a divorce where no sexual sin appears at all — and the grounds are the symbol laid bare.
Queen Vashti is summoned by the king, __“but the queen Vashti *refused to come* at the king’s commandment”__ (Esther 1:12).
The case is heard __“according to *law*”__ (Esther 1:15), and the concern of the court is not jealousy but obedience across the whole realm: __“this deed of the queen shall come abroad unto *all women*, so that they shall *despise their husbands*”__ (Esther 1:17).
The verdict:

[quote.scripture, Esther 1:19]
____
…That Vashti *come no more* before king Ahasuerus; and let the king give her *royal estate unto another that is better than she*.
____

That sentence is the Bible’s standing formula for a deposed covenant partner.
Samuel to Saul: __“The LORD hath rent the kingdom of Israel from thee this day, and hath given it to a neighbour of thine, *that is better than thou*”__ (1 Samuel 15:28).
Jesus to the husbandmen of the vineyard: __“The kingdom of God shall be *taken from you, and given* to a nation bringing forth the sym:sym-fruit[fruits] thereof”__ (Matthew 21:43).
And Solomon — the very case Nehemiah cited — hears it over his strange wives: __“I will surely *rend the kingdom* from thee, and will *give it* to thy servant”__ (1 Kings 11:11).
One formula, one lesson: the King’s wife must obey, or the estate passes — not because the King is petty, but because the whole land learns from the queen; the covenant marriage is public, and its breach teaches rebellion to every house in the empire.

Next comes the replacement, and she is the deposed queen’s exact inversion.
Esther — a bride taken from the scattered exiles — is __“made queen *instead of* Vashti”__ (Esther 2:17); and where Vashti refused to come when summoned, Esther goes in _unsummoned_, at the peril of her life, to intercede for her people: __“I will go in unto the king, which is not according to the law: and *if I perish, I perish*”__ (Esther 4:16).
The queen who would not come, and the bride who comes at the cost of her life: the two wives of the whole symbolic story, side by side in one Persian court.

[discrete]
=== God’s Own Case File

Now open the greatest divorce case in Scripture — God’s own — and watch Him keep His own law at every step.
His wife committed adultery, endlessly, __“with stones and with stocks.”__
The law says death; He is the Judge; and He does not stone her:

[quote.scripture, Jeremiah 3:8]
____
And I saw, when for all the causes whereby backsliding Israel committed *adultery* I had *put her away*, and given her a *bill of divorce*; yet her treacherous sister Judah feared not, but went and played the sym:sym-harlot[harlot] also.
____

The bill of divorce is the exile — the wife sent __“out of his house,”__ scattered among the nations — and God holds the paperwork up to her children (Isaiah 50:1).
But now the Husband has a legal problem, and He states it Himself, citing His own statute:

[quote.scripture, Jeremiah 3:1]
____
They say, If a man put away his wife, and she go from him, and become another man’s, *shall he return unto her again?* shall not that land be greatly polluted? but thou hast played the sym:sym-harlot[harlot] with many lovers; *yet return again to me*, saith the LORD.
____

Deuteronomy 24:4 bars the road home: the first husband may not take her again.
God announces His intention to do the one thing His own law forbids — and He does not waive the law to do it; the whole testimony of this book is that He never does.
Listen to Paul find the door:

[quote.scripture, Romans 7:2-4]
____
For the woman which hath an husband is bound by the law to her husband *so long as he liveth*; but *if the husband be dead*, she is loosed from the law of her husband…
Wherefore, my brethren, ye also are become *dead to the law by the body of Christ*; that ye should be *married to another*, even to him that is *raised from the dead*…
____

Death dissolves the bond — and the death that dissolves this one is the _Husband’s_.
The wife earned the stoning; the Husband takes the stroke; and rising, He is free to wed her again in a renewed marriage bond.
The covenant is no contract renegotiated among peers: its Head establishes the law and terms, which remain; what changes is who stands within the covenant, and whether its law is broken outside the heart or kept from within it.

The Husband’s death is why the renewed covenant is announced in remarriage language: __“I will make a new covenant… not according to the covenant… which my covenant they brake, *although I was an husband unto them*”__ (Jeremiah 31:31-32).
That is why Hosea, God’s sign-and-similitude marriage, must not only endure his wife’s adultery but _buy her back_ — __“So I *bought her* to me for fifteen pieces of silver”__ (Hosea 3:2). The reunion is a fresh betrothal in the vocabulary this book keeps finding at the center: __“I will *betroth thee* unto me for ever; yea, I will betroth thee unto me in sym:sym-righteousness[righteousness], and in sym:sym-judgment[judgment]… and thou shalt sym:sym-knowing[know] the LORD”__ (Hosea 2:19-20).

It is why the forsaken wife is told her shame is over:

[quote.scripture, Isaiah 54:4-7]
____
Fear not; for thou shalt not be ashamed: neither be thou confounded; for thou shalt not be put to shame: for thou shalt forget the shame of thy youth, and shalt not remember the reproach of thy sym:sym-widow[widowhood] any more.
For thy *Maker* is thine *husband*; the LORD of hosts is his sym:sym-name[name]; and thy Redeemer the Holy One of Israel; The God of the whole earth shall he be called.
For the LORD hath called thee as a woman forsaken and grieved in spirit, and a wife of youth, when thou wast refused, saith thy God.
For a small sym:sym-moment[moment] have I forsaken thee; but with great mercies will I *gather* thee.
____

Her reproach is named _widowhood_: the bond was dissolved the one way the law allows — by the Husband’s death — and the Maker who bore that death is the Husband who gathers her back.

It is why, when they dragged a woman taken __“in the very act”__ of adultery before Jesus and quoted the death penalty at Him (John 8:4-5), the only Man present with the right to cast the first stone stooped, wrote in the dust, and let her accusers file out — __“Neither do I condemn thee: go, and sym:sym-sin[sin] *no more*”__ (John 8:11).
The trap was also lawless on its face: the statute they quoted requires *both* — __“they shall *both* of them die, both the *man* that lay with the woman, and the woman”__ (Deuteronomy 22:22; Leviticus 20:10) — and a woman taken in the very act was taken with a man they knew and did not bring.
To stone her alone would have broken the very law they invoked; He could not lawfully condemn her on their case.

He was not waiving the penalty.
He was on His way to pay it.

[discrete]
=== The Burning and the Wedding

The Bible closes its marriage file the way the law requires — with an execution and a wedding, in that order.
The false wife, __“the great sym:sym-harlot[whore]”__ who corrupted the earth with her sym:sym-fornication[fornication], is judged at last: __“true and righteous are his judgments: for he hath sym:sym-judgment[judged] the great sym:sym-harlot[whore]”__ (Revelation 19:2), and she is __“utterly *burned with fire*”__ (Revelation 18:8) — the law’s own sentence for the priest’s daughter who plays the whore (Leviticus 21:9).
And in the very next breath:

[quote.scripture, Revelation 19:7-8, ASV]
____
Let us rejoice and be exceeding glad, and let us give the glory unto him: for the *marriage of the* sym:sym-lamb[Lamb] is come, and his *wife hath made herself ready*.
And it was given unto her that she should array herself in *fine linen, bright and pure*: for the fine linen is the sym:sym-righteousness[righteous acts] of the saints.
____

The counterfeit wife burned; the true bride wed, dressed in _righteous acts_footnote:fn12righteousacts[The Greek is plural and active. The KJV reads __“the righteousness of saints,”__ while the ASV and NKJV preserve __“righteous acts.”__] — the commandments kept, worn: the sym:sym-garment[garment] whose full reading has its own chapter ahead.

Paul had named the mystery long before:

[quote.scripture, Ephesians 5:31-32]
____
For this cause shall a man leave his father and mother, and shall be joined unto his wife, and they two shall be *one flesh*.
This is a *great mystery*: but I speak concerning *Christ and the church*.
____

Every marriage since Eden has been a similitude of this one — which is why the law guards marriage so fiercely, and why the prophets grieve its breaking in the language of heaven’s own wounds.
__“For I am jealous over you with godly jealousy: for I have espoused you to one husband, that I may present you as a chaste sym:sym-virgin[virgin] to Christ”__ (2 Corinthians 11:2).

The symbols return their verdict on the common reading.
Divorce for adultery is not the law’s remedy and was never Jesus’ concession — adultery’s wage is death, and the Husband paid it.
The putting-away Scripture allows is the one it commands: the union that is itself sym:sym-fornication[fornication], the marriage to the daughter of a strange god, the covenant God never joined.
And the marriage Scripture will not let go of is the covenant one — defended in the law, mourned by the prophets, kept by God Himself through His wife’s adultery, His own bill of divorce, His death, and the wedding feast He has already announced.

The gospel, read through this symbol, is a Husband who would not quit: __“Turn, O backsliding children, saith the LORD; *for I am married unto you*”__ (Jeremiah 3:14).
The marriage is the covenant between one God and one people — and the wing the bride came under, the covenant’s own hem, is the next symbol.

description: "One Hebrew word — kanaph — is scattered across English as wing, skirt, border, corner, quarter, end, uttermost part, even 'overspreading': 108 occurrences under eighteen renderings, and the thread is lost in the spread. It is the edge where God commanded the fringes bound, 'that ye may remember all the commandments... and do them' — so wherever kanaph hides, look for the commandments. The ark of the covenant sits under the wings of the cherubim; the covenant is cut by spreading the wing; the kingdom tears when the skirt tears; the dispersed wait at the four corners of the earth; and there is healing in his wings."
og_title: "Wings — MEAT The Bible's Symbolic Language"
epigraphs:
  - quote: "Unto you that fear my name shall the Sun of righteousness arise with healing in his wings."
    ref: "Malachi 4:2"
---
A woman who had bled for twelve years pressed through a crowd to touch the edge of Jesus’ robe, and __“immediately her flow of blood stopped”__ (Luke 8:44, NKJV).
The Gospels are precise about what she touched — not the cloak, but its __“border”__ (Luke 8:44), its __“hem”__ (Matthew 9:20).
She was reaching for a particular part of the garment, and to see why, you must follow one Hebrew word that English has scattered into more than a dozen.

The word is _kanaph_, and the scatter is worth counting.
It falls one hundred and eight times in the Hebrew Scriptures, and the King James renders it _wing_, _skirt_, _border_, _corner_, _quarter_, _end_, _uttermost part_ — once even __“overspreading”__ (Daniel 9:27).
It is the eagle’s _wing_ on which God __“bare you… unto myself”__ (Exodus 19:4), the _skirt_ Boaz spread over Ruth, the _border_ of a garment, the four _corners_ of the earth.
One word: the outermost edge of a thing, where it meets the world.

Because the English keeps changing, the reader who works only in English can miss the thread.
Learn this word, and you gain a signal: wherever a verse says _skirt_, _border_, _corner_, or _the ends of the earth_, lift the English and look underneath.
If _kanaph_ is there, the commandments may be near — for reasons the next section makes plain.

[discrete]
=== The Fringe on the Wing

God commanded something bound to that edge:

[quote.scripture, Numbers 15:38-39]
____
…bid them that they make them *fringes in the borders of their* sym:sym-garment[garments]… that ye may look upon it, and *remember all the commandments of the LORD, and do them*; and that ye seek not after your own heart and your own eyes…
____

Those fringes — the _tzitzit_ — hang at the _kanaph_: the reminder of the law is tied to every corner of the covenant garment.
Their purpose is stated flatly — to _remember the commandments and do them_, and not to follow __“your own eyes”__ (there is the man who is right in his own eyes — we will meet him properly in the sym:sym-fool[Fool and the Wise] chapter ahead).

Notice how well the command itself hides in English: here the kanaph is __“borders,”__ and when the command is repeated — __“thou shalt make thee fringes upon the four *quarters* of thy vesture”__ (Deuteronomy 22:12) — it is __“quarters.”__
Neither verse says _wing_; so the English reader never connects the commandment-fringe to the wings of refuge in the Psalms, though they are one word and one thing.
That is the signal to carry through Scripture: the kanaph is where the *reminder* of the commandments is bound — the fringe is a memory-device, not the law itself — so the kanaph in a verse is a flag that the verse may be speaking of remembering — or forgetting — the commands.

Be precise about what __“remember”__ asks, for in Scripture remembering is not recalling; it is *doing*.
The Torah defines forgetting as disobedience outright — __“Beware that thou *forget* not the LORD thy God, *in not keeping* his commandments”__ (Deuteronomy 8:11): to forget *is* to not keep — and the psalm gives the other side in a single phrase: __“those that remember his commandments *to do them*”__ (Psalm 103:18).
Even God's remembering moves His hand: __“God *remembered* Noah… and God *made a* sym:sym-wind[wind] *to pass over* the earth”__ (Genesis 8:1); __“God heard their groaning, and God *remembered his covenant*”__ (Exodus 2:24) — and the Exodus follows.
So the fringe on the wing is not an aid to reflection; it is a trigger for obedience — __“not a forgetful hearer, but a *doer* of the work”__ (James 1:25).

Strip the vowel points, and the word gives up one more secret.
The points — and Strong’s numbering after them — split the consonants into two entries: a noun for the wing, and a verb that acts only once in all of Scripture.
Unpointed they are one word, and the lone verse where it moves as a verb shows what a kanaph _does_:

[quote.scripture, Isaiah 30:20-21]
____
And though the Lord give you the sym:sym-bread[bread] of adversity, and the water of affliction, yet shall not thy *teachers* be *removed into a corner* any more, but thine eyes shall *see thy teachers*:
And thine ears shall hear a word behind thee, saying, This is the sym:sym-way[way], walk ye in it…
____

To be _kanaph_-ed is to be tucked into the corner — and what Israel had tucked away there was its teachers of the law.
Read it beside the fringe-command and the two verses answer each other: the tzitzit were tied at the corner __“that ye may *look upon it*, and remember,”__ and restoration is promised in the same grammar — eyes that __“*see* thy teachers”__ again, and ears that hear __“this is the way.”__
The corner is where the teaching waits: hidden in judgment, seen in mercy — which is exactly where God tied it.

The counterfeit obliges by aiming at exactly this spot: the Pharisees __“make broad their phylacteries, and *enlarge the borders of their* sym:sym-garment[garments]”__ (Matthew 23:5) — bigger fringes, __“to be seen of men,”__ and the weightier matters of the law undone.
A tassel grown large to advertise an obedience that is not there.

[discrete]
=== Healing in His Wings

Now the woman’s reach makes sense.
She did not grab at random cloth; she took hold of the _tzitzit_ — the corner where the law hangs.
The word the Gospels use for what she touched, the __“hem”__ or __“border”__ of His garment, is _kraspedon_ — the very word the Greek Old Testament uses for the _tzitzit_ of Numbers 15.
She laid hold of His fringes, and the prophet had foretold exactly where healing would be:

[quote.scripture, Malachi 4:2]
____
But unto you that sym:sym-fear[fear] my sym:sym-name[name] shall the sym:sym-sun[Sun] of sym:sym-righteousness[righteousness] arise with *healing in his wings*…
____

Healing _in his wings_ — in the _kanaph_, the corner where the tzitzit hang.
The healing is not loose in the air; it is at the fringe, where the commandments are.
She reached for the law made flesh and laid hold of its corner — __“If I may but touch his sym:sym-garment[garment], I shall be whole”__ (Matthew 9:21) — and she was; and she was not alone: __“as many as touched were made *perfectly whole*”__ (Matthew 14:36).

[discrete]
=== The Covenant Under the Wings

If the wing carries the tassels that remind the wearer of the commandments, the sanctuary should show that reminder — and it does, in furniture.
When Solomon brought the ark home, Scripture places it with this phrase:

[quote.scripture, 1 Kings 8:6]
____
And the priests brought in the *ark of the covenant* of the LORD unto his place, into the oracle of the house, to the most holy place, even *under the wings of the cherubims*.
____

The covenant dwells _under the wings_ — Scripture’s own words.
And the pattern was set at Sinai: the cherubim stretch their wings __“covering the mercy seat”__ (Exodus 25:20), the testimony — the tablets of the law — goes _inside_ the ark beneath (Exodus 25:21), and God tells Moses where He will speak from:

[quote.scripture, Exodus 25:22]
____
And there I will meet with thee, and I will commune with thee from above the mercy seat, *from between the two cherubims* which are upon the ark of the testimony, of all things which I will give thee *in commandment* unto the children of Israel.
____

The commanding voice speaks from between the wings, above the law: the whole architecture of the most holy place is Numbers 15 built in gold — commandments kept under the kanaph.

Even the burning ones wear the covering: the seraphim, six-winged, use four of their wings not to fly but to cover themselves before the fire (Isaiah 6:2).
And the psalm that promises refuge names what the covering is made of: __“under his wings shalt thou trust: his sym:sym-truth[truth] shall be thy shield and buckler”__ (Psalm 91:4) — and the truth, this book has shown, is the law.
To hide __“under the sym:sym-shadow[shadow] of thy wings”__ (Psalm 17:8) is not to hide from the law; it is to hide _inside_ it.

This is why the eagle’s wings of the Exodus land where they land:

[quote.scripture, Exodus 19:4-5]
____
Ye have seen what I did unto the Egyptians, and how I *bare you on eagles’ wings*, and brought you *unto myself*.
Now therefore, *if ye will obey my voice* indeed, and *keep my covenant*, then ye shall be a *peculiar treasure* unto me above all people…
____

The wings carry Israel to Sinai, to the commandments — __“so the LORD alone did lead him”__ (Deuteronomy 32:12).
At the end of the story the flight is replayed: the woman is given __“two *wings* of a great eagle, that she might fly into the wilderness”__ (Revelation 12:14) — the Exodus again, wings again, out of the serpent’s reach and into the place where God keeps His own.

[discrete]
=== Spread Your Wing Over Me

The edge that carries the law is the edge that makes covenant.
To spread your _kanaph_ over someone is to take them into covenant — we saw it last chapter, where the whole wedding was built on it: God __“spread [his] skirt”__ over Israel and __“entered into a covenant”__ (Ezekiel 16:8).
Ruth asks it of Boaz in the same word:

[quote.scripture, Ruth 3:9]
____
…spread therefore thy *skirt* over thine handmaid; for thou art a near kinsman.
____

To dwell under the wing, then, is to dwell under the covenant — and to uncover the wrong one is to violate it: the law forbids a man his father’s wife with the words __“nor *discover his father’s skirt*”__ (Deuteronomy 22:30), the kanaph as the covenant boundary itself, in the very chapter that commands the fringes.

Here is the grief of it: again and again He longed to gather His people under His wing, as a mother bird her young, and again and again they would not.
Jesus laments it over Jerusalem in that very image:

[quote.scripture, Matthew 23:37]
____
O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, thou that killest the prophets, and stonest them which are sent unto thee, how often would I have *gathered thy children together*, even as a hen gathereth her chickens *under her wings*, and *ye would not!*
____

That lament closes the same chapter that opened with the enlarged fringes of the Pharisees (Matthew 23:5) — Matthew 23 begins with the kanaph counterfeited and ends with the kanaph refused.
The wing offered is the covenant offered; to refuse it is rebellion, and it leaves the house bare — __“Behold, your house is left unto you desolate”__ (Matthew 23:38).

Refuge does not disappear when God’s wing is refused; it is replaced.
Assyria comes on wings of its own — __“the stretching out of his *wings* shall fill the breadth of thy land, O Immanuel”__ (Isaiah 8:8) — and Ezekiel’s empires are __“great eagles with great wings”__ carrying off the top of the sym:sym-cedar[cedar] (Ezekiel 17:3, 7).
Everyone ends up under some wing; the question is whose.

[discrete]
=== The Torn Skirt

Because the kanaph carries covenant, what happens to the skirt happens to the kingdom — and Scripture stages it twice in one book.
When Samuel turned to leave, Saul __“laid hold upon the *skirt* of his mantle, and it *rent*”__ — and Samuel reads the torn kanaph on the spot:

[quote.scripture, 1 Samuel 15:27-28]
____
And Samuel said unto him, The LORD hath *rent the kingdom* of Israel from thee this day, and hath given it to a neighbour of thine, that is *better than thou*.
____

The torn skirt _is_ the torn kingdom — the deposed-covenant verdict of the sym:sym-marriage[marriage] chapter, enacted in cloth.

David, hiding in the cave, __“cut off the *skirt* of Saul’s robe privily.
And it came to pass afterward, that *David’s heart smote him*, because he had cut off Saul’s skirt”__ (1 Samuel 24:4-5).
His men saw a missed kill; David felt what he had actually done — put a knife into the covenant edge of the LORD’s anointed.
Yet the same cut skirt becomes his evidence: __“see the *skirt of thy robe in my hand*: for in that I cut off the skirt… and killed thee not… *I have not sinned* against thee”__ (1 Samuel 24:11) — the kanaph held up in court, the covenant kept where it could have been cut.

For the skirt is where a people’s covenant record is kept.
__“In thy *skirts* is found the *blood of the souls of the poor innocents*”__ (Jeremiah 2:34); __“her filthiness is in her *skirts*; she remembereth not her last end”__ (Lamentations 1:9) — what is carried in the kanaph is what the covenant sees.
Haggai’s priests rule that holiness does _not_ rub off through the skirt, but uncleanness does (Haggai 2:12-13) — the fringe transmits no merit; it testifies.
And when almost everything is judged, the kanaph is where the sym:sym-remnant[remnant] rides out the fire: __“Thou shalt also take thereof a *few in number*, and *bind them in thy skirts*”__ (Ezekiel 5:3).

[discrete]
=== The Corners of the Earth

Scale the garment up, as this book keeps doing, and the earth itself wears one — with corners.
The dispersed of Israel wait at them: God will __“gather together the dispersed of Judah from the *four corners of the earth*”__ (Isaiah 11:12) — the four _kanaph_.
Songs rise __“from the *uttermost part* of the earth”__ (Isaiah 24:16) — the kanaph again.
Judgment arrives at them: __“An end, the end is come upon the *four corners* of the land”__ (Ezekiel 7:2).
And in Job, God handles the whole earth exactly like the garment it is:

[quote.scripture, Job 38:13]
____
That it might take hold of the *ends of the earth*, that the *wicked* might be *shaken out of it*?
____

The dawn grips the earth by its kanaph and shakes the wicked out of it, as a man shakes out a garment.
The world has edges the way the covenant garment has edges — and the scattered people of God are kept at them, like the few hairs bound in the prophet’s skirt, until the gathering.

[discrete]
=== The Corner of the Field

The same shape appears at the edge of a sym:sym-field[field] — though the word now changes, for a field’s corner is _pe’ah_, not _kanaph_.
That is the symbol working as it always does: by structure, not by spelling.
The reserved edge may be a wing, a border, or a corner; what repeats is the shape — the boundary kept back, not reaped for oneself.
And that edge God reserved:

[quote.scripture, Leviticus 19:9-10]
____
…thou shalt not wholly reap the *corners of thy* sym:sym-field[field]… thou shalt leave them for the sym:sym-poor[poor] and sym:sym-stranger[stranger]…
____

The forgotten sheaf and the field’s corner are not the owner’s; they belong __“for the sym:sym-stranger[stranger], for the sym:sym-fatherless[fatherless], and for the sym:sym-widow[widow]”__ (Deuteronomy 24:19).
A field is people — humanity is sown and reaped like grain — and the corner is only a thin border of the whole.
Yet that thin edge is enough to live on: it is where Ruth gleaned (Ruth 2:3), and where she was redeemed.
The remnant is fed at the edge.

The wing gathers this book to a single edge, and hands the reader a working tool.
The law is sewn into the kanaph, and there is healing in it; the ark of the covenant sits beneath it; the covenant is made by spreading it and is read in what it carries; the kingdom tears when it tears; the dispersed wait at the earth’s four corners, and the poor glean at the field’s.
From here on, when your English Bible says _skirt_, _border_, _corner_, _quarter_, or _the ends of the earth_, check the word underneath: if the wing is there, the commandments are near — remembered, refused, or waiting to be done.
And the stranger, the fatherless, the widow who glean the corner are the next symbols to define — and after them, the remnant they add up to.

sources.name: 14-orphans-widows-and-the-fatherless.adoc
sources.content:
---
title: "Orphans, Widows, and the Fatherless"
slug: orphans-widows-and-the-fatherless
order: 14
permalink: /books/meat-bibles-symbolic-language/orphans-widows-and-the-fatherless/
description: "Everyone honors caring for widows and orphans — even the godless do it — and assumes himself among the helpers. But Scripture turns the symbol: the covenant people, cut off from their Husband, are themselves the widow and the fatherless (Lamentations 5:3). God defends them, feeds them, and gathers them home — and the food He gives is His word, the clothing His righteousness. The stranger is no mere foreigner but the one outside the covenant, drawn in at the field's open edge. And the poor — the fourth name at that same corner — are the bowed-humble to whom the kingdom is promised, set against the self-made rich who have need of nothing."
og_title: "Orphans, Widows, and the Fatherless — MEAT The Bible's Symbolic Language"
epigraphs:
  - quote: "We are orphans and fatherless, our mothers are as widows."
    ref: "Lamentations 5:3"
---
Few commands are easier to applaud than the care of widows and orphans. __“Pure religion and undefiled,”__ says James, is __“to visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction”__ (James 1:27); even the godless agree, funding the work through the state.
It is a good thing, and we are commanded to it.
But it is so plainly good that we read past it — and we read past it assuming one thing: that we stand among the givers, never the widow, never the orphan.
The symbolic language overturns the assumption.

[discrete]
=== We Are the Widow

A widow is a woman whose husband is dead or has put her away; the fatherless are children left without their father.
Now hear how God speaks of His own people when they break covenant.
He hands them a bill of divorce:

[quote.scripture, Isaiah 50:1]
____
…Where is the bill of your mother’s sym:sym-divorce[divorcement], whom I have *put away*?… for your iniquities have ye sold yourselves…
____

The city, cut off from her Husband, sits alone: __“how is she become as a widow!”__
(Lamentations 1:1).
Her children take up the cry: __“We are orphans and fatherless, our mothers are as widows”__ (Lamentations 5:3).
Here the symbol turns.
The widow and the fatherless are not only the poor down the street; they are the covenant people themselves, severed from the God who was their Husband and their Father.
We are the widow; we are the orphans.

In the Bible’s symbolic language this confession has an exact opposite, and she is a queen.
__“I sit a *queen*, and am *no widow*, and shall see no sorrow”__ (Revelation 18:7) — the boast in her heart, quoted word for word from Isaiah’s oracle against the *daughter of Babylon* (Isaiah 47:1):

[quote.scripture, Isaiah 47:8-9]
____
Therefore hear now this, thou that art given to pleasures, that dwellest carelessly, that sayest in thine heart, I am, and none else beside me; I shall *not sit as a widow*, neither shall I know the *loss of children*:
But these two things shall come to thee *in a* sym:sym-moment[moment] *in one day*, the loss of children, and *widowhood*…
____

She assumes herself married to the King — Vashti’s posture, the deposed queen of the sym:sym-marriage[marriage] chapter — and the sentence answers the boast in kind, repeated in Revelation: __“therefore shall her plagues come *in one day*, death, and mourning, and famine”__ (Revelation 18:8) — the sym:sym-moment[moment] itself has a study of its own in Part Five.

Two women, one word: the covenant people who *confess* their widowhood are the ones the Redeemer remarries — and the queen who *denies* hers is made a widow in a moment.
The whole difference is the confession.

[discrete]
=== Thy Maker Is Thine Husband

Which is why God’s fierce defense of the widow and the fatherless is no generic charity — it is a Husband and a Father moving toward His own:

[quote.scripture, Isaiah 54:5]
____
For thy *Maker* is thine *husband*; the LORD of hosts is his name; and thy *Redeemer* the Holy One of Israel…
____

He __“doth execute the sym:sym-judgment[judgment] of the fatherless and widow, and loveth the stranger, in giving him food and raiment”__ (Deuteronomy 10:18).
And the corner of the field left unreaped from the last chapter was reserved for exactly these: __“for the stranger, for the fatherless, and for the widow”__ (Deuteronomy 24:19).
The widowed sym:sym-remnant[remnant] gleans the sym:sym-wings[edge], as Ruth did, and is brought home by the Redeemer.

[discrete]
=== The Stranger

The third name in that gleaning law is a defined symbol, and Scripture fixes its meaning by setting it against its exact opposite:

[quote.scripture, Ephesians 2:19]
____
Now therefore ye are *no more strangers and foreigners*, but *fellowcitizens* with the saints, and of the household of God.
____

The opposite of a stranger is a _fellowcitizen_; so a stranger is a non-citizen — one who belongs to another commonwealth than the one he stands in.
And Paul names the commonwealth in the verse just before: the Gentiles had been __“aliens from the commonwealth of Israel, and strangers from the covenants of promise, having no hope, and without God”__ (Ephesians 2:12).
The covenant is the commonwealth, and to be a stranger is to hold no citizenship in it.

The key turns both ways.
Outside the covenant, a man is a stranger to God’s commonwealth — and the law leaves the field’s corner to draw him in.
The gleaning stranger is the _ger_, the sojourner who has left his own people to dwell among God’s; Israel had been one in Egypt — __“ye were strangers in the land of Egypt”__ (Leviticus 19:34) — so they must love him, and bring him toward citizenship: let him keep the Passover, and __“he shall be as one that is born in the land”__ (Exodus 12:48).
This is the whole of Ruth, a Moabite stranger who gleans the corner and is grafted into the line of the Redeemer, until the far-off are __“no more strangers… but fellowcitizens.”__

Once a man is made a citizen of God’s commonwealth, the symbol inverts: he becomes a stranger to the _world_.
The patriarchs __“confessed that they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth,”__ and Hebrews gives the reason — __“they seek a country… an heavenly”__ (Hebrews 11:13-16); __“our conversation”__ — the word is _citizenship_ — __“is in heaven”__ (Philippians 3:20); even in the land God says, __“ye are strangers and sojourners with me”__ (Leviticus 25:23).
The stranger to the world keeps the one law that is now his: __“I am a stranger in the earth: hide not thy commandments from me”__ (Psalm 119:19).
The covenant that ends a man’s estrangement from God begins his estrangement from the world.

[discrete]
=== The Poor and the Rich

There is a fourth name at that unreaped corner.
The gleaning law itself sets it beside the stranger — __“thou shalt leave them for the *poor* and stranger”__ (Leviticus 19:10) — and Zechariah gathers the whole defended household in one breath:

[quote.scripture, Zechariah 7:10]
____
And oppress not the sym:sym-widow[widow], nor the sym:sym-fatherless[fatherless], the sym:sym-stranger[stranger], nor the sym:sym-poor[poor]; and let none of you imagine evil against his brother in your heart.
____

Widow, fatherless, stranger, poor: one company, gleaning one corner.
The final member of the defended household seems at first to differ from the rest — the first three names are losses of kin and country, the fourth sounds like money.
Yet Scripture unfolds the *poor* by the same pattern: we read the word as the man with less money than we have, count ourselves among the givers — and then open the promises and find the poor holding all of them:

[quote.scripture, Luke 6:20]
____
Blessed be ye *poor*: for yours is the *kingdom of God*.
____

Why should the poor inherit a kingdom?
They should not, and they do not — because the wallet was never the measure.
The Hebrew words rendered __“poor”__ in these promises form a close family whose members are also rendered __“meek”__ and __“humble”__ — Strong’s calls its two chief members __“practically the same”__ — and the family grows from a root that means _bowed down_.
The poor of the promises are the bowed.

Watch the two renderings trade places across the same texts.
The psalm says __“the *meek* shall inherit the earth”__ (Psalm 37:11), and Jesus repeats it word for word: __“Blessed are the *meek*: for they shall inherit the earth”__ (Matthew 5:5).
Isaiah says the Anointed comes __“to preach good tidings unto the *meek*”__ (Isaiah 61:1) — and when Jesus stands up in Nazareth and reads that very verse, it comes out __“to preach the sym:sym-gospel[gospel] to the *poor*”__ (Luke 4:18): the same people under either rendering.
Matthew’s beatitude names the state outright: __“Blessed are the *poor in spirit*: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven”__ (Matthew 5:3) — bowed before God, nothing in the hand held up to Him.

Hear God say whom He means:

[quote.scripture, Isaiah 66:2]
____
…but to this man will I look, even to him that is *poor* and of a *contrite spirit*, and *trembleth at my word*.
____

The poor man God looks to is defined by his posture toward the word, not his balance.
He is the sym:sym-remnant[remnant]: __“I will also leave in the midst of thee an afflicted and *poor* people, and they shall trust in the sym:sym-name[name] of the LORD”__ (Zephaniah 3:12).
Hannah sang his future — __“He raiseth up the *poor* out of the dust… to make them inherit the throne of glory”__ (1 Samuel 2:8) — and James states it flat: __“Hath not God chosen the *poor* of this world *rich in* sym:sym-faith[faith], and heirs of the kingdom?”__
(James 2:5).
When John the Baptist sent from prison to ask whether Jesus was the One, the closing credential of the answer was this: __“the *poor* have the sym:sym-gospel[gospel] preached to them”__ (Matthew 11:5).

Now the other column.
If the poor are the bowed, the sym:sym-rich[rich] of the symbol are the unbowed — the self-sufficient who have need of nothing.
Solomon wrote the proverb: __“There is that maketh himself *rich*, yet hath nothing: there is that maketh himself *poor*, yet hath great riches”__ (Proverbs 13:7) — and two churches in Revelation act out its two halves.
To suffering Smyrna: __“I know thy… *poverty*, (but thou art *rich*)”__ (Revelation 2:9).
To comfortable Laodicea:

[quote.scripture, Revelation 3:17]
____
Because thou sayest, I am *rich*, and increased with goods, and *have need of nothing*; and knowest not that thou art wretched, and miserable, and *poor*, and blind, and sym:sym-naked[naked]…
____

The counsel that follows prices heaven’s currency: __“buy of me gold tried in the fire, that thou mayest be rich; and white raiment, that thou mayest be clothed”__ (Revelation 3:18) — faith tried in the fire, and the sym:sym-garment[garment] of righteousness.

Jesus names the true wealth in a phrase — the fool who filled his barns was __“not *rich toward God*”__ (Luke 12:21) — and pronounces the woe: __“woe unto you that are *rich*! for ye have received your consolation”__ (Luke 6:24).
And the exchange at the center of the sym:sym-gospel[gospel] is stated in exactly these terms: __“though he was *rich*, yet for your sakes he became *poor*, that ye through his *poverty* might be *rich*”__ (2 Corinthians 8:9).

Here a long-standing paradox dissolves.
If the poor of the promises are the bowed, then the rich of the woes are the proud — the unbowed — and the hardest saying about them was never about a balance sheet: __“How hardly shall they that have riches enter into the kingdom of God!”__
(Mark 10:23).
The disciples were astonished, and Jesus answered again with the symbol opened: __“Children, how hard is it for them that *trust in riches* to enter into the kingdom of God!”__
(Mark 10:24) — the trust, not the treasure.

Read the camel and the needle as a statement about money, and Scripture contradicts itself on its face: Abraham was __“very rich in cattle, in silver, and in gold”__ (Genesis 13:2), Job’s latter end was blessed with double, Joseph administered an empire’s wealth and David a kingdom’s — and all of them heirs.
Read it as the symbol reads — the unbowed cannot pass the low door — and the paradox was never there: __“with men this is impossible; but with God all things are possible”__ (Matthew 19:26), and what God does with the proud is bow them.

As always, the symbol does not dissolve the literal command; it deepens it.
__“The poor shall never cease out of the land: therefore I command thee… thou shalt open thine hand wide unto thy brother, to thy poor”__ (Deuteronomy 15:11).
The corner stays unreaped and the hand stays open — but the giver now knows what he is handling, and where he himself stands.
Before God, every man is the beggar lifted from the dunghill (Psalm 113:7); the only question is whether he knows it, as Smyrna did, or says __“I have need of nothing.”__

[discrete]
=== Food and Raiment

He gives the widow food and raiment (Deuteronomy 10:18) — and by now neither word is bare.
Scripture makes bread the word of God — __“man doth not live by sym:sym-bread[bread] only, but by every word that proceedeth out of the mouth of the LORD”__ (Deuteronomy 8:3) — and the sym:sym-garment[garment], as the sym:sym-marriage[marriage] chapter showed, is the righteous deeds of the saints — deeds He ordains and grants her to do (Ephesians 2:10; Revelation 19:8).
So to feed and clothe His widowed people is to give them the word, and the works the word produces.
The worst famine is not of bread:

[quote.scripture, Amos 8:11]
____
…I will send a famine in the land, not a famine of bread… but of *hearing the words of the LORD*.
____

This is why the charge to the shepherd is __“Feed my sym:sym-sheep[sheep]”__ (John 21:17); why the faithful servant is the one who gives the household __“sym:sym-meat[meat] in due season”__ (Matthew 24:45); why the commission is to teach the nations __“to observe all things whatsoever I have commanded”__ (Matthew 28:20).
To feed is to teach the commandments; to clothe is to grant the righteous deeds the word teaches.

The covenant itself is taken the same way — by eating His flesh and drinking His blood: __“the sym:sym-bread[bread] that I will give is my flesh”__ (John 6:51), and his words are spirit and life (John 6:63).
His body is the bread, the word to be eaten and kept; His blood is what washes the garment clean.
The crowd could not bear it — link:/books/symbolic-language/introduction/[the scene this book opened with] — and many walked no more with him (John 6:66), because they took the symbol for the flesh.footnote:fn11capernaum[The hard saying at Capernaum is walked in full in the link:/books/symbolic-language/introduction/[Introduction].]

The command to care for the widow and the fatherless therefore reaches all the way down.
They are God’s own people, cut off and gleaning at the edge; to feed them is to bring them the word, to clothe them is to robe them in righteousness, and to gather them is the work of the Husband who will not leave them widowed.
The next time Scripture says _feed the hungry_, hear what is handed across: the bread of His word, to a people hungrier than they know.
