---
title: "The Moment"
slug: the-moment
order: 38
permalink: /books/meat-bibles-symbolic-language/the-moment/
description: "Babylon boasts, 'I sit a queen, and am no widow' — and Scripture answers with a single word: in a MOMENT the loss of children and widowhood shall come upon her, in one day. The Hebrew for that moment is built on the same root as the wink of an eye, and the same image crosses into the Greek: 'in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye.' It is the word of Babylon's fall, of Korah's swallowing, of the last trumpet, and of God's own anger toward His people — never long, and never slow. Judgment does not creep; it blinks."
edition: digital
og_title: "The Moment — MEAT The Bible's Symbolic Language"
epigraphs:
  - quote: "But these two things shall come to thee in a moment in one day, the loss of children, and widowhood."
    ref: "Isaiah 47:9"
---
Babylon fell in the middle of a boast.
__“I sit a queen, and am no sym:sym-widow[widow], and shall see no sorrow”__ (Revelation 18:7) — and the verse that supplies her exact words, seven centuries earlier, supplies the timing of her answer too:

[quote.scripture, Isaiah 47:9]
____
But these two things shall come to thee *in a moment* in one day, the loss of children, and sym:sym-widow[widowhood]: they shall come upon thee in their perfection…
____

__“In a moment.”__
Not a slow decline, not a siege that could be watched approaching for years — a moment, and both children and husband are gone.
This book has followed one Hebrew word into a dozen chapters now; this one is smaller and sharper than any of them, and once you have it, an entire vocabulary of sudden things in Scripture turns out to be one thing.

[discrete]
=== The Wink of an Eye

The Hebrew behind __“moment”__ is _rega_, and its root meaning is exact: to wink, to blink — the very motion of an eyelid.
It is the shortest interval Scripture has a word for, and it never describes a process.

God tells Moses what would happen if He walked with a stiff-necked people even one stage of the journey: __“I will come up into the midst of thee in a moment, and consume thee”__ (Exodus 33:5).
When Korah’s company rose up against Moses, God did not say _I will judge them in time_; He said, __“Separate yourselves from among this sym:sym-assembly[congregation], that I may consume them in a moment”__ (Numbers 16:21) — and when the plague broke out among the people themselves, the same word is used again: __“that I may consume them *as in a moment*”__ (Numbers 16:45).
Job draws the general rule from such scenes: __“In a moment shall they die, and the people shall be troubled at midnight, and pass away: and the mighty shall be taken away *without hand*”__ (Job 34:20) — no visible weapon, no army, no hand at all; the moment does the work alone.

Scripture makes sure you cannot mistake this for a merely human turn of phrase.
The Greek New Testament reaches for the identical image, unprompted, to describe the resurrection:

[quote.scripture, 1 Corinthians 15:52]
____
In a *moment*, in the *twinkling of an eye*, at the last trump: for the trumpet shall sound, and the dead shall be raised incorruptible…
____

__“Moment”__ here is _atomos_ — literally an _uncut_ thing, an atom of time, indivisible — paired with __“the twinkling of an eye,”__ the eye’s own glance.
Two languages, centuries apart, reach for the same picture: the blink of an eye is Scripture’s unit for _instantaneous_, whether the news is a resurrection or a ruin.
The moment is not vague; it is the shortest thing a human body can do.

[discrete]
=== Suddenly

Beside _rega_ stands its constant companion, _pithom_ — __“suddenly”__ — and Strong’s traces it back to the same family of roots: a wink, an unguarded instant, __“used only adverbially, quickly or unexpectedly.”__
The two words travel together so often that they read as one idea wearing two names.
Watch them arrive in the same verse over the ruin of a land: __“suddenly are my tents spoiled, and my curtains *in a moment*”__ (Jeremiah 4:20).
And watch the word do its full work on Babylon herself:

[quote.scripture, Jeremiah 51:8]
____
*Babylon is suddenly fallen* and destroyed: howl for her; take balm for her pain, if so be she may be healed.
____

No warning shot, no visible siege in the sentence — she is simply, suddenly, fallen.
Revelation counts the same fall by the clock rather than the eye, and repeats the number until it cannot be missed: __“for in *one hour* is thy judgment come”__ (Revelation 18:10); __“for in *one hour* so great riches is come to nought”__ (18:17); __“for in *one hour* is she made desolate”__ (18:19).
Three times in one chapter, the mourners themselves keep saying the word — because the thing that stuns them most is not that Babylon fell, but how fast.

The same suddenness that ends the wicked announces the LORD Himself: __“the Lord, whom ye seek, shall *suddenly* come to his temple”__ (Malachi 3:1) — the true King’s arrival keeps the same timing as the false queen’s fall.
Neither is a process you can watch coming.
Both are a wink.

[discrete]
=== No Remedy in the Wink

Scripture is careful to note what the moment does not allow: appeal, delay, or repair.

[quote.scripture, Proverbs 29:1]
____
He, that being often reproved hardeneth his neck, shall *suddenly* be destroyed, and that *without remedy*.
____

The warnings can run for years; the destruction, when it lands, allows none.
Paul names the same collapse waiting behind the world’s most confident sentence:

[quote.scripture, 1 Thessalonians 5:3]
____
For when they shall say, sym:sym-peace[Peace] *and safety*; then *sudden destruction* cometh upon them, as *travail upon a woman with child*; and they shall not escape.
____

The image is deliberately double-edged, and worth holding next to Babylon’s own boast of childlessness (Isaiah 47:8-9): travail is sudden, unstoppable once it starts, and ends in a birth the mother cannot delay — but here it ends the one who is unprepared, __“as a thief in the night”__ (1 Thessalonians 5:2; 2 Peter 3:10).
Jesus warns His own not to be caught the same way — __“lest… that day come upon you *unawares*”__ (Luke 21:34), the Greek _aiphnidios_, the exact cousin of the __“suddenly”__ that fells Babylon.
The moment does not ask whether you are ready.

[discrete]
=== The Moment That Blesses

The shortness of the word is not only a threat, and Scripture will not let the reader forget it.
The same _rega_ that consumes Korah’s company also measures God’s own anger toward His covenant people — and measures it as mercy:

[quote.scripture, Isaiah 54:7-8]
____
For a *small moment* have I forsaken thee; but with great mercies will I *gather thee*.
In a little wrath I hid my face from thee *for a moment*; but with *everlasting kindness* will I have mercy on thee…
____

The wrath is a moment; the kindness is everlasting — the same asymmetry David sings: __“his anger endureth but a *moment*; in his favour is life: weeping may endure for a night, but joy cometh in the morning”__ (Psalm 30:5).
And Paul, under the weight of real suffering, reaches for the identical word to shrink it: __“our light affliction, which is but *for a moment*, worketh for us a far more exceeding and eternal weight of glory”__ (2 Corinthians 4:17).
The moment cuts both ways because it is not itself good or evil; it is simply the unit in which God acts — decisively, without process, whether the act is a judgment or a rescue.

Even the devil's temptation borrows the word, and gives away more than he intends by doing so.
He takes Jesus __“up into an *exceeding high mountain*”__ (Matthew 4:8) and shows Him __“all the kingdoms of the world *in a moment of time*”__ (Luke 4:5) — and by now every term of the offer is plain.
The sym:sym-mountain[mountain] is an empire, and Scripture knows one mountain that link:/books/symbolic-language/mountain/[holds all the kingdoms at once]: the destroying mountain that destroys all the earth (Jeremiah 51:25) — sym:sym-babel[Babylon], the composite kingdom.footnote:fn31mountain[The mountain-as-kingdom derivation — Jeremiah 51:25 beside Daniel 2 and Revelation 17 — is made in the link:/books/symbolic-language/mountain/[Mountain] chapter.]
And the offer arrives priced in Babylon's own doom-unit: he shows the kingdoms in a *moment* — the very measure by which they fall.
What the devil could display in a _rega_, God can end in one; the Lord declined the mountain that falls in a moment.

What changes hands in that moment is not what the devil was holding.
The trumpet that raises the dead __“*in a moment*, in the twinkling of an eye, at the *last trump*”__ (1 Corinthians 15:52) is the seventh, at which __“The kingdoms of this world are become the kingdoms of our Lord, and of his Christ”__ (Revelation 11:15) — and the next breath tells how: __“the *nations were angry*, and *thy wrath is come*”__ (Revelation 11:18).

The world's kingdoms are not transferred; they fall — Daniel's sym:sym-stone[stone] grinds them to sym:sym-chaff[chaff] and the sym:sym-wind[wind] carries them off, no place found for them (Daniel 2:35) — and what is given to the Son is another kingdom entirely, the kingdom the God of heaven sets up to break and consume all these (Daniel 2:44): __“there was *given him* dominion, and glory, and a kingdom”__ (Daniel 7:14).
The devil offered the mountains as they stood — __“that is *delivered unto me*,”__ he claimed (Luke 4:6); the Father's grant arrives only over their dust.
At the moment Babylon falls, the nations of the world fall with her — and the kingdom is given to the Son of man.

Take the phrase as a marker wherever you meet it: *in a moment*, *suddenly* — when Scripture hangs those words on a kingdom, it is speaking the judgment of Babylon, or a similitude of it.

[discrete]
=== The Sign That Was Not Sudden

Set against all this, one long-fused word makes its point by contrast.
The vision that seems slow is not therefore false: __“the vision is yet for an *appointed time*, but at the end it shall speak, and not lie: though it tarry, *wait for it*; because it will *surely come*, it will not tarry”__ (Habakkuk 2:3).
God’s patience and God’s suddenness are not opposites; they are the same character seen at two distances.
He can hold back for centuries and then close the account in a single wink, because the tarrying was never uncertainty — it was the appointed time, running its full course before the moment falls.

[discrete]
=== The Queen’s Clock Is Not Her Own

Return, then, to the queen who claimed she would never be a widow.
The moment is not a separate judgment laid on top of Babylon’s fall; it is that judgment’s own timer.
Isaiah addresses her as the *daughter* of Babylon (Isaiah 47:1) — not the empire itself, but the covenant wife who wears its name.
The wife of the covenant is warned, pleaded with, given generation after generation to return — the long, patient _tarrying_ of Habakkuk’s vision — but when the sentence at last falls, it falls the only way Scripture ever lets it fall on the unrepentant: __“in a moment, in one day”__ (Isaiah 47:9), __“in one hour”__ (Revelation 18:10, 17, 19), __“suddenly”__ (Jeremiah 51:8).
The years of warning and the instant of ruin are not in tension; they are the same pattern this book keeps meeting — in the sym:sym-remnant[remnant] of Part Two, in the sym:sym-shadow[shadow] beside it — every symbol that turns out to turn on one small, decisive word.

God is not slow, and He is not sudden by accident.
He simply does not need more than a wink — and neither, Scripture keeps insisting, will the trumpet that raises the dead.
And if the account can close in a wink, the vocabulary had best be in hand before it does.
The case studies are next — the rest of the symbols, one by one, beginning where Daniel's image began: with the sym:sym-mountain[mountain].

sources.name: 39-mountain.adoc
sources.content:
---
title: "Mountain"
slug: mountain
order: 39
permalink: /books/meat-bibles-symbolic-language/mountain/
description: "Scripture defines the mountain as a kingdom — Revelation, Daniel, Isaiah, and Jeremiah agree — and that one key unlocks dozens of passages, from the burning mountain cast into the sea to the command to flee to the mountains."
og_title: "Mountain — MEAT The Bible's Symbolic Language"
epigraphs:
  - quote: "…the stone that smote the image became a great mountain, and filled the whole earth."
    ref: "Daniel 2:35"
---
The first case study is __“mountain,”__ which represents kingdoms or power structures.
The pyramid-like structure of a mountain mirrors the power structure of delegated authority and is an apt analogy — but subjective aptness is not a basis for defining a symbol.
Thankfully, in this case Scripture comes right out and defines it:

[quote.scripture, Revelation 17:9-10]
____
This calls for a mind with wisdom.
The seven heads are *seven mountains* on which the woman sits.
They are also *seven kings* (kingdoms).
____

Revelation tells us that mountains mean kingdoms, and by analogy hills are cities.
The question is whether Scripture consistently uses mountain with the same symbolic meaning, or whether this is a one-off.
Other times in Scripture we are given a vision and an interpretation, which establishes the definition by analogy:

[quote.scripture, Daniel 2:35 (NKJV)]
____
Then the iron, the clay, the bronze, the silver, and the gold were crushed together, and became like sym:sym-chaff[chaff] from the summer threshing floors; the sym:sym-wind[wind] carried them away so that no trace of them was found.
And the sym:sym-stone[stone] that struck the sym:sym-image[image] became a *great mountain* and *filled the whole earth*.
____

[quote.scripture, Daniel 2:44-45 (NKJV)]
____
And in the days of these kings the God of heaven will set up a *kingdom* which shall never be destroyed; and the kingdom shall not be left to other people; it shall break in pieces and *consume all these kingdoms*, and it shall stand forever.
Inasmuch as you saw that the sym:sym-stone[stone] was cut out of the *mountain* without hands, and that it broke in pieces the iron, the bronze, the clay, the silver, and the gold — the great God has made known to the king what will come to pass after this.
The dream is certain, and its interpretation is sure.
____

In this case Daniel explains a vision of a statue with layers of gold, silver, bronze, and feet of clay and iron, and explains that this statue represents successive kingdoms.
When God’s kingdom comes as a stone, it destroys the statue and consumes all the kingdoms the statue represents.
The stone then grows into a mountain that fills the entire earth, and God’s kingdom rules forever and ever.

[quote.scripture, Daniel 2:38-39 (NKJV)]
____
You are this head of gold.
After you shall arise another *kingdom* inferior to yours; then another, a third *kingdom* of bronze, which shall *rule over all the earth*.
____

Daniel's own explanation lets a ruler stand for the kingdom he heads: __“You are this head of gold,”__ followed immediately by __“another kingdom.”__
The sym:sym-stone[Stone] follows the same scale.
It enters the vision as one appointed Head and becomes the sym:sym-mountain[Mountain] as a people and kingdom gather under Him.

Rock and Stone are related, but they do not hold the same office.
The sym:sym-rock[Rock] is the bedrock beneath the house and kingdom — its sym:sym-covenant[covenant] Head, source, and foundation: __“that Rock was Christ”__ (1 Corinthians 10:4).
Isaiah gives the relationship at the human scale:

[quote.scripture, Isaiah 51:1-2]
____
Look unto the *rock whence ye are hewn*…
Look unto *Abraham your father*, and unto Sarah that bare you…
____

The rock is the father and source; the stones hewn from it are his people.
Peter carries the same order into the house of Christ: Jesus is the __“living sym:sym-stone[stone]”__ rejected by men, and those who come to Him __“also, as lively sym:sym-stone[stones], are built up a spiritual house”__ (1 Peter 2:4-5).
Jesus is the Rock beneath the house and the chief Stone within it; His people are the other living stones built under His authority.

The chief corner stone is the *Head* in authority while remaining at the foundation in position.
Isaiah lays the tried corner stone __“for a foundation”__ (Isaiah 28:16), and Paul says the house is __“built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Jesus Christ himself being the chief corner stone”__ (Ephesians 2:20).
Placed at the foundation corner, the Head Stone establishes the line to which every other stone must be fitted.
Zechariah's physically upper stone uses a different expression: Psalm 118:22 calls Christ _rosh pinnah_, __“the head of the corner,”__ while Zechariah 4:7 calls the completing top stone _ha-even ha-roshah_, __“the headstone.”__
The cornerstone governs the building from beneath; the capstone crowns it from above.

Daniel's sym:sym-stone[Stone] cut without hands is therefore Christ as the Head appointed by God, not a kingdom assembled by men.
As the living stones are built under Him, the single Stone becomes the great Mountain — the kingdom that fills the earth.

The fact that the mountain is described as growing and covering the entire earth is another clue that this isn’t a physical mountain.
The analogy from Daniel is carried on in Isaiah.

[quote.scripture, Isaiah 2:2-3]
____
It shall come to pass in the latter days that the *mountain* of the house of the Lord shall be established as the highest of the *mountains*, and shall be lifted up above the *hills*; and all the *nations* shall flow to it, and many peoples shall come.
____

See the same symbolic meaning applied in Jeremiah, describing Babylon the Great, which rules over the whole earth and destroys nation after nation.
Here Jeremiah tells us this destroying mountain will become a burnt mountain.

[quote.scripture, Jeremiah 51:25]
____
Behold, I am against you, O *destroying mountain*, Who destroys all the earth,” says the Lord.
“And I will stretch out My hand against you, Roll you down from the rocks, And make you a *burnt mountain*.
____

Now we have Daniel, Revelation, Isaiah, and Jeremiah all agreeing on the meaning of this symbol of a Mountain as a Kingdom.
With this knowledge we can now gain greater insight into many other Scriptures.
Consider the account in Revelation of a flaming mountain thrown into the sea:

[quote.scripture, Revelation 8:8-9]
____
Then the second angel sounded his trumpet, and something like a *huge mountain*, all ablaze, was *thrown into the* sym:sym-sea[sea].
A third of the *sea* turned into blood, a third of the *living creatures* in the sea died….
____

The common readings rank this way:

.How the “mountain” is usually read (Revelation 8:8)
[.prevalence-table%unbreakable, frame=topbot, grid=none, cols="^2,8", options="header"]
|===
| Rank | Common interpretation

| 1 | Literal asteroid or meteor impact
| 2 | Literal volcano hurled into the sea
| 3 | Nuclear blast or modern warfare
| 4 | A nation or world empire
|===

How do we know that this isn’t a literal mountain in this context?
The answer is in the phrase __“thrown into the sea,”__ the __“sea turning into blood,”__ and the __“creatures in the sea,”__ all in the same sentence.
In a later chapter I will show the evidence that sym:sym-sea[sea] is a symbol that means the masses of people, the population of the earth, and that sym:sym-living[living creatures], sym:sym-beast[beast], and sym:sym-beast[animals] represent gentile nations.

Symbolically, Revelation 8:8-9 is saying that when a __“huge mountain”__ — a world empire — is thrown down, a third of the people will die and a third of the nations will be destroyed.

One final supporting piece of evidence is that a __“stone, rock, mountain, etc.”__ being __“thrown into the sea”__ to __“never rise again”__ is the prophetic symbol tied to the fall of Babylon the Great.
And thus symbols can be composed of both words and catchphrases.

[quote.scripture, Matthew 17:20]
____
So Jesus said to them, “Because of your unbelief; for assuredly, I say to you, if you have sym:sym-faith[faith] *as a mustard* sym:sym-seed[seed], you will say to this *mountain*, ‘Move from here to there,’ and it will move; and nothing will be impossible for you.”
____

[quote.scripture, Matthew 21:21]
____
So Jesus answered and said to them, “Assuredly, I say to you, if you have sym:sym-faith[faith] and do not doubt, you will not only do what was done to the sym:sym-fig[*fig tree*], but also if you say to this *mountain*, ‘Be removed and be *cast into the* sym:sym-sea[sea],’ it will be done.”
____

[quote.scripture, Mark 11:23]
____
For assuredly, I say to you, whoever says to this *mountain*, ‘Be removed and be *cast into the sea*,’ and does not doubt in his heart, but believes that those things he says will be done, he will have whatever he says.
____

The common readings rank this way:

.How the “mountain” Jesus moves is usually read
[.prevalence-table%unbreakable, frame=topbot, grid=none, cols="^2,8", options="header"]
|===
| Rank | Common interpretation

| 1 | A personal obstacle or problem
| 2 | A literal mountain, used as hyperbole
| 3 | The Mount of Olives or Temple Mount
| 4 | A spiritual stronghold or doubt
| 5 | The corrupt temple or religious system
| 6 | A national power or kingdom
|===

How do we know that this mountain is not a literal mountain, or merely an impossible obstacle, in this context?
Because the context is a fig tree and a mustard tree — and sym:sym-tree[trees] are rooted covenant lives that can stand for peoples or nations — and of course __“thrown into the sea”__ is a symbol clearly referring to Babylon the Great, as the link:/books/symbolic-language/the-fall-of-babylon/[Fall of Babylon] chapter demonstrated — and as the next chapter will trace from the Song of the Sea onward.

What we learn from this is that the symbolic language of the Bible is interconnected: symbols are defined in terms of symbols and phrases, as well as the verbs, adjectives, and other personifications used with the symbol.
For this reason, we often see the same set of symbols connected over and over.

[quote.scripture, Psalm 46:2-3]
____
Though the *mountains* be carried into the midst of the sym:sym-sea[sea]; though the waters thereof roar and be troubled, though the *mountains* shake with the swelling thereof.
____

The common readings rank this way:

.How the “mountains” are usually read (Psalm 46)
[.prevalence-table%unbreakable, frame=topbot, grid=none, cols="^2,8", options="header"]
|===
| Rank | Common interpretation

| 1 | Literal earthquakes or natural disaster
| 2 | Life’s troubles and instability
| 3 | Cosmic or end-times upheaval
| 4 | Nations or kingdoms shaken
|===

Now consider this poetic picture from Joel:

[quote.scripture, Joel 2:2]
____
A day of darkness and gloom, A day of clouds and of thick [dark] mist, Like the *dawn* spread over the *mountains*;
____

The picture is of __“dawn,”__ __“mist,”__ or __“fog”__ spread over the __“mountains,”__ which is quite common in early morning and aligns with the visual of a __“day of clouds and thick dark mist.”__
The Hebrew word for __“dawn,”__ _shachar_, link:/books/symbolic-language/lucifers-declared-plan/[names the dark before sunrise].footnote:fn33shachar[Derived — _shachar_ written on the letters of blackness — in the link:/books/symbolic-language/lucifers-declared-plan/[Lucifer's Declared Plan] chapter.] It names the first light while the sky is still quite dark, before the sun burns away the fog.
Now, with the greater context, we have dark clouds of smoke spread over the nations.
This is just one of dozens of verses that gain new meaning when you apply the symbolic meaning of mountain.

[quote.scripture, Matthew 24:15-16]
____
So when you see the abomination of desolation spoken of by the prophet Daniel, standing in the holy place (let the reader understand), then let those who are in Judea *flee to the mountains*.
____

Here is a verse that contains instructions for the future, and to understand the instructions it is helpful to know that __“mountains”__ means nations.
In other words: get out of Judea.
In AD 70, those who survived the fall of Jerusalem were scattered to the nations, so this prophecy has been fulfilled in this sense already.

[quote.scripture, Luke 21:20-21]
____
When you see Jerusalem being surrounded by armies, you will know that its desolation is near.
Then let those who are in Judea *flee to the mountains*, let those in the *city* get out, and let those in the country not enter the city.
____

Another verse sounds poetic on the surface, but carries a far more practical message when read by Scripture’s own symbols:

[quote.scripture, Jeremiah 50:6]
____
My people have been sym:sym-lost[lost sheep]; their *shepherds* have led them astray, in the *mountains* they have turned them away. *From mountain to hill* they have gone; they have forgotten their resting place.
____

Here His people are the sheep; the shepherds are the pastors and teachers who led people astray among the nations they were scattered to.
His people have gone from nation to city and have forgotten their home.

[quote.scripture, Isaiah 40:4]
____
Every sym:sym-valley[valley] shall be exalted, and every *mountain and hill* shall be made low.
____

This verse from Isaiah now has far deeper meaning: the nations and cities will be humbled (brought low).
And those who are humble, obedient even to death, will be exalted and lifted up.
The mountains are high places, proud places, and they contrast with their opposite, the valleys — those enslaved by the mountains.

[quote.scripture, Jeremiah 16:16]
____
Behold, I will send for many *fishers*, said the LORD, and they shall fish them; and after will I send for many *hunters*, and they shall hunt them from *every mountain*, and from *every hill*, and out of the *holes of the rocks*.
____

Here is another case where mountains (nations) are used with other symbols: fishermen and hunters.
Here Jeremiah is prophesying about Jesus calling people to be fishers of men.
Then, those who are not caught as fish will be hunted down from among the nations, in every city, and out of every bunker.
The holes of the rocks are then referenced in Revelation:

[quote.scripture, Revelation 6:14-16]
____
And the heaven departed as a scroll when it is rolled together; and *every mountain and* sym:sym-island[island] were moved out of their places.
And the kings of the earth, and the great men, and the rich men, and the chief captains, and the mighty men, and every slave, and every free man, hid themselves in the dens and in the *rocks of the mountains*; and said to the *mountains and rocks*, Fall on us, and hide us.
____

Now that you know that mountain means a kingdom, we should ask ourselves: what does an sym:sym-island[island] represent?

[quote.scripture, Revelation 16:19-20]
____
And great *Babylon* came in remembrance before God, to give to her the cup of the wine of the fierceness of his wrath.
And *every* sym:sym-island[island] *fled away*, and the *mountains were not found*.
____

Are literal mountains going to disappear, or is this clearly talking about the third of the nations thrown into the sea, never to rise again?
When I read this, it struck me as odd that an island could flee, or escape.
It is the personification of the island that led me to research the sym:sym-island[island] symbol, which we will cover in a future chapter.

I will close this chapter on mountains with one final notable use, when Jesus was tested in the desert:

[quote.scripture, Matthew 4:8]
____
Again, the devil takes him up into an *exceeding high mountain*, and shows him *all the kingdoms of the world*, and the glory of them;
____

Here we see an exceedingly high mountain from which all the other kingdoms of the earth can be seen.
In other words, he is taken to a kingdom ruling over all the other kings of the earth — likely Babylon the Great.

By now you should see the pattern: Scripture reliably and consistently uses the word mountain as a way to say __“nation”__ or __“kingdom”__ in many different contexts across the whole of Scripture.
I have only addressed a few of the notable uses, but once you internalize this symbol you will find it used in countless other places in profound ways.

In the process of exploring the mountain symbol, we came across many other symbols: the sym:sym-sea[sea] (the masses of mankind), the hills (cities), the sym:sym-tree[tree] and the fig tree (kingdoms and Israel), the sym:sym-stone[stones] (people built into a house), the sym:sym-rock[Rock] (Christ, the foundation beneath it), the sym:sym-beast[beasts] and living creatures (the gentile nations), the sym:sym-island[island], the fishers and the hunters, the valley, and Babylon the Great.
The sea, the trees and their beasts, and the island are taken up in the chapters just ahead, each defined the same way we defined the mountain — by letting Scripture interpret Scripture.
Babylon the Great we have already traced through Part Five, and the glossary carries the rest.

The meaning is already there, recoverable by following the repeated relationships rather than leaning on inherited opinion.
What forces the answer is not the cleverness of the reader but the discipline of the process.

sources.name: 40-sea-and-waters.adoc
sources.content:
---
title: "Sea & Waters"
slug: sea-and-waters
order: 40
permalink: /books/meat-bibles-symbolic-language/sea-and-waters/
description: "If mountains are kingdoms, the sea is the peoples they rise from and rule over. Revelation 17 defines both — the waters are 'peoples, and multitudes, and nations, and tongues' — and that key unlocks the beasts from the sea, the flood that is an invading army, the two waters of creation — a restless sea of nations below, and the sea of glass above where the redeemed stand — and the 'no more sea' of the new creation."
og_title: "Sea & Waters — MEAT The Bible's Symbolic Language"
epigraphs:
  - quote: "The LORD on high is mightier than the noise of many waters, yea, than the mighty waves of the sea."
    ref: "Psalm 93:4"
---
The next symbol we will investigate is the sea.
The sea is a symbol that comes up over and over again in Scripture.
The symbol appears in the beasts coming out of the sea, mountains and trees being thrown into it, Jonah, Jesus walking on it, and disciples fishing in it.
Understanding how its symbolic meaning is consistent across so many different situations is critical for understanding the prophecies, miracles, and less notable references to the sea.

The sea is sometimes called sym:sym-sea[waters] or sym:sym-sea[waves] and is related to sym:sym-flood[floods].
This chapter gathers those uses and shows how they clarify verses often read as mere poetic ornament.

Like the _mountain_ symbol, Scripture directly tells us the meaning of “waters” and “sea” in several different verses across the Old and New Testaments.
Let’s start with Revelation.

[quote.scripture, Revelation 17:1]
____
…the judgment of the great sym:sym-harlot[whore] that sitteth upon sym:sym-sea[many waters]:
____

[quote.scripture, Revelation 17:15]
____
And he saith unto me, The sym:sym-sea[waters] which thou sawest, where the sym:sym-harlot[whore] sitteth, are *peoples, and multitudes, and nations, and tongues*.
____

Here we do not have to guess: the messenger is interpreting the vision for John, just as he interpreted the seven mountains a few verses earlier.
The waters are peoples, multitudes, nations, and tongues — humanity in the mass, described four ways so that nothing slips between the words.

Notice that this is the very same chapter that defined the mountain (Revelation 17:9-10).
One chapter of Revelation hands us both halves of the map: the woman sits on seven sym:sym-mountain[mountains] — kingdoms — and upon sym:sym-sea[many waters] — the peoples those kingdoms rise from and rule over.
In the mountain chapter I deferred the evidence that the sea means the masses of people; this chapter is that evidence.

The picture is natural enough that English keeps it to this day: we still speak of a sea of faces, a wave of immigration, a flood of refugees.
But as we learned with the mountain, an apt analogy is not the basis for defining a symbol — and neither is a familiar idiom.
The question is whether Scripture itself uses the sea this way consistently, or whether Revelation 17 is a one-off.

In answering it I can show you one of the most useful tools for discovering symbols on your own: Hebrew poetry rhymes ideas instead of sounds.
A verse says a thing once, then says it again in other words — so the second line is an inspired gloss on the first, Scripture defining its own terms in parallel columns.
Watch Isaiah do it:

[quote.scripture, Isaiah 17:12-13]
____
Woe to the multitude of *many people*, which make a noise like the noise of the sym:sym-sea[seas]; and to the rushing of *nations*, that make a rushing like the rushing of mighty sym:sym-sea[waters]!
The *nations* shall rush like the rushing of sym:sym-sea[many waters]…
____

People are set against seas; nations against waters.
The Psalms do the same:

[quote.scripture, Psalm 65:7]
____
Which stilleth the noise of the sym:sym-sea[seas], the noise of their sym:sym-sea[waves], and the *tumult of the people*.
____

Seas, waves, and the tumult of the people — three phrases, one meaning.
Once you know to look for these parallel columns, definitions turn up in verses you have sung right past.
Here is one sitting in plain sight in a praise psalm:

[quote.scripture, Psalm 98:7]
____
Let the sym:sym-sea[sea] roar, and the *fulness thereof*; the *world*, and *they that dwell therein*.
____

The sea is matched to the world, and the fulness of the sea to them that dwell in the world.
What fills the sea is people.

The witnesses are not a handful of hand-picked verses.
The word __“sea”__ appears in 376 verses of Scripture, and __“waters”__ and __“floods”__ in hundreds more.
Gather the sea verses and sort them, and the shape of the whole is striking: roughly three of every four either connect the sea to people outright, put the symbol to work — kingdoms rising out of it, armies as floods, men as fish, multitudes as sand — or take on a second depth once the symbol is known.
Only about eighty are plain geography: borders, coastlines, harbors, and shipping.
No figure of speech stays that consistent by accident — dozens of authors, some fifteen centuries apart, all speaking one vocabulary.

Jesus uses the symbol exactly the same way, and even supplies the gloss in the same sentence:

[quote.scripture, Luke 21:25]
____
And there shall be sym:sym-sign[signs] in the sym:sym-sun[sun], and in the sym:sym-moon[moon], and in the sym:sym-stars[stars]; and upon the earth *distress of nations*, with perplexity; the sym:sym-sea[sea] and the sym:sym-sea[waves] roaring;
____

The common readings rank this way:

.How the “sea and waves roaring” is usually read (Luke 21:25)
[.prevalence-table%unbreakable, frame=topbot, grid=none, cols="^2,8", options="header"]
|===
| Rank | Common interpretation

| 1 | Literal ocean upheaval — tsunamis, rising seas, disasters
| 2 | General end-times chaos and dread
| 3 | Stock apocalyptic imagery with no specific meaning
| 4 | The nations in turmoil
|===

The meaning is not hidden: __“distress of nations, with perplexity”__ and __“the sym:sym-sea[sea] and the sym:sym-sea[waves] roaring”__ are the same parallel columns Isaiah used — the symbol and its meaning side by side in a single sentence.
Haggai does the same thing across two verses:

[quote.scripture, Haggai 2:6-7]
____
…I will *shake* the heavens, and the earth, and the sym:sym-sea[sea], and the dry land;
And I will *shake all nations*…
____

Shaking the sea is shaking the nations.

What kind of thing, then, is this sea?
Isaiah tells us its nature:

[quote.scripture, Isaiah 57:20]
____
But the *wicked* are like the troubled sym:sym-sea[sea], when it cannot rest, whose sym:sym-sea[waters] cast up mire and dirt.
____

The wicked are the sea: restless, churning, casting up their own filth.
Jude says the ungodly are __“raging sym:sym-sea[waves of the sea], foaming out their own shame”__ (Jude 13).
And the symbol scales all the way down to a single person:

[quote.scripture, James 1:6]
____
But let him ask in faith, nothing wavering.
For he that wavereth is like a sym:sym-sea[wave of the sea] driven with the sym:sym-wind[wind] and tossed.
____

One doubting man is one wave — part of the mass, driven by whatever wind blows across it.
That sym:sym-wind[wind] returns later in the chapter.

The next texts show where kingdoms come from.

[quote.scripture, Daniel 7:2-3]
____
…the sym:sym-four[four winds] of the heaven strove upon the great sym:sym-sea[sea].
And four great sym:sym-beast[beasts] came up from the sym:sym-sea[sea], diverse one from another.
____

Daniel is given the interpretation directly: link:/books/symbolic-language/trees/[the beasts are kings] (Daniel 7:17) — kingdoms — and they come up out of the sea.footnote:fn34beastkings[The beast symbol is taken up in full in the link:/books/symbolic-language/trees/[Trees] chapter.]
Empires do not fall from the sky; they take shape out of the churning mass of peoples.

What churns the mass?
The four winds of heaven — the __“four spirits of the heavens, which go forth from standing before the Lord of all the earth”__ (Zechariah 6:5) — for throughout Scripture sym:sym-wind[wind] is spirit.
Unseen powers sent from God’s throne agitate the nations, and out of the agitation kingdoms rise.
The winds had their chapter at the head of Part Five; here it is enough to see the pattern working.
Revelation reuses the image exactly:

[quote.scripture, Revelation 13:1]
____
And I stood upon the sym:sym-sand[sand] of the sym:sym-sea[sea], and saw a sym:sym-beast[beast] rise up out of the sym:sym-sea[sea], having seven heads and ten horns…
____

Even the Psalms know this sea is full of beasts:

[quote.scripture, Psalm 104:25-26]
____
So is this great and wide sym:sym-sea[sea], wherein are sym:sym-beast[things creeping] innumerable, both *small and great* sym:sym-beast[beasts].
There go the ships: there is that sym:sym-dragon[leviathan], whom thou hast made to *play therein*.
____

Small beasts and great — petty powers and empires — swarming in the sea of peoples, with the sym:sym-dragon[dragon] himself at play among them.

Now the verse from the mountain chapter pays out in full.
A burning mountain is __“cast into the sym:sym-sea[sea],”__ and __“the third part of the sym:sym-sea[sea] became blood; And the third part of the sym:sym-living[creatures] which were in the sym:sym-sea[sea], and had life, died”__ (Revelation 8:8-9).
A kingdom is thrown down into the mass of peoples, and a third of the people die — which is exactly how the judgment reads when a vial is poured on the sea:

[quote.scripture, Revelation 16:3]
____
And the second angel poured out his vial upon the sym:sym-sea[sea]; and it became as the *blood of a dead man*: and *every living soul died* in the sym:sym-sea[sea].
____

Souls live in this sea.
No literal ocean has souls in it; the sea of peoples has nothing else.

There is a particular motion of this sea to watch for.
When the waters rise, overflow, and sweep across the land, the symbol is a nation on the move — an invading army.
Isaiah names the flood outright:

[quote.scripture, Isaiah 8:7]
____
…the Lord bringeth up upon them the sym:sym-flood[waters of the river], strong and many, *even the king of Assyria*, and all his glory…
____

The flood is the king of Assyria — the verse says so in the same breath — and the next verse follows the water up to Judah’s neck: __“he shall overflow and go over, he shall reach even to the neck”__ (Isaiah 8:8).
Egypt gets the same picture, and this time the flood speaks:

[quote.scripture, Jeremiah 46:7-8]
____
Who is this that cometh up as a sym:sym-flood[flood], whose sym:sym-sea[waters] are moved as the rivers?
*Egypt* riseth up like a sym:sym-flood[flood], and his waters are moved like the rivers; and he saith, I will go up, and will *cover the earth*; I will *destroy the city and the inhabitants* thereof.
____

A flood that talks, boasts, and plans a campaign is not weather.
Jeremiah asks the riddle — who is this flood? — and answers it in the next line: Egypt.
So too __“sym:sym-sea[waters] rise up out of the sym:sym-north[north], and shall be an overflowing sym:sym-flood[flood], and shall overflow the land”__ (Jeremiah 47:2) — the army out of Babylon.
The armies even sound like what they are: __“their voice roareth like the sym:sym-sea[sea]”__ (Jeremiah 6:23); and when Babylon’s own turn comes, the identical sentence is turned back on her, word for word — __“their voice shall roar like the sym:sym-sea[sea]… against thee, O daughter of sym:sym-babel[Babylon]”__ (Jeremiah 50:42).
And in Revelation the dragon attacks the woman with this very weapon:

[quote.scripture, Revelation 12:15-16]
____
And the sym:sym-serpent[serpent] cast out of his mouth sym:sym-flood[water as a flood] after the woman… And the earth helped the woman, and the earth opened her mouth, and swallowed up the sym:sym-flood[flood]…
____

A sym:sym-flood[flood] sent after the woman is a hostile people set in motion to sweep her away, and the earth swallowing it is her deliverance.
Once you see that a flood is a nation in motion, dozens of __“overflowing”__ and __“drowning”__ passages become legible.

The flood is not only the enemy’s weapon; it is also how the enemy ends.
Daniel seals his prophecy of the seventy sevens with this symbol.
The destroying verb of the verse is singular, and link:/books/symbolic-language/daniel-unsealed/[its subject is the Messiah]: he will destroy the people of the coming ruler, __“and the end thereof shall be with a sym:sym-flood[flood]”__ (Daniel 9:26).footnote:fn34dan926[The word-by-word case for this reading — the singular verb, its subject, and the seventy sevens entire — is made in the link:/books/symbolic-language/daniel-unsealed/[Daniel Unsealed] chapter.]

The corrected reading does not bend the symbol; it completes it.
A flood is a people in motion — and the Messiah has a people of his own: __“the Lord cometh with ten thousands of his saints”__ (Jude 14), and __“the armies which were in heaven followed him”__ (Revelation 19:14).
The city is not destroyed by the coming ruler’s people; his people are destroyed — swept away by the Lord’s own host, the flood turned around.
And that is exactly what happened to the first army that pursued God’s people into the sea.

We can now return to that most famous sea event and read it with new eyes.
Habakkuk read it this way long before us, and he asks the question for us:

[quote.scripture, Habakkuk 3:8]
____
Was the LORD displeased against the rivers? was thine anger against the rivers? was thy wrath against the sym:sym-sea[sea], that thou didst ride upon thine sym:sym-horse[horses] and thy chariots of salvation?
____

Was God’s wrath really against water?
Of course not.

Notice who rides against it: the LORD upon __“thine sym:sym-horse[horses] and thy chariots of salvation”__ — heaven’s own cavalry on the move.
Then look at the last word of the verse in Hebrew: __“salvation”__ is _yeshuah_ — the very sym:sym-name[name] the angel would give the Son (Matthew 1:21), and Jonah's last word out of the belly of Sheol (Jonah 2:9).
The LORD rides against the sea on the chariots of Yeshua — His army rides in His salvation — and when the armies of heaven follow Him __“upon white horses”__ (Revelation 19:14), they ride those same chariots.

At the Red Sea, the flood that had been drowning Israel’s sons — Egypt, the nation that __“riseth up like a sym:sym-flood[flood]”__ — was itself drowned in the sea:

[quote.scripture, Exodus 15:4-5]
____
Pharaoh’s chariots and his host hath he *cast into the* sym:sym-sea[sea]: his chosen captains also are drowned in the Red sea.
The depths have covered them: they sym:sym-cast-into-sea[sank into the bottom as a stone].
____

The phrase joins two actions: cast into the sea, sank as a stone.
Not every symbol is a single word; some are whole phrases, and this is one of Scripture’s most loaded.
The sym:sym-cast-into-sea[sinking stone] is the fall of sym:sym-babel[Babylon] — a ruling power sunk into the sea of peoples, never to rise (Jeremiah 51:63-64; Revelation 18:21) — and the Song of the Sea sang it first, centuries before either prophet wrote.

Now run Egypt’s plagues from first to last, because Revelation does.
The judgment opened with water turned to blood: Pharaoh had commanded, __“Every son that is born ye shall cast into the river”__ (Exodus 1:22), and the first plague turned that very river to blood, and __“the sym:sym-fish[fish] that was in the river died”__ (Exodus 7:21) — the waters that had swallowed the sons were made to show what they held.
And it closed with the drowners drowned: an army dead in the sea.

Revelation replays the sequence on the whole world: the burning mountain turns a third of the sea to blood (Revelation 8:8), the vials finish it — __“every living soul died in the sym:sym-sea[sea]”__ (Revelation 16:3), and the rivers become blood — and this time the interpretation is spoken aloud:

[quote.scripture, Revelation 16:6]
____
For they have *shed the blood* of saints and prophets, and thou hast given them *blood to drink*; for they are worthy.
____

Waters turned to blood are the bloodshed of the peoples given back to them to drink.

The last battle ends the way Egypt’s story ended: __“blood came out of the winepress, even unto the horse bridles”__ (Revelation 14:20) — a river of blood where an army stood — exactly what Ezekiel promised Pharaoh, the sym:sym-dragon[dragon] of the sym:sym-sea[sea]: __“I will water with thy blood the land… and the rivers shall be full of thee”__ (Ezekiel 32:6).
Egypt was the rehearsal; Revelation is the performance.

Revelation even names the cast: the victors over the sym:sym-beast[beast] stand on the sea of glass singing the song of Moses and the sym:sym-lamb[Lamb] — the Red Sea anthem, struck up at Babylon’s fall (Revelation 15:2-3) — and the call to come out of Babylon is the Exodus call, plagues and all (Revelation 18:4; Jeremiah 51:45).
The Exodus is link:/books/symbolic-language/the-fall-of-babylon/[the typology of the fall] of sym:sym-babel[Babylon]: the plagues, the call to come out, the sinking of the pursuer, the song.footnote:fn34exodusbabylon[The two stories are laid side by side, scene for scene, in the link:/books/symbolic-language/the-fall-of-babylon/[Fall of Babylon] chapter.]

Even the sea’s name carries the freight: our Bibles call it the Red Sea, after the Greek (Acts 7:36), but the Hebrew is _yam suph_ — and the consonants of _suph_, reeds, are the very consonants of _soph_, the end.
The Sea of Reeds is, on its letters, the Sea of the End — and there the oppressor’s army met it.

The plague did not retire with Moses; Revelation hands the same power to the two witnesses:

[quote.scripture, Revelation 11:5-6]
____
And if any man will hurt them, fire proceedeth out of their mouth, and devoureth their enemies…
These have power to shut heaven, that it rain not in the days of their prophecy: and have *power over* sym:sym-sea[waters] *to turn them to blood*, and to smite the earth with all plagues, as often as they will.
____

The common readings rank this way:

.How the witnesses’ power is usually read (Revelation 11:6)
[.prevalence-table%unbreakable, frame=topbot, grid=none, cols="^2,8", options="header"]
|===
| Rank | Common interpretation

| 1 | Literal plague-power — water to blood, as Moses did
| 2 | A cue that the witnesses are Moses and Elijah figures
| 3 | A general emblem of divine judgment
| 4 | Authority to bring death upon the peoples, with waters as peoples
|===

The allusion to Moses invites a literal plague reading, but run the symbols: the waters are the peoples, and to turn the waters to blood is to bring death upon the peoples — the witnesses carry the power to kill, and they carry it in their testimony.

Scripture has already defined the fire of their mouth the same way:

[quote.scripture, Jeremiah 5:14]
____
…I will make *my words* in thy mouth *fire*, and this people *wood*, and it shall devour them.
____

Look how much that one sentence defines: the fire is His words, and __“this people”__ is the wood — for wood is the stuff of a sym:sym-tree[tree], and at this collective scale a tree is a nation, as its own chapter will show.
Word-fire devours people-wood; word-plague turns people-waters to blood.
The fire is the word; the plague is the word; the first plague of Moses, wielded __“as often as they will,”__ by speaking.

Moses himself was told his wonders would speak — __“they will sym:sym-belief[believe] the sym:sym-voice[voice] of the latter sym:sym-sign[sign]”__ (Exodus 4:8): signs have voices.
And hear the voice of his first sign.

The staff cast to the ground became a serpent (Exodus 4:3) — and the Hebrew for staff, _matteh_, is a branch-word, the same word by which Israel’s tribes are named: a branch of the family sym:sym-tree[tree].
The tribe, cast down, becomes a sym:sym-serpent[serpent]; taken up by the hand, it is a staff again (Exodus 4:4).
Israel corrupted; Israel restored — a prophecy spoken in a wonder, and read aloud at its ripening: __“O generation of vipers”__ (Matthew 3:7; 12:34).

When the sign was replayed in Pharaoh’s court, it spoke at the scale of empires.
The magicians cast down _their_ staffs — the nations in the service of the sym:sym-harlot[whore], ruled, ridden, and consumed by her — and __“they became sym:sym-serpent[serpents]: but Aaron’s rod swallowed up their rods”__ (Exodus 7:12).
One tribe swallows the corrupted nations whole — the very promise Daniel heard of the kingdom of God, that it shall __“consume all these kingdoms, and it shall stand for ever”__ (Daniel 2:44, from the mountain chapter).
First to last, the signs of Egypt are sayings: the tribe turned serpent, the nations swallowed, the waters turned to blood.

This verse shows how the letter and the symbol can stand together.
Moses’ plague was literal — real blood in a real river, real fish dead on the water — and it was at the same time the symbol enacted: the river that had swallowed the sons shown for what it held.
The witnesses may yet turn literal water to literal blood; nothing in the symbol forbids it.
The symbolic reading does not cancel the literal one — the two are often true together, and the symbol is the deeper reason that particular literal event was chosen.

Writing on two levels at once is also the signature of the Author.
To write one verse that is true on both levels is craft; to sustain it across dozens of interlocking symbols — sea, flood, fish, mountain, wind — each keeping its meaning in every other verse where it appears, through sixty-six books and some fifteen centuries of writers, is an equation with more simultaneous variables than any human author could hold.
The consistency is not a reader’s trick; it is the fingerprint of a single mind above the text.

Paul then reads the crossing itself as a symbol:

[quote.scripture, 1 Corinthians 10:1-2]
____
…all our fathers were under the cloud, and all *passed through the* sym:sym-sea[sea]; And were all *baptized* unto Moses in the cloud and in the sea;
____

The people pass through the sea and come out God’s own; their old master goes under it.
That is what baptism pictures, and Micah completes the thought — what God did to Pharaoh’s host He will do to our sins:

[quote.scripture, Micah 7:19]
____
He will turn again, he will have compassion upon us; he will subdue our iniquities; and thou wilt *cast all their* sym:sym-sin[sins] *into the depths of the* sym:sym-sea[sea].
____

Micah has just invoked the Exodus — __“according to the days of thy coming out of the land of Egypt”__ (Micah 7:15) — so the picture is exact: our sins go down like Pharaoh’s army, cast into the sea, link:/books/symbolic-language/the-fall-of-babylon/[never to rise].footnote:fn34neverrise[Why the verdict is the not-rising — Babylon sinks and shall not rise; the righteous come up — is proved in the link:/books/symbolic-language/the-fall-of-babylon/[Fall of Babylon] chapter.]

Notice the flag that marks these verses as symbolic — the same flag that stopped me at the fleeing island in the mountain chapter: personification.

[quote.scripture, Psalm 114:3-5]
____
The sym:sym-sea[sea] *saw it, and fled*: Jordan was driven back.
The sym:sym-mountain[mountains] *skipped like rams*, and the little hills like lambs.
What ailed thee, O thou sym:sym-sea[sea], that thou *fleddest*? thou Jordan, that thou wast driven back?
____

When Scripture has the sea seeing, fleeing, speaking, or travailing, it is telling you the sea is not water.

Return now to Babylon.
She is a destroying sym:sym-mountain[mountain] (Jeremiah 51:25), and she is enthroned on the sea:

[quote.scripture, Jeremiah 51:13]
____
O thou that *dwellest upon* sym:sym-sea[many waters], abundant in treasures, thine end is come…
____

Yet the throne becomes the grave:

[quote.scripture, Jeremiah 51:42]
____
The sym:sym-sea[sea] is come up upon sym:sym-babel[Babylon]: she is covered with the *multitude of the* sym:sym-sea[waves] thereof.
____

The verse glosses itself — covered with the *multitude*.
The peoples she sat on rise and swallow her; and in the same oracle God promises, __“I will dry up her sym:sym-sea[sea], and make her springs dry”__ (Jeremiah 51:36) — her supporting mass of peoples drained away — which is why Isaiah’s burden against Babylon is addressed to __“the desert of the sym:sym-sea[sea]”__ (Isaiah 21:1): a sea already sentenced to become desert.

Tyre is drawn with the same pen.
God brings __“many nations”__ against her __“as the sym:sym-sea[sea] causeth his sym:sym-sea[waves] to come up”__ (Ezekiel 26:3) — the nations are the waves; her rulers are __“the princes of the sym:sym-sea[sea]”__ (Ezekiel 26:16); she is __“a merchant of the people for many sym:sym-island[isles]”__ (Ezekiel 27:3) — her cargo is people; and her prince boasts, __“I sit in the seat of God, in the midst of the sym:sym-sea[seas]”__ (Ezekiel 28:2) — a throne amid the peoples, claiming God’s chair.
Isaiah even lets Tyre’s sea speak as a barren mother: __“I travail not, nor bring forth children, neither do I nourish up young men, nor bring up virgins”__ (Isaiah 23:4) — for when this sea does bear, it bears people.

Her sentence reads:

[quote.scripture, Isaiah 23:11]
____
He stretched out his *hand over the* sym:sym-sea[sea], he *shook the kingdoms*: the LORD hath given a commandment against the merchant city, to destroy the strong holds thereof.
____

Hand over the sea; kingdoms shaken.
By now that equation should feel familiar.

If the sea is the peoples, then the people in it are sym:sym-fish[fish] — and Scripture says exactly that: God makes men as the fishes of the sea, creatures with no ruler over them (Habakkuk 1:14) — the scattered, ungoverned mass, exposed to every net link:/books/symbolic-language/the-parables-of-the-kingdom/[dragged through the waters].footnote:fn34fishnet[The fish and the net are derived in the link:/books/symbolic-language/the-parables-of-the-kingdom/[Parables of the Kingdom] chapter.]
Now listen to Jesus recruit His disciples, and watch the interpretation arrive in the very next verse:

[quote.scripture, Matthew 4:18-19]
____
And Jesus, walking by the sea of Galilee, saw two brethren… casting a net into the sym:sym-sea[sea]: for they were fishers.
And he saith unto them, Follow me, and I will make you *fishers of men*.
____

Reading the next verse is another habit worth forming: when a symbol appears, Scripture often sets the interpretation right beside it.
The kingdom itself is then described as a net cast into the sym:sym-sea[sea] and gathering of every kind (Matthew 13:47-48) — swept through the sea of humanity, sorted on the shore.

Recall from the mountain chapter that Jeremiah’s fishers and hunters work __“from every sym:sym-mountain[mountain], and from every hill”__ (Jeremiah 16:16); the fishers also work the sea, because the catch lives in both — people among the kingdoms, people among the nations.
In the end the sea even yields up its wealth to Zion: __“the abundance of the sym:sym-sea[sea] shall be converted unto thee, the forces of the Gentiles shall come unto thee”__ (Isaiah 60:5) — the verse glossing itself once more, the abundance of the sea being the Gentiles — and Moses had promised exactly that, when the tribes would __“call the people unto the sym:sym-mountain[mountain]”__ and __“suck of the abundance of the sym:sym-sea[seas]”__ (Deuteronomy 33:19).

Through all of this, one figure stands over the sea and is not moved by it.

[quote.scripture, Psalm 89:9-10]
____
Thou *rulest the raging of the* sym:sym-sea[sea]: when the sym:sym-sea[waves] thereof arise, thou stillest them.
Thou hast *broken Rahab in pieces*, as one that is slain; thou hast scattered thine *enemies* with thy strong arm.
____

The next-verse rule again: ruling the raging sea is glossed as breaking Rahab and scattering enemies — and Rahab is Scripture’s name for Egypt (Psalm 87:4), the dragon cut in pieces when the sea was dried before the ransomed (Isaiah 51:9-10).
Job adds that God alone __“treadeth upon the sym:sym-sea[waves of the sea]”__ (Job 9:8).
Those two facts set the terms for the boat scene:

[quote.scripture, Mark 4:39-41]
____
And he arose, and rebuked the sym:sym-wind[wind], and said unto the sym:sym-sea[sea], Peace, be still…
And they feared exceedingly, and said one to another, What manner of man is this, that even the sym:sym-wind[wind] and the sym:sym-sea[sea] obey him?
____

The common readings rank this way:

.How the stilling of the storm is usually taught (Mark 4:39)
[.prevalence-table%unbreakable, frame=topbot, grid=none, cols="^2,8", options="header"]
|===
| Rank | Common interpretation

| 1 | Jesus calms the storms of your life
| 2 | A display of deity — power over nature
| 3 | A historical miracle, nothing more
| 4 | A sign of authority over the raging nations
|===

Comfort in personal storms and the display of power over nature are not false readings, but they stop short.
The disciples’ question is the point of the account: what manner of man is this?
The Scriptures they knew had already answered it — the One who stills the noise of the seas and the tumult of the people (Psalm 65:7), the One who rules the raging of the sea and breaks Rahab (Psalm 89:9-10).

When Jesus rebukes the sea, He is signing His name.
The miracle on the water is a claim of dominion over the nations, and the claim is repeated when He comes to them __“walking on the sym:sym-sea[sea]”__ (Matthew 14:26), doing what Job said God alone does.
Asaph had already seen Him there:

[quote.scripture, Psalm 77:19-20]
____
Thy sym:sym-way[way] is in the sym:sym-sea[sea], and thy path in the great sym:sym-sea[waters], and thy *footsteps are not known*.
Thou *leddest thy people* like a flock by the hand of Moses and Aaron.
____

A way in the sea, footsteps unknown — and the next line: thou leddest thy people.
He walks the sea, and the people are led through it.

Mark adds a detail no one would think to invent: walking on the sea, he __“would have passed by them”__ (Mark 6:48) — and the same chapter of Job joins those two acts:

[quote.scripture, Job 9:8, 11]
____
Which alone spreadeth out the heavens, and *treadeth upon the* sym:sym-sea[waves of the sea]…
Lo, he *goeth by me*, and I see him not: he *passeth on* also, but I perceive him not.
____

Treading the waves, passing by, unperceived — the disciples were watching Job 9 climb into their boat.

Isaiah supplies the reason His path runs where ours cannot: __“as the heavens are higher than the earth, so are my ways higher than your ways”__ (Isaiah 55:9).
Our way lies through the sea, at its mercy; His way is upon it — the LORD __“which maketh a sym:sym-way[way] in the sym:sym-sea[sea], and a path in the mighty sym:sym-sea[waters]”__ (Isaiah 43:16).
And sym:sym-way[the way] is itself a symbol — the walk, a man’s covenant conduct — with a chapter of its own back in Part Two; here His walk runs over the very waters ours drowns in.

Even the staging of Jesus’ ministry acts the symbol out.

[quote.scripture, Mark 4:1]
____
And he began again to teach by the sym:sym-sea[sea] side: and there was gathered unto him a great *multitude*, so that he entered into a ship, and *sat in the* sym:sym-sea[sea]; and the whole *multitude was by the* sym:sym-sea[sea] *on the land*.
____

The scene is precise: he sat in the sea, and the multitude stood on the land.
The teacher of the nations takes his seat upon the sea, and the multitude — drawn out of it to hear him — stands on solid ground.
The arrangement is a parable before he speaks a word.

In the country of the Gadarenes the symbol turns violent: the demons answer, __“My name is Legion: for we are many”__ (Mark 5:9) — Legion, a Roman army word; many, a multitude word — and the many rush down __“a steep place into the sym:sym-sea[sea]”__ and are __“choked in the sym:sym-sea[sea]”__ (Mark 5:13), drowned like Pharaoh’s host.
There is one more sea story of this kind — a prophet thrown into the raging sea so that it ceased, and swallowed by what waited beneath — but it carries a whole sign with it, and Part One read it scene by scene as the sign of Jonah; recall it here with the sea’s meaning in hand.

There is one more turn to the symbol, and it goes back to the first page of the Bible.

[quote.scripture, Genesis 1:9-10]
____
And God said, Let the sym:sym-sea[waters] under the heaven be *gathered together* unto one place, and let the *dry land* appear: and it was so.
And God called the dry land Earth; and the *gathering together of the* sym:sym-sea[waters] called he sym:sym-sea[Seas]: and God saw that it was good.
____

Notice what a sea is by definition: a gathering of waters.
And notice what God does with it: he separates dry land out of it.
From the first page the pattern is set — the undifferentiated mass gathered on one hand, and what God draws up out of the mass on the other.

Genesis also divides the waters vertically: waters under the firmament, and waters above it (Genesis 1:6-7).
Water drawn up from the sea below into the heavens above joins the two.
Jeremiah tells us — twice, word for word (Jeremiah 10:13; 51:16) — how the drawing up works:

[quote.scripture, Jeremiah 10:13]
____
…there is a *multitude of* sym:sym-sea[waters] *in the heavens*, and he causeth the *vapours to ascend from the ends of the earth*…
____

A multitude of waters above, filled by vapours drawn up from below — the pattern Elijah’s servant watched as the little cloud arose out of the sym:sym-sea[sea] like a man’s hand (1 Kings 18:44).

Now run the symbol through it.
The waters below are the peoples; the vapour God draws up out of the sea is people drawn up out of the mass; and the multitude gathered in the heavens is exactly what John sees before the throne — __“a sym:sym-sea[sea of glass] like unto crystal”__ (Revelation 4:6), with __“them that had gotten the victory over the sym:sym-beast[beast]”__ standing on it, __“having the harps of God”__ (Revelation 15:2).
Two seas of people: below, the restless nations, roaring; above, the gathered assembly, still as glass.
And when that upper assembly speaks, listen to what its voice sounds like:

[quote.scripture, Revelation 19:6]
____
And I heard as it were the *voice of a great multitude*, and as the *voice of* sym:sym-sea[many waters]… saying, Alleluia: for the Lord God omnipotent reigneth.
____

The voice of a great multitude is the voice of many waters — the definition of Revelation 17:15 running in reverse.
Solomon knew about the two seas.
He built one — a __“molten sym:sym-sea[sea]”__ (1 Kings 7:23), holding two thousand baths (1 Kings 7:26), lifted up on __“twelve oxen”__ facing the four quarters of the earth (1 Kings 7:25) — twelve, the number of the tribes — and it stood in the court of God’s house __“for the priests to wash in”__ (2 Chronicles 4:6).
A sea stilled, bounded, raised on twelve, set in the sanctuary for cleansing: the sea of glass rendered in brass.

Moses' court held the casting before him: the laver, made __“of the *lookingglasses* of the women assembling at the door of the tabernacle”__ (Exodus 38:8) — the basin the priests washed in was not merely bright; it was cast from *mirrors*.
And one word welds the copies to the original: the temple's sea is __“a *molten* sea”__ (1 Kings 7:23), and Job asks of the sky itself — the _shachaq_ where the sym:sym-faithful-witness[faithful witness] stands (Psalm 89:37) — __“Hast thou with him spread out the sky… as a *molten* looking glass?”__ (Job 37:18): one casting verb, _yatsaq_, pours them both.
John's __“before the throne”__ is _enōpion_ — *in the face of* (Revelation 4:6) — and a mirror returns only what it faces: the sea of glass is the mirror-sea, the stilled waters giving back the light of the One enthroned above them, as the mirror-made basin stood facing the door of His house.
And when the kingdom fell, the Chaldeans broke the sea in pieces and __“carried the brass of them to Babylon”__ (2 Kings 25:13) — even the emblem of the gathered people went into captivity with them.

Thus, the symbol runs to its end.
In the mountain chapter, Daniel’s stone became a mountain that __“filled the whole earth”__ (Daniel 2:35).
Here is the same consummation seen from the sea’s side:

[quote.scripture, Revelation 21:1]
____
And I saw a new heaven and a new earth… and there was *no more* sym:sym-sea[sea].
____

The common readings rank this way:

.How “no more sea” is usually read (Revelation 21:1)
[.prevalence-table%unbreakable, frame=topbot, grid=none, cols="^2,8", options="header"]
|===
| Rank | Common interpretation

| 1 | Literal — the new earth has no oceans
| 2 | The sea as chaos or evil, now abolished
| 3 | No more separation — John exiled on Patmos, cut off by sea
| 4 | The end of restless, rebellious humanity — the nations
|===

Will the new creation really lack oceans, or is this the end of the restless mass of ungoverned humanity?
The chapter itself has already told us who the sea is.
When the mountain has filled the whole earth, there is no sea left for it to rise over: no restless mass outside the kingdom, no waters for a beast to climb out of, no flood to send after the woman.
Habakkuk paints the same end as a flood of another kind:

[quote.scripture, Habakkuk 2:14]
____
For the earth shall be filled with the *knowledge of the glory of the LORD*, as the sym:sym-sea[waters] *cover the* sym:sym-sea[sea].
____

The last flood to sweep the earth is the knowledge of the glory of the LORD — and the sea it covers is us.

[discrete]
=== Sand

The sym:sym-sand[sand] is where the sea meets the land — grains beyond all counting, heaped at the boundary.
That is why __“the sand of the sea”__ is Scripture’s byword for a multitude past numbering: Abraham’s seed __“as the sym:sym-sand[sand] which is upon the sym:sym-sea[sea] shore”__ (Genesis 22:17); Israel __“as the sym:sym-sand[sand] of the sym:sym-sea[sea], which cannot be measured nor numbered”__ (Hosea 1:10); and the last enemy horde, Gog and Magog, __“the number of whom is as the sym:sym-sand[sand] of the sym:sym-sea[sea]”__ (Revelation 20:8).
It is also why John watches the beast rise while standing __“upon the sym:sym-sand[sand] of the sym:sym-sea[sea]”__ (Revelation 13:1) — on the shore of multitudes, at the edge of the mass the beast climbs out of.
And God uses the sand to preach to His people:

[quote.scripture, Jeremiah 5:22-23]
____
Fear ye not me? saith the LORD… which have placed the sym:sym-sand[sand] for the *bound of the* sym:sym-sea[sea] by a perpetual decree, that it cannot pass it: and though the sym:sym-sea[waves] thereof toss themselves, yet can they not prevail; though they *roar*, yet can they not pass over it?
But *this people* hath a revolting and a rebellious heart; they are revolted and gone.
____

The next-verse rule once more: the raging sea that cannot cross its bound is set against __“this people,”__ who will not stay within theirs.
Take the comfort in it: the waves may toss and roar, but the raging of the nations has a decreed limit it cannot pass.
But sand is loose and forever shifting, and that makes it the one ground a man must never build on:

[quote.scripture, Matthew 7:26-27]
____
…a sym:sym-fool[foolish man], which built his house upon the sym:sym-sand[sand]: And the rain descended, and the sym:sym-flood[floods] came, and the sym:sym-wind[winds] blew, and beat upon that house; and it *fell*: and great was the fall of it.
____

The sym:sym-rock[rock] is the covenant; the sand is the multitude.
To build on sand is to found your house on the many — the crowd, the consensus, whatever most people think — and when the flood comes (a nation in motion) and the winds blow (the spirits sent forth), the house built on the crowd goes down with the crowd.
The house on the covenant-rock __“fell not”__ (Matthew 7:25).

Isaiah shows what the sand was meant to be: __“O that thou hadst hearkened to my commandments!… thy seed also had been as the sym:sym-sand[sand]”__ (Isaiah 48:18-19) — the innumerable multitude God desired, bound to His commandments instead of lying loose on the shore.
(The two builders are weighed in the Fool & Wise chapter.)

[discrete]
=== Islands

If the sea is the nations, ask what an sym:sym-island[island] must be — the question I promised to answer back in the mountain chapter, when it struck me as odd that an island could flee.
An island is land standing up out of the sea: the head of a mountain, a rock breaking the surface.
Both of those we have already fixed: the mountain is a kingdom, and the rock is the covenant.
So the island is covenant ground standing out of the sea of peoples — a people set apart, which is what holy means: separated.

The Hebrew word is _iy_, and Scripture’s usage never bends.
The first __“isles”__ are the nations distinguished __“every one after his tongue”__ (Genesis 10:5) — peoples marked off from one another, not a swarm.

God summons them as those who answer to Him: __“Keep silence before me, O sym:sym-island[islands]… let us come near together to judgment”__ (Isaiah 41:1); __“Listen, O sym:sym-island[isles], unto me”__ (Isaiah 49:1).
They wait for His law — __“the sym:sym-island[isles] shall wait for his law”__ (Isaiah 42:4; so too 51:5; 60:9) — for it is by the truth, the law, that men are sanctified (__“thy word is sym:sym-truth[truth],”__ John 17:17).
They glorify Him — __“glorify ye the LORD… in the sym:sym-island[isles] of the sym:sym-sea[sea]”__ (Isaiah 24:15); __“let the multitude of sym:sym-island[isles] be glad”__ (Psalm 97:1).
And they are gathered home — the remnant recovered __“from the sym:sym-island[islands] of the sym:sym-sea[sea]”__ (Isaiah 11:11), His glory sent __“unto the sym:sym-island[isles] afar off”__ (Isaiah 66:19).
Summoned, waiting, glorifying, gathered: across the prophets the isles are one thing — the set-apart peoples, turned toward the God who set them apart.

When the last judgment shakes the world, watch the islands and the mountains part ways:

[quote.scripture, Revelation 16:20]
____
And every sym:sym-island[island] *fled away*, and the sym:sym-mountain[mountains] *were not found*.
____

The kingdoms are __“not found”__ — thrown down, dissolved into the sea.
The islands __“fled away”__ — removed, carried out of harm, delivered before the sea is judged (so also __“every sym:sym-mountain[mountain] and sym:sym-island[island] were moved out of their places,”__ Revelation 6:14).
Job names them in a phrase that the vowel points later buried: __“the sym:sym-island[island] of the innocent,”__ delivered __“by the pureness of thine hands”__ (Job 22:30 — the unpointed consonants, _iy_, are the very letters that name the isles).

In the new creation there is no more sea — and so no more islands: not because the set-apart vanish, but because nothing remains to be set apart from.

One caution before we close.
The same word __“water”__ carries a second, opposite symbol, and the difference is the source.
The gathered, salt, restless waters are the peoples; but __“living water”__ — water that springs and flows from God (__“the fountain of sym:sym-living-2[living waters],”__ Jeremiah 2:13; __“rivers of sym:sym-living-2[living water],”__ John 7:38) — is the Spirit and word of God going out to give life.
The two meet in Ezekiel’s vision, and the living water wins:

[quote.scripture, Ezekiel 47:8-9]
____
These sym:sym-living-2[waters] issue out… and go into the sym:sym-sea[sea]: which being brought forth into the sea, the sym:sym-sea[waters] *shall be healed*.
And it shall come to pass, that every thing that liveth, which moveth, whithersoever the rivers shall come, shall live: and there shall be a very great *multitude of* sym:sym-fish[fish]…
____

The river from the temple flows into the sea, the sea is healed, and the healed sea teems with a very great multitude of fish — the nations made alive, and full of people to be gathered.
The living water is a symbol in its own right, and the glossary carries it; for now, simply note that a sea of salt and a river of life are not the same symbol, and the context tells you which is which.

Set this chapter beside the mountain and the structure of power comes into view.
The sea is the peoples; the winds stir it; the beasts — kingdoms — rise out of it; the mountains are those kingdoms enthroned; Babylon sits on the sea and is at last covered by it; and God stills the sea, walks on it, draws His people up out of it, and finally makes an end of it.
Mountain and sea are not two unrelated pictures but two halves of one map: the governing and the governed, the rule and the ruled.

By now you should also have three habits that will let you make these discoveries yourself: read the parallel columns, read the next verse, and treat personification as a flag that a symbol is in play.

Along the way we have again gathered symbols, and each now has its home.
The sym:sym-flood[flood] that is an army in motion, the sym:sym-fish[fish], the sym:sym-sand[sand] and the sym:sym-island[island], the sym:sym-dragon[dragon] at play in the deep, and the living water that heals the sea were defined in these pages, and the glossary carries each of them.
The sym:sym-four[four winds] of Daniel 7 had their chapter at the head of Part Five; the sym:sym-way[way] He makes in the sea had its own back in Part Two.
And the sym:sym-beast[beasts] that rose out of this sea are next, taken up with the sym:sym-tree[trees] and defined the same way we have defined the mountain and the sea: by letting Scripture interpret Scripture.
