sources.content:
---
title: "Garments & Armor"
slug: garments
order: 43
permalink: /books/meat-bibles-symbolic-language/garments/
description: "A garment in Scripture is righteousness — 'the fine linen is the righteous acts of the saints' (Revelation 19:8, NKJV), the covenant covering worn as righteous deeds. The man cast out of the wedding feast had none. The righteous acts are clean; sin only stains the cloth — so the garment is to be washed, not cast off, and kept by keeping the commandments. A covering of one's own cut is fig leaves, refused. To be without it is to be naked — the covenant stripped, the shame seen."
og_title: "Garments & Armor — MEAT The Bible's Symbolic Language"
epigraphs:
  - quote: "He hath clothed me with the garments of salvation, he hath covered me with the robe of righteousness."
    ref: "Isaiah 61:10"
---
A man is bound hand and foot and thrown out of a wedding feast into the dark — and his offense was his clothing.
The feast is no ordinary supper: it is a king’s, made __“for his son”__ (Matthew 22:2) — a parable of the kingdom, and the wedding is the sym:sym-marriage[marriage] of the Lamb.

The man __“had not on a wedding garment”__ (Matthew 22:11), and when the king asks how he entered so, he has no answer; __“he was speechless”__ (Matthew 22:12) — the Greek is stronger than the English: _phimoō_, to *muzzle*, the same word Paul uses of the ox that treads out the grain (1 Corinthians 9:9) and the very word Jesus speaks to the storm and to unclean spirits, __“Peace, be still”__ (Mark 4:39), __“Hold thy peace”__ (Mark 1:25).
He was not merely at a loss for words; he was muzzled — silenced the way a power greater than his own silences what it overrules, with no defense in his mouth because he had none on his back.

He was not stopped at the gate — he was invited, seated, and only then found out, for __“many are called”__ (Matthew 22:14).
What condemns him is what he has on.
At that very marriage Scripture halts to name the garment.

[quote.scripture, Revelation 19:8, NKJV]
____
And to her it was granted to be arrayed in fine linen, clean and bright, for the fine linen is the *righteous acts* of the saints.
____

The fine linen _is_ the righteous _acts_ of the saints — the things they did.
The Greek is _dikaiōmata_, righteous deeds, and the NKJV keeps the plural action visible.
The King James shortens it to __“the righteousness of saints,”__ and on that one narrowed word a long confusion is built: _righteousness_ gets turned from something you _do_ into a state you merely _have_, sanctification folded into justification until the garment seems to require no weaving at all.
But the word is plural and active — righteous _acts_.

The garment is righteousness performed; to be clothed is to have done it, to be bare is to stand in your sins.
Nor is the doing self-made: the verse's first clause says the linen __“was *given* unto her”__ — deeds God __“hath before ordained that we should *walk in* them”__ (Ephesians 2:10) — granted, then worn.
So the man who came to the wedding with no garment came with no righteous acts on him at all — invited, seated, and naked.

Scripture says plainly what those acts are, for _righteousness_ is itself a word men stumble over — taken for a vague goodness, or a verdict merely received.
Put plainly, righteousness is *right-living*.
For a creature under God's authority, the commandments name what right-living is: __“it shall be our sym:sym-righteousness[righteousness], if we observe to do all these commandments”__ (Deuteronomy 6:25), for __“all thy commandments are righteousness”__ (Psalm 119:172).
Lest anyone make it a state without deeds, John says it in one line: __“he that doeth sym:sym-righteousness[righteousness] is righteous”__ (1 John 3:7).
The garment of righteous acts is therefore right-living made visible — the law kept, and worn.

God's own righteousness does not break the definition.
God obeys no superior; His ways are the measure of right: __“all his ways are judgment: a God of truth and without iniquity, just and right is he”__ (Deuteronomy 32:4), and __“the LORD is righteous in all his ways, and holy in all his works”__ (Psalm 145:17).
God is Right-Living by definition.
When Isaiah sees Him put on righteousness as a breastplate, God is going forth to do right — to judge, repay, and save where no man could (Isaiah 59:16-18).

Romans 4 and Philippians 3, often read as if reckoned righteousness had no life inside it, were treated with Paul's wage, debt, faith, and obedience vocabulary in link:/books/symbolic-language/the-end-of-the-law/[The End of the Law].
Righteousness is God's gift in source and right-living in substance: granted, then worn.

This is why the song over this chapter sings the way it does: __“he hath clothed me with the *garments of salvation*, he hath covered me with the *robe of* sym:sym-righteousness[righteousness]”__ (Isaiah 61:10) — garments of _yeshuah_: the covering He gives is salvation-wear, and its fabric is righteousness.
And it is the robe the father calls for when the prodigal comes home: __“Bring forth the *best robe*, and put it on him”__ (Luke 15:22) — the covenant covering restored on repentance, before the boy can finish his speech.

[discrete]
=== The Covering Is the Covenant

Behind the garment stands the covenant.
When God first took Israel for His own, He told it as the clothing of a newborn cast out naked in the open field:

[quote.scripture, Ezekiel 16:8]
____
…I spread my *skirt* over thee, and *covered thy nakedness*… and entered into a *covenant* with thee… and thou becamest mine.
____

Three phrases for one act: to spread the skirt, to cover the nakedness, to enter the covenant.
That spread skirt is the _kanaph_, the sym:sym-wings[wing], link:/books/symbolic-language/wings/[doing both of its offices]: the edge that carries the fringe bound as the reminder to keep the commandments and do them (Numbers 15:39), and the shade a refuge shelters under.footnote:fn37kanaph[The kanaph — wing, skirt, border, corner — and the fringe at its edge are derived in the link:/books/symbolic-language/wings/[Wings] chapter.]
The covenant contains the commands; faithfulness to them gains the covering — and what it covers is the nakedness, the sin.

What follows is a *second* gift, given inside the covenant:

[quote.scripture, Ezekiel 16:9-10]
____
Then *washed I thee* with water; yea, I throughly washed away thy blood from thee, and I anointed thee with sym:sym-oil[oil].
I *clothed thee* also with broidered work… and I girded thee about with *fine linen*…
____

First the covering of the covenant; then the clothing of the covered.
Revelation keeps the same grammar at the wedding — __“to her was *granted* that she should *array herself*”__ (Revelation 19:8): given, and put on by her; deeds God __“before ordained that we should *walk in them*”__ (Ephesians 2:10), worked in her by His word, and washed whiter than snow when she stains them.

The righteous acts that make up the garment, then, are not scattered good turns — they are the covenant lived out, the law kept and worn where every eye can see it.
As the sym:sym-name[name] is the covenant _owned_, the garment is the covenant _worn_.

The first garment was cut at the cost of blood.
The man and his wife stood naked by their sin, and God makes them __“coats of skins”__ and __“clothed them”__ (Genesis 3:21) — a covering that cost a life, the first blood shed to clothe the guilty, and the first shadow of the Lamb to come.
So nakedness is a symbol in its own right, the exact opposite of the garment: the clothed are covered by covenant, the naked stand exposed in their breach — and every verse that defines the one defines the other.

[discrete]
=== Filthy Rags

The garment is woven of righteous acts, and the acts themselves are clean — but the cloth can be soiled.
One verse is pressed into service to deny this:

[quote.scripture, Isaiah 64:6]
____
But we are all as an *unclean thing*, and all our sym:sym-righteousness[righteousnesses] are as *filthy rags*…
____

It is read as if obedience itself were filth — as if the more law a man keeps, the dirtier he grows.
But read the whole line: __“we are all as an unclean thing,”__ and so even __“our righteousnesses”__ come out stained.
It is not the righteous act that is filthy; it is the sin it is worked in.
The rag is blood-stained — fouled by the very iniquities the verse goes on to name — not because doing right is wrong, but because the doer is unclean.
A clean deed from a stained hand comes away marked.

The answer to a dirty garment is not to take it off; it is to wash it. __“Wash you, make you clean,”__ God says in the same prophet, and then, __“though your sym:sym-sin[sins] be as sym:sym-scarlet[scarlet], they shall be as white as snow”__ (Isaiah 1:16-18).
The saints __“washed their robes, and made them white in the blood of the sym:sym-lamb[Lamb]”__ (Revelation 7:14); Joshua the high priest stands __“clothed with filthy garments”__ until the word goes out, __“Take away the filthy garments from him… I will clothe thee with change of raiment”__ (Zechariah 3:4) — the iniquity removed, the robe made clean.
The keeping is itself commanded: the last beatitude in Scripture is for __“they that do his commandments, that they may have right to the tree of life”__ (Revelation 22:14).
Those who take no responsibility for their robe — who neither weave nor wash — are the ones found bare.

The Lord enacted it the night before He died.
He girded a towel and washed the disciples’ feet, and when Peter refused, He warned, __“If I wash thee not, thou hast no part with me”__ (John 13:8).
Then the key:

[quote.scripture, John 13:10]
____
He that is *washed* needeth not save to wash his sym:sym-feet[feet], but is *clean every whit*.
____

The bath is baptism — washed once into the Name, and so into the covenant: __“as many of you as have been baptized into Christ have put on Christ”__ (Galatians 3:27).
A man is not bathed again and again; he is not baptized over and over, and the robe is put on once.

Yet his feet gather the dirt of the road and must be washed — the sym:sym-feet[feet] are the walk, the conduct that is a man’s sym:sym-way[way].
Jesus therefore stooped to wash them: not a second baptism, but the daily cleansing of the walk that keeps the garment clean.
And __“ye also ought to wash one another’s feet”__ (John 13:14).

There is an opposite error, and it is the older one.
In the garden the man and his wife __“sewed sym:sym-fig[fig] leaves together, and made themselves aprons”__ (Genesis 3:7) — a covering of their own cut and their own measure, what was right in their own eyes.
Scripture marks that road: __“There is a sym:sym-way[way] which seemeth right unto a man, but the end thereof are the ways of death”__ (Proverbs 14:12); __“Every way of a man is right in his own eyes: but the LORD pondereth the hearts”__ (Proverbs 21:2).

God strips the fig leaves off and clothes them Himself, at the cost of blood.
The covering must be cut to His pattern, not to ours.

The fig tree itself shows what such a covering is worth.
Jesus came to one __“having leaves”__ and __“found nothing thereon, but leaves only”__; He cursed it — __“Let no sym:sym-fruit[fruit] grow on thee henceforward for ever”__ — and it withered away (Matthew 21:19; Mark 11:13-14).
The leaves are the show; the fruit is the substance.
A tree hung with leaves and bearing no fruit is the fig-leaf covering in one picture — the look of righteousness where the works God came seeking are not.
He is not fed by leaves; He looks for fruit.

[discrete]
=== Keep Your Garments

A garment given can still be defiled, so it must be kept.
The Lord commends the few in Sardis __“which have not defiled their garments,”__ and promises __“they shall walk with me in white”__ (Revelation 3:4); Jude speaks of __“hating even the garment spotted by the flesh”__ (Jude 23); and the watchword for the last hour is just this:

[quote.scripture, Revelation 16:15]
____
Behold, I come as a thief.
Blessed is he that watcheth, and *keepeth his garments*, lest he *walk naked*, and they see his shame.
____

To keep the garment is to go on doing the righteousness it is made of.
This is why the apostles speak of it as something you _put on_: __“put ye on the Lord Jesus Christ”__ (Romans 13:14); __“put on the new man,”__ and with him __“bowels of mercies, kindness… meekness, longsuffering”__ (Colossians 3:10-12); as Job said long before, __“I put on sym:sym-righteousness[righteousness], and it clothed me”__ (Job 29:14).
The clothing is conduct.

The wardrobe is God’s own: Isaiah watched Him dress — __“he put on *righteousness* as a breastplate, and an helmet of *salvation* upon his head”__ (Isaiah 59:17) — and Paul issues the same suit to the soldier: the breastplate of righteousness, the helmet of salvation, truth for a belt and the word for a sword (Ephesians 6:14-17).
The armour of God is not a figure borrowed from Rome; it is God’s own clothing from the prophets, lent to the man who will wear it.
A robe is not framed and admired; it is worn, kept clean, and worn again tomorrow.

[discrete]
=== Naked

To be without the garment is to be naked, and nakedness, from the garden onward, is not nudity but exposure — the covenant covering gone, the shame seen.
Laodicea is __“wretched, and miserable, and sym:sym-poor[poor], and blind, and naked”__ and does not feel it (Revelation 3:17); the warning __“lest he walk naked, and they see his shame”__ (Revelation 16:15) is aimed at a way of life, not a state of undress.
When God judges a covenant-breaker, He strips her: __“Thy nakedness shall be uncovered, yea, thy shame shall be seen”__ (Isaiah 47:3).
And Paul’s one dread for the day of resurrection is to be caught uncovered — __“if so be that being clothed we shall not be found naked”__ (2 Corinthians 5:3).
The naked are those with no righteousness to show and no covenant to plead — exactly the man at the wedding, speechless in his bare skin before the king.

[discrete]
=== The War-Dress

The wardrobe has a battle form.
The helmet of salvation is commonly treated as a state of mind: confidence and assurance that guard the believer from doubt, fear, and lies.
Now run the words through the whole of Scripture instead.
The phrase is not Paul's; it is a quotation, and its first wearer is not the believer:

[quote.scripture, Isaiah 59:16-17]
____
And he saw that there was *no man*, and wondered that there was no intercessor: therefore *his arm* brought *salvation* unto him; and his righteousness, it sustained him.
For *he* put on righteousness as a *breastplate*, and an *helmet of salvation upon his head*; and he put on the garments of vengeance for clothing, and was clad with zeal as a cloke.
____

The armor is God's own war-dress, put on because no man could — which is what __“the whole armour *of God*”__ (Ephesians 6:11) says when it is allowed to mean it: not armor from His stores, but the armor He wears, lent to the soldier.
And the Hebrew under __“salvation”__ is the word this book met on the mountains of the link:/books/symbolic-language/gospel/[Gospel] chapter: _yeshuah_ — the helmet of *Yeshuah*.
The head, covered with Him.

David had already defined the piece without naming it: __“the strength of my *salvation*, thou hast *covered my head* in the day of battle”__ (Psalm 140:7) — a covered head, _yeshuah_, and a battle; and the covering verb is the _sukkah_ root: a booth pitched over the head, and pitched by God's hand — __“*thou* hast covered.”__
And what covers a man's head? __“the *head* of every man is *Christ*”__ (1 Corinthians 11:3).
The armor verbs are this chapter's verbs — clothing verbs — and their object is a Person: __“*put ye on* the Lord Jesus Christ”__ (Romans 13:14).

The forehead seals it.
The high priest's mitre carried a graven plate __“upon Aaron's *forehead*,”__ reading HOLINESS TO THE LORD, __“that they may be *accepted*”__ (Exodus 28:36-38); the word is bound __“as frontlets *between thine eyes*”__ (Deuteronomy 6:8); and the redeemed wear __“his sym:sym-name[name]… in their foreheads”__ (Revelation 22:4) — while the counterfeit is issued for the same head: the beast's mark __“in their foreheads”__ (Revelation 13:16).
The helmet is the Name and word of Jesus covering the mind; the enemy makes helmets too.

Scripture even stages the two armors side by side, in a fitting room before a duel.
Saul dresses David in his own gear — __“and he put an *helmet of brass* upon his head”__ — and the shepherd takes it all off again: __“I cannot go with these; for I have not *proved* them”__ (1 Samuel 17:38-39).
The word under __“proved”__ is _nasah_ — tested; the King James even says David __“*assayed* to go”__ — and the armor of a man failed the assay.
David walks to the giant in what he had tested: __“The LORD that delivered me out of the paw of the lion, and out of the paw of the bear, he will deliver me”__ (1 Samuel 17:37) — *test all things; hold fast what is good*, worn as battle-dress.

Even the weight teaches.
Man's armor is heavy on the wearer, and the tradition it stands for binds __“*heavy burdens* and grievous to be borne”__ on other men's shoulders (Matthew 23:4).
God's armor runs the other way: __“my yoke is easy, and my burden is *light*”__ (Matthew 11:30); __“his commandments are *not grievous*”__ (1 John 5:3) — and it is the armor *of light* (Romans 13:12).
In English the two senses share one word, and the pun is ours, not the Hebrew's: _or_ is the light that shines, _qal_ the light that weighs nothing, and the Greek splits them the same way. Even without the pun, the doctrine stands: the armor made of light is also the armor that is light, because the One who wore it first carries the weight.

Now walk down Paul's whole list with the Glossary of this book open: the girdle of sym:sym-truth[truth], the breastplate of sym:sym-righteousness[righteousness], the feet shod with the sym:sym-gospel[gospel] of sym:sym-peace[peace], the shield of sym:sym-faith[faith], the helmet of _yeshuah_, and the sym:sym-sword[sword] of the Spirit, __“which is the *word of God*”__ (Ephesians 6:17).
Every piece is a defined symbol: the whole armour of God is the symbolic vocabulary of Scripture, worn as clothing.
The milk reading arms a man with his own feelings; the word read whole dresses him in Christ from head to foot.

The symbol takes its place with the rest.
The sym:sym-gospel[gospel] is the covenant announced; the sym:sym-way[way], the sym:sym-truth[truth], and the sym:sym-life[life] are the covenant embodied; the sym:sym-name[name] is the covenant owned; and the garment is the covenant _worn_ — righteous acts done, granted in the blood of the Lamb and kept clean to the end.

The marriage of the Lamb is set, and the call has gone out to many.
But __“many are called… few are chosen”__ (Matthew 22:14): the chosen are the few found on the sym:sym-highway[highway] of holiness, properly dressed.
The one who walks some other road, or comes to the feast in a covering of his own cut, is the man without a garment — speechless at the door, and cast into the dark.
And how a covenant binds not one wearer but a whole people together is the next symbol: the bow.

sources.content:
---
title: "The Bow"
slug: the-bow
order: 44
permalink: /books/meat-bibles-symbolic-language/the-bow/
description: "The rainbow is a bow — a weapon of war, laid down. The Hebrew qesheth is one word for the warrior's bow, the covenant token of Genesis 9, and a binding bond. So the bow is the covenant that binds a people: Babel forged its own ('make us a name, lest we be scattered'), and God breaks such bows — the bow of Elam, the bows of Babylon — scattering the kingdom strung against Him."
og_title: "The Bow — MEAT The Bible's Symbolic Language"
epigraphs:
  - quote: "And the bow shall be in the cloud… that I may remember the everlasting covenant between God and every living creature."
    ref: "Genesis 9:16"
---
Everyone knows the rainbow as God’s sign after the flood.
But the Hebrew names it plainly: it is a _qesheth_, a *bow* — the same word used everywhere else for the warrior’s weapon.
Scripture states outright what this bow is:

[quote.scripture, Genesis 9:13]
____
I do set my *bow* in the cloud, and it shall be for a *token of a covenant* between me and the earth.
____

__“A token of a covenant.”__
This is not an analogy we are reading into the text; the text sets the war-bow in the sky and names it the sign of God’s covenant.
The bow is the covenant.

See its reach.
God makes this first covenant __“between me and you and every sym:sym-living[living creature] of all flesh”__ (Genesis 9:15) — and in the language of these symbols a living creature is a nation: the sym:sym-beast[beasts] of Daniel’s sym:sym-sea[sea] are kingdoms, and the living creatures of Revelation are peoples.
The very first bow-covenant, then, is struck not with one tribe but with _every nation on earth_ — a universal covenant of sym:sym-peace[peace], set over all the families of the ground.
That reach governs what follows.

[discrete]
=== The Bow Is the Covenant

Once you see it here, the symbol runs everywhere, because _qesheth_ is never merely hardware.
It is a kingdom’s _might_: __“the bow of sym:sym-elam[Elam], the chief of their might”__ (Jeremiah 49:35).
And it is a _binding bond_: Isaiah pictures fleeing rulers __“bound”__ — the Hebrew is _asar_, to yoke, the root of the word for a *vow* — __“by the bow”__ (Isaiah 22:3, where the KJV hides the word as “archers”).

Weapon, might, covenant, vow: one word carries them all, because they are one thing.
A kingdom’s armed power is the outward face of the covenant that holds it together.
The bow is what a people is _strung together_ by.

The New Testament keeps the symbol whole.
Its single bow — _toxon_, the only bow in the New Testament — belongs to the conqueror on the sym:sym-horse[white horse]:

[quote.scripture, Revelation 6:2]
____
…he that sat on him had a *bow*; and a *crown* was given unto him: and he went forth *conquering, and to conquer*.
____

He carries a bow, yet no arrow is ever loosed.
He conquers not by the shot but by the bow itself — he wins the nations by _covenant_.
(Whether this rider is the true King binding the nations to Himself or a counterfeit binding them to a lie is a question this book leaves open; either way, the instrument of conquest is a covenant.)

Scripture even stages the symbol inside a covenant scene.
__“Then Jonathan and David *made a covenant*, because he loved him as his own soul”__ — and the cutting is sealed by a handover of arms: __“Jonathan stripped himself of the robe that was upon him, and gave it to David… even to his sword, and to his *bow*, and to his girdle”__ (1 Samuel 18:3-4).
The bow passes when the covenant is cut.
And when Jonathan fell, David commanded Judah to learn his lament — __“he bade them teach the children of Judah the *bow*”__ (2 Samuel 1:18): the Song of the Bow, sung for the covenant-brother whose __“bow turned not back”__ (2 Samuel 1:22).

Habakkuk writes the whole equation in a single verse:

[quote.scripture, Habakkuk 3:9]
____
Thy *bow* was made quite naked, according to the *oaths* of the tribes, even thy *word*.
____

God’s bow unsheathed _is_ His sworn word to the tribes, riding out beside the __“chariots of salvation”__ we met in the sym:sym-sea[sea] chapter (Habakkuk 3:8).
And when God draws, look what fills His hand: __“I have *bent Judah* for me, *filled the bow with* sym:sym-ephraim[Ephraim]”__ (Zechariah 9:13) — the covenant is the weapon, and the covenant people are its string and its arrows.

[discrete]
=== Make Us a Name

If the bow that holds a kingdom together is finally a covenant, then the bond can be made of nothing but a word.
So it was with the first kingdom built against heaven: it was founded not on a weapon but on a name.
At Babel men gather to build, and they name their purpose:

[quote.scripture, Genesis 11:4]
____
…let us make us a sym:sym-name[name], lest we be *scattered abroad* upon the face of the whole earth.
____

The reason they give is a _name_ — __“lest we be scattered.”__
The name is the bond that holds them as one people; cut it, and they fly apart.
And a **name**footnote:name[_Name_ — the covenant that binds a people; established in the chapter link:/books/symbolic-language/the-name/[The Name].], as the link:/books/symbolic-language/the-name/[Name] chapter showed, _is_ a covenant — the binding constitution of a people.
Babel’s project is a self-made covenant, a bow of their own stringing, forged to bind a kingdom together in defiance of the God who set the nations apart.
And God answers in kind: He does not topple the tower, He cuts the bond.

[quote.scripture, Genesis 11:9]
____
…the LORD did there *confound the language* of all the earth: and from thence did the LORD *scatter them abroad* upon the face of all the earth.
____

Their one speech was the string of their bow; God cuts it, and the kingdom springs apart.
The very scattering they built a name to prevent is the scattering He brings.
Break the bond, and the people disperse.

[discrete]
=== Elam and the Mortar of Babel

This is the system Scripture calls _Babylon_, and it has a partner that shares its judgment: _Elam_.
The two stand together in the first war in the Bible — four kings against five, the coalition led by __“Chedorlaomer king of Elam”__ alongside __“Amraphel king of Shinar”__ (Genesis 14:1, 9), and Shinar _is_ Babel (Genesis 10:10).
And where do they fight?
In a valley __“full of slimepits”__ (Genesis 14:10) — where the word for that slime, _chemar_, is the very word for the mortar of Babel’s tower: __“slime had they for morter”__ (Genesis 11:3).
The Elam-Babylon war is fought on ground paved with Babel’s own building-material.

Against them stands Abram with his household and his allies, __“confederate”__ with him (Genesis 14:13) — in the Hebrew, literally _masters of a covenant_ with Abram: a true covenant set against the self-covenant.
So when the prophets take up Elam, they take up Babel’s old confederate — Jeremiah’s oracle against Elam stands as the prologue to his great prophecy of Babylon’s fall, and the sentence on both is the same: the bow broken.

[discrete]
=== Break the Bow

How, then, does God bring down a kingdom bound by such a bow?
He breaks the bow.
Hear it where it cannot be missed — bow-breaking set side by side with covenant-making:

[quote.scripture, Hosea 2:18]
____
And in that day will I *make a covenant* for them… and I will *break the bow* and the sword and the battle out of the earth, and will make them to *lie down safely*.
____

To break the bow is covenant work: the violent self-bond shattered, God’s own covenant of sym:sym-peace[peace] put in its place — and Hosea says it in the very scene where God re-betroths His divorced wife (Hosea 2:19), the wedding we met in the link:/books/symbolic-language/marriage-and-divorce/[Marriage and Divorce] chapter.
So the sentence on the Babylon-system reads exactly so:

[quote.scripture, Jeremiah 49:35]
____
Behold, I will *break the bow of Elam*, the chief of their might.
____

Against Babylon herself, __“every one of their bows is broken”__ (Jeremiah 51:56).
The might, the constitution, the binding covenant of the kingdom are all that one bow, and God snaps it — __“he breaketh the bow, and cutteth the spear in sunder”__ (Psalm 46:9).
The kingdom that strung itself together against Him comes unstrung, and scatters.

Nor is the breaking reserved for the heathen.
When Israel’s own covenant was strung against Him, the same sentence fell on His own house: __“I will *break the bow of Israel* in the valley of Jezreel”__ (Hosea 1:5).
For the covenant-breaker has a bow-name in Scripture: __“they *dealt unfaithfully*… they were turned aside like a *deceitful bow*”__ (Psalm 78:57); __“they return, but not to the most High: they are like a *deceitful bow*”__ (Hosea 7:16).
A deceitful bow looks strung and true, and betrays the archer at full draw — the exact figure of a people wearing the covenant and failing it in the hand.

[discrete]
=== Two Names, Two Bows

Set the two covenants side by side and the whole symbol stands clear.
At Babel men say, __“let us _make us_ a name”__ — a covenant seized, self-strung, to bind a kingdom against heaven; and God scatters it.
In the very next breath of Scripture He turns to one man and says the opposite:

[quote.scripture, Genesis 12:2]
____
…I will *make of thee a great nation*, and I will bless thee, and *make thy* sym:sym-name[name] *great*; and thou shalt be a blessing.
____

Not _make us_ a name but _I will make thy_ name — a covenant given, not grasped; and where Babel’s name was built to keep one people from scattering, Abraham’s name is given to bless _all the families of the earth_.

The bow God first hung in the cloud is hanging there still — __“the everlasting covenant”__ (Genesis 9:16), His war-bow bent in peace over every nation on earth.
Scripture sights it twice more, exactly where a covenant should hang.
Ezekiel sees the glory ringed __“as the appearance of the *bow* that is in the cloud in the day of rain”__ (Ezekiel 1:28); John sees __“a *rainbow* round about the throne”__ (Revelation 4:3), and the mighty angel comes down crowned with one (Revelation 10:1).
The war-bow of Noah’s sky encircles the throne of judgment itself: every verdict rendered from that seat is rendered from inside the everlasting covenant.

Notice what the sign is made of.
A rainbow has no substance of its own; it is sym:sym-light[light] shining through water — Ezekiel says exactly that, __“the appearance of the *brightness*”__ in __“the day of *rain*”__ (Ezekiel 1:28).
In this book’s vocabulary neither ingredient is neutral: light is the commandment made visible — __“the commandment is a lamp; and the law is light”__ (Proverbs 6:23) — and the rain is the word poured out — __“my *doctrine* shall drop as the *rain*”__ (Deuteronomy 32:2).
So the token of the everlasting covenant appears exactly where God’s law shines through His outpoured word: the sign is drawn in the sky out of the covenant’s own two ingredients.

Joseph’s blessing names the secret of a bow that never breaks: __“his *bow abode in strength*… by the hands of the mighty God of Jacob”__ (Genesis 49:24).
The bow’s universal reach is the very thing Babel grasped after to bind one people, and that Abraham was given to carry as blessing to all.

Two names, two covenants, two bows: one strung by men and broken, one set in the heavens by God and kept; every bow drawn against Him comes, in the end, unstrung.
The covenant is the bow; and the only bow that abides is the one He strings.

sources.content:
---
title: "Jacob, Israel, and Ephraim"
slug: jacob-israel-and-ephraim
order: 45
permalink: /books/meat-bibles-symbolic-language/jacob-israel-and-ephraim/
description: "Jacob — the heel-grabbing supplanter — is the crooked human heart; Israel is the new name given to that same man for prevailing with God. The names do not divide flesh from spirit; they tell one story, the crooked made straight. So Israel is covenant and character, not blood — 'they are not all Israel, which are of Israel.' And Ephraim, the firstborn whose seed becomes 'a multitude of nations,' is that people scattered into all the earth as fruit, and regathered into one."
og_title: "Jacob, Israel, and Ephraim — MEAT The Bible's Symbolic Language"
epigraphs:
  - quote: "Thy name shall be called no more Jacob, but Israel: for as a prince hast thou power with God and with men, and hast prevailed."
    ref: "Genesis 32:28"
---
A man wrestles God through the night, will not let go, and at daybreak is given a new name:

[quote.scripture, Genesis 32:28]
____
Thy name shall be called no more *Jacob*, but *Israel*: for as a prince hast thou power with God and with men, and hast *prevailed*.
____

What does that change of name mean?
The common readings rank this way:

.How Jacob’s change to Israel is usually read
[.prevalence-table%unbreakable, frame=topbot, grid=none, cols="^2,8", options="header"]
|===
| Rank | Common interpretation

| 1 | Jacob the carnal “old man” put off; Israel the spiritual “new man” put on
| 2 | Simply the patriarch — and his nation — renamed; a plain name change
| 3 | From sinner to saint: a conversion at the brook
| 4 | A title earned for prevailing in the wrestling
|===

The first reading makes Jacob the flesh and Israel the spirit, the old self traded for the new — Paul's __“put off… the old man”__ and __“put on the new man”__ (Ephesians 4:22-24) read back into the patriarch.
It is half right and wholly misread, for Scripture will not let the change be a swap of two men.

God first gives him the name Israel after the wrestling (Genesis 32:28).
Later, at Bethel, God reaffirms it: __“thy name shall not be called any more Jacob”__ (Genesis 35:10).
Yet Scripture keeps right on calling him Jacob, and God names Himself to the end __“the God of Jacob.”__
Isaiah even trades the titles between the two names — __“Israel… my servant, Jacob whom I have chosen”__ (Isaiah 41:8), then __“Jacob my servant; and Israel, whom I have chosen”__ (Isaiah 44:1); and each name runs the whole range, for He __“hath not beheld iniquity in Jacob”__ (Numbers 23:21) and yet __“Israel is defiled”__ (Hosea 5:3).

The names are not flesh and spirit, the bad man traded for the good.
There is a real change — but it is the straightening of one heart, not the swapping of two selves.
They are one man told in two words, and between them lies the whole work of God on a human heart.

[discrete]
=== Jacob: The Crooked

The first name is a verdict.
He was born gripping his brother’s heel — __“his name was called Jacob”__ (Genesis 25:26), _heel-grabber_ — and he lived up to it, seizing the birthright and stealing the blessing, until Esau cries out:

[quote.scripture, Genesis 27:36]
____
Is not he rightly named *Jacob*? for he hath *supplanted* me these two times…
____

The root of the name throws off a second word, _aqob_ — _crooked, deceitful_ — and that word lands on every one of us: __“The heart is deceitful [_aqob_] above all things”__ (Jeremiah 17:9).
Jacob is not one crooked man; he is the crooked heart itself, the grasping, scheming nature every son of Adam is born wearing.
To be named Jacob is only to be human.

[discrete]
=== Israel: The Crooked Made Straight

The second name is what God does with such a heart. _Israel_ — to _prevail_ with _God_ — is given not for bloodline but for what happened in the dark: he held on, __“and prevailed.”__
Hosea tells how:

[quote.scripture, Hosea 12:4]
____
…he had power over the angel, and *prevailed*: he *wept, and made supplication* unto him…
____

The prevailing was not sharper cunning; it was the supplanter brought to the end of himself, weeping, clinging, asking.
And the very root that named him crooked names the cure — __“the _crooked_ [_aqob_] shall be made straight”__ (Isaiah 40:4).
Israel is Jacob made straight.

Which is why the new name is never simply handed over; it begins with a confession of the old.
God asks, __“What is thy name?”__ Jacob answers, __“Jacob”__ (Genesis 32:27) — name the crooked thing, and only then receive the new.

The end of the work is a man with the grasping gone, and Jesus names him the moment He sees him: __“Behold an Israelite indeed, in whom is no guile!”__ (John 1:47) — Jacob, with the Jacob taken out.

[discrete]
=== The Renewed Covenant

The new name is a renewed covenant.
We have seen that a sym:sym-name[name] _is_ a covenant, and a sym:sym-new[new name] a covenant renewed — and that is exactly what Jacob received.
Going out to the nations, he had been given the covenant of his fathers at Bethel: __“I am the LORD God of Abraham thy father, and the God of Isaac… the land whereon thou liest, to thee will I give it”__ (Genesis 28:13).
Coming home, God renews it and seals it to the new name:

[quote.scripture, Genesis 35:10-12]
____
…*Israel shall be thy name*: and he called his name Israel.
And God said unto him, I am God Almighty: be fruitful and multiply; a *nation and a company of nations* shall be of thee…
And the *land which I gave Abraham and Isaac*, to thee I will give it, and to thy seed after thee will I give the land.
____

The covenant of the fathers, renewed with the son, under the new name — and already carrying the company of nations the scattered house will become.

See _when_ it is won.
The wrestling lasts __“until the breaking of the day”__ (Genesis 32:24): Jacob holds on through the whole night — __“I will not let thee go, except thou bless me”__ (Genesis 32:26) — and the new name, the renewed covenant, comes with the dawn.

Here is the pattern of the people who bear the name.
Israel holds to God through the night — the long night among the nations, the scattering of his own house — and will not loosen his grip until the day breaks and the covenant is renewed.
The one who holds on through the dark receives, in the morning, the new name and the covenant of his fathers made his own.

For the morning is when the long sorrow turns — __“weeping may endure for a night, but joy cometh in the morning”__ (Psalm 30:5) — and it is the hour the Lord Himself, held in the heart of the earth through His own night, rose __“very early in the morning… at the rising of the sun”__ (Mark 16:2), __“the firstfruits of them that slept”__ (1 Corinthians 15:20).
Hold on through the night, and the morning brings the new name, the renewed covenant, joy, and life.

[discrete]
=== They Are Not All Israel

Israel, then, was never a matter of descent.
It is the new name of the one who overcomes, and the New Testament says so flatly:

[quote.scripture, Romans 9:6]
____
…For they are not all *Israel*, which are of Israel:
____

The Jew is __“one inwardly”__ (Romans 2:28-29) — and Paul's definition carries Judah's name inside it: Judah means *praise* — __“Now will I *praise* the LORD: therefore she called his name Judah”__ (Genesis 29:35) — and the verse lands exactly there: the Jew inwardly is he __“whose *praise* is not of men, but of God.”__
The word wears three coats — ethnic, religious, covenant — and as with every symbol, the context tells you which one it is wearing.

The blessing rests on __“the Israel of God,”__ as many as __“walk according to this rule”__ (Galatians 6:16); and the wild branch is __“graffed in”__ to the same tree (Romans 11:17) — for here the tree is the nation, and this nation receives whoever is joined to it by covenant.
This is the new name promised to every overcomer — __“a sym:sym-new[new] sym:sym-name[name]… which no man knoweth saving he that receiveth it”__ (Revelation 2:17).
Jacob at the ford is the first of them: the natural man who contends with God, is brought low, and rises bearing the covenant name.

[discrete]
=== Ephraim: Fruit in the Land of Affliction

Within Israel there is a firstborn, and his name carries a prophecy.
Joseph calls his second son _Ephraim_ — _double fruit_:

[quote.scripture, Genesis 41:52]
____
…Ephraim: For God hath caused me to be *fruitful in the land of my affliction*.
____

Fruit, and fruit in affliction — the name is the story.
God sets this son above his elder (__“Ephraim is my firstborn,”__ Jeremiah 31:9), and over him aged Jacob speaks the strangest blessing in Genesis:

[quote.scripture, Genesis 48:19]
____
…his seed shall become a *multitude of nations*.
____

A multitude of nations out of one tribe — the Hebrew is _melo ha-goyim_, the _fulness of the nations_.

The way it comes to pass is by scattering.
Ephraim __“mixed himself among the people”__ and became __“a cake not turned”__ (Hosea 7:8), until he was __“broken, that it be not a people”__ (Isaiah 7:8).
The judgment looks like his end — but it is how the seed reaches every nation: he is lost on purpose, sown into all the earth.
And Paul names the harvest in the very words of the blessing — __“the fulness of the Gentiles”__ (Romans 11:25): _melo ha-goyim_, come in at last.

[discrete]
=== Two Sticks, One Nation

The scattered are lost to men, never to God; beneath the judgment runs a Father’s grief:

[quote.scripture, Hosea 11:8]
____
How shall I *give thee up, Ephraim*?… mine heart is turned within me, my *repentings* are kindled together.
____

The lost are sought — Jesus is sent __“unto the sym:sym-lost[lost sheep] of the house of Israel”__ (Matthew 15:24) — and the divided are made one.
The word for the two __“sticks”__ Ezekiel is handed is _ets_ — the same word Scripture uses for a _tree_ — and he is told to make the two one:

[quote.scripture, Ezekiel 37:19]
____
…Behold, I will take the *stick of Joseph*, which is in the hand of *Ephraim*, and the tribes of Israel his fellows, and will put them with him, even with the *stick of Judah*, and make them *one stick*, and they shall be *one in mine hand*.
____

At this scale a tree is a nation; so these are two nation-trees — Judah and Joseph-Ephraim — made one tree, __“one in mine hand,”__ that __“they shall be no more two nations, neither shall they be divided into two kingdoms any more at all”__ (Ezekiel 37:22).

The sentence on the scattered is reversed:

[quote.scripture, Hosea 1:10]
____
…in the place where it was said unto them, *Ye are not my people*, there it shall be said unto them, Ye are the *sons of the living God*.
____

Peter says it of the gathered church: __“which in time past were not a people, but are now the people of God”__ (1 Peter 2:10).

The two sticks have a second portrait, painted in the same orchard.
The olive-tree name was given jointly — __“The LORD called thy name, A green sym:sym-olive[olive] tree, fair, and of goodly sym:sym-fruit[fruit]”__ — and the next verse names those who wear it: __“the house of Israel and… the house of Judah”__ (Jeremiah 11:16-17).
Two houses under one green name; so when Zechariah is shown __“*two* sym:sym-olive[olive] *trees*”__ flanking the golden candlestick, emptying __“the golden sym:sym-oil[oil] out of themselves”__ through pipes into its lamps (Zechariah 4:3, 12), the two trees of the one name stand where the two sticks stood.
Revelation seals the reading: the two witnesses __“are the *two olive trees*, and the *two candlesticks*”__ (Revelation 11:4) — and a candlestick, by the book's own key, is an assembly (Revelation 1:20): not two men, but two covenant peoples bearing witness.

The trees supply sym:sym-oil[oil] — the pressed, proven works of the olive — the oil burns in the sym:sym-lamp[lamp], and the lamp, Scripture says, is __“the *commandment*”__ (Proverbs 6:23); what comes out is sym:sym-light[light].
For whom?
Isaiah answers in one breath — to __“raise up the tribes of Jacob, and to *restore the preserved of Israel*,”__ and __“I will also give thee for a sym:sym-light[light] *to the Gentiles*”__ (Isaiah 49:6); __“this is your sym:sym-wisdom[wisdom] and your sym:sym-understanding[understanding] *in the sight of the nations*”__ (Deuteronomy 4:6).
The two sticks become one in His hand; the two olive trees feed one lamp.

The three names are one road.
Jacob is the crooked heart every man is born with; Israel is that heart made straight, prevailing with God and given the covenant name; Ephraim is that people made fruitful in affliction, scattered as seed into all the nations, and gathered home into one.
Israel was never a bloodline to be born into.
It is a new name to be given — to the supplanter who weeps and holds on, in whom at last there is no guile.

sources.content:
---
title: "The Foreskin"
slug: foreskin
order: 46
permalink: /books/meat-bibles-symbolic-language/foreskin/
description: "Take away the foreskins of your heart, says Jeremiah — so the foreskin is a symbol the reader is expected to know. Scripture decodes it out loud: what the circumcision made without hands removes is 'the body of the sins of the flesh.' The foreskin is the blocking flesh over a covenant member — the uncircumcised heart cannot be humbled or love, the uncircumcised ear cannot hearken, uncircumcised lips cannot be heard, and a young tree's fruit is orlah, uncircumcised, until the covenant year. God himself performs the surgery, and the covenant's own wordplay states the alternative: cut it away, or be cut off."
og_title: "The Foreskin — MEAT The Bible's Symbolic Language"
epigraphs:
  - quote: "Circumcise yourselves to the LORD, and take away the foreskins of your heart, ye men of Judah and inhabitants of Jerusalem: lest my fury come forth like fire."
    ref: "Jeremiah 4:4"
---
Jeremiah lays a double command on the same field: __“Break up your fallow ground, and sow not among sym:sym-bramble[thorns]… take away the foreskins of your heart”__ (Jeremiah 4:3-4).
Plowing and circumcising, one operation in two figures — but the second figure assumes something: that a heart can wear a foreskin, and that the reader knows what one means.
So gather the uses, as this book does with every candidate, and let Scripture define it.

[discrete]
=== Scripture's Own Decode

Paul names what the circumcision of the heart removes, in so many words:

[quote.scripture, Colossians 2:11]
____
In whom also ye are circumcised with the circumcision *made without hands*, in *putting off the body of the* sym:sym-sin[sins] *of the flesh* by the circumcision of Christ.
____

What is cut away is __“the body of the sins of the flesh.”__
That is the foreskin's meaning, stated out loud: the sym:sym-foreskin[foreskin] is the blocking flesh — the layer of the natural man that covers a covenant member and stops its work.
Test the definition against every member Scripture attaches it to.

[discrete]
=== The Blocked Members

The heart.
Moses commands, __“Circumcise therefore the foreskin of your heart, and be *no more stiffnecked*”__ (Deuteronomy 10:16) — the covered heart is the stiff neck.
Leviticus pairs it with pride: exile runs its course __“if then their *uncircumcised hearts* be *humbled*”__ (Leviticus 26:41).
And when God himself performs the surgery, the freed function is love: __“the LORD thy God will circumcise thine heart… *to* sym:sym-love[love] *the LORD thy God with all thine heart*, and with all thy soul, that thou mayest live”__ (Deuteronomy 30:6).

The ear.
__“To whom shall I speak, and give warning, that they may hear? behold, their *ear is uncircumcised*, and they *cannot hearken*: behold, the word of the LORD is unto them a reproach; they have no delight in it”__ (Jeremiah 6:10).
The flesh over the ear blocks the word from the organ of hearing — and to hear, this book has shown, is to obey.
Here is the Old Testament's own diagnosis of the crowd at Capernaum, who ate the loaves and could not hear the hard saying: the word arrived at ears still covered.

The lips.
Moses protests his commission twice with the same figure — __“how then shall Pharaoh hear me, who am of *uncircumcised lips*?”__ (Exodus 6:12, 30) — speech blocked at the member that should carry it.

Even the fruit of a tree.
__“And when ye shall come into the land, and shall have planted all manner of trees for food, then ye shall count the sym:sym-fruit[fruit] thereof as *uncircumcised*: three years shall it be as uncircumcised unto you: it shall not be eaten of”__ — and __“in the fourth year all the fruit thereof shall be *holy to praise the LORD*”__ (Leviticus 19:23-24).
The word is _orlah_, the foreskin word: a young sym:sym-tree[tree]’s produce is its foreskin until the covenant year — sym:sym-fruit[fruit] blocked from acceptable use, then released holy.

Stephen gathers the members into one indictment: __“Ye *stiffnecked* and *uncircumcised in heart and ears*, ye do always *resist* the Holy Ghost: as your fathers did, so do ye”__ (Acts 7:51).

[discrete]
=== Cut, or Be Cut Off

The covenant states the alternative in its own wordplay:

[quote.scripture, Genesis 17:14]
____
And the uncircumcised man child whose flesh of his sym:sym-foreskin[foreskin] is not circumcised, that soul shall be *cut off* from his people; he hath *broken my covenant*.
____

Cut the flesh away, or be cut away from the people — the choice is which cutting.

The sign's placement also teaches, although this remains observation rather than derivation: the literal mark sits on the member where *seed* passes, and the seed, in the language of this book, is the word.
The circumcision of the heart clears the same obstruction one member up: __“circumcision is that of the *heart*, in the spirit, and not in the letter”__ (Romans 2:29).

Jeremiah's two figures thus close into one.
Break up the fallow ground; take away the foreskin: plow and knife, both removing the barrier so the sym:sym-seed[seed] can enter the heart and bear.
The sower's soils share one condition — unplowed, unbroken, choked — and the cure was published with the command: let God circumcise the heart, __“that thou mayest live.”__

sources.name: 46x-the-anointing.adoc
sources.content:
---
title: "The Anointing"
slug: the-anointing
order: 46.5
permalink: /books/meat-bibles-symbolic-language/the-anointing/
description: "Anointing is a church word often left undefined. Scripture uses it for appointment: a person or thing is marked as God's own and assigned to an office or work. Priests, kings, prophets, altars, and vessels are anointed; Saul remains the LORD's anointed after the Spirit departs, and Cyrus is God's anointed though he does not know Him. The oil marks the appointment, while the Spirit supplies its power — and Exodus keeps lamp oil and the compounded anointing oil distinct."
og_title: "The Anointing — MEAT The Bible's Symbolic Language"
epigraphs:
  - quote: "Thou shalt anoint them, and consecrate them, and sanctify them, that they may minister unto me in the priest's office."
    ref: "Exodus 28:41"
---
Anointing is a church word everyone recognizes and few define.
It has gathered oil, the Spirit, healing, power, and a feeling of divine presence into one religious fog.
Scripture uses the word more exactly.

[discrete]
=== Marked for a Work

The Hebrew verb is _mashach_: to smear or rub.
The Greek sacred-use verb is _chriō_, carrying the same act.
The action is physical at first, but its purpose is stated in the sentence where Aaron and his sons receive it:

[quote.scripture, Exodus 28:41]
____
…thou shalt *anoint* them, and *consecrate* them, and *sanctify* them, *that they may minister unto me in the priest's office*.
____

The final clause defines the first: anoint them _that they may minister_ in the office appointed to them.
Anointing marks a person as God's own and installs him in a stated work.
Kings are anointed to rule, priests to minister, and Elisha __“to be prophet”__ in Elijah's place (1 Kings 19:16).

The same verb is laid on things that can hold no spiritual gift:

[quote.scripture, Exodus 40:9]
____
Thou shalt take the anointing sym:sym-oil[oil], and *anoint* the tabernacle, and all that is therein, and shalt *hallow it*, and all the vessels thereof: and it shall be holy.
____

The tabernacle, ark, altar, laver, and vessels are all anointed (Exodus 30:26-29; 40:9-11).
No one imagines the altar received the Holy Spirit.
Its anointing removed it from ordinary use, marked it as the LORD's, and appointed it to the service for which it was made.

[discrete]
=== Anointed After the Spirit Departed

David receives both appointment and power, in 2 clauses Scripture keeps distinct: Samuel __“anointed him in the midst of his brethren: and the Spirit of the LORD came upon David from that day forward”__ (1 Samuel 16:13).
The oil marks the chosen king; the Spirit equips him for the kingdom.
Related does not mean identical, and Saul proves the difference.

The next verse says __“the Spirit of the LORD departed from Saul”__ (1 Samuel 16:14).
Years afterward David still refuses to kill him:

[quote.scripture, 1 Samuel 24:6]
____
The LORD forbid that I should do this thing unto my master, *the LORD'S anointed*, to stretch forth mine hand against him, seeing he is the *anointed of the LORD*.
____

Saul remained the anointed king after the Spirit departed.
His appointment still stood until God removed him from the office; his empowerment did not.

Cyrus separates the terms even farther.
God calls the Persian ruler __“his anointed”__ and commissions him to subdue nations and release Israel (Isaiah 45:1), then says twice that Cyrus __“hast not known me”__ (Isaiah 45:4-5).
Scripture records no priest pouring Israel's holy compound on his head, and the text grants him no indwelling Spirit.
God nevertheless chose him, took his right hand, and assigned his work.
God's appointment is enough for the title: Cyrus is anointed because he is God's appointed instrument.

The patriarchs bear the same name without a recorded oiling.
God guards Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob from kings under the command __“Touch not mine anointed, and do my prophets no harm”__ (Psalm 105:9-15).
The status rests on God's choice and claim, not on oil remaining in the hair.

[discrete]
=== Anointed With the Spirit

The New Testament states the relationship without collapsing it:

[quote.scripture, Acts 10:38]
____
God *anointed* Jesus of Nazareth *with the Holy Ghost and with power*: who went about doing good, and healing all that were oppressed of the devil; for God was with him.
____

God appoints; Jesus is the appointed; the Holy Spirit and power equip Him; doing good and healing are the assigned work made visible.
The Spirit does not define the verb any more than the priesthood defines it in Exodus.
He is the power with which God furnishes the Anointed for His work.

Isaiah's prophecy follows the same order: __“The Spirit of the Lord GOD is upon me; because the LORD hath anointed me to preach good tidings”__ (Isaiah 61:1; Luke 4:18).
The anointing has an infinitive attached — _to preach_ — because an appointment names a work.
Paul likewise places the acts side by side without making them synonyms: God __“hath anointed us,”__ __“sealed us,”__ and __“given the earnest of the Spirit in our hearts”__ (2 Corinthians 1:21-22).

English hides another distinction.
When the New Testament speaks of putting oil on the sick, perfume on a guest, or ointment on a body, it ordinarily uses _aleiphō_ (Mark 6:13; Luke 7:46; John 12:3; James 5:14).
When it speaks of God's appointment of Jesus or His people, it uses _chriō_ (Luke 4:18; Acts 4:27; 10:38; 2 Corinthians 1:21).
One English word, _anoint_, covers both the ordinary smearing and the sacred appointment, and religious speech has blurred them back together.

[discrete]
=== Oil for the Light, Oil for the Office

The law refuses the final confusion in one inventory:

[quote.scripture, Exodus 25:6]
____
*Oil for the light*, spices for *anointing oil*, and for sweet incense.
____

Lamp oil and anointing oil stand as separate provisions.
The lamp receives __“pure oil olive beaten for the light”__ so that it will burn continually (Exodus 27:20).
The holy anointing oil is a compounded ointment: olive oil carrying myrrh, cinnamon, calamus, and cassia, forbidden on ordinary flesh and forbidden to be copied (Exodus 30:22-33).
The shared olive does not erase the different preparation or work.

Zechariah's lampstand joins oil and Spirit without making them the same thing.
The word to Zerubbabel is __“Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit”__ because the work in view is the temple his hands will finish (Zechariah 4:6-9).
When Zechariah asks what the 2 olive branches are, the angel answers, __“These are the two anointed ones”__ (Zechariah 4:11-14); he never answers, “the oil is the Spirit.”
The Spirit is the power behind the appointed servants and their completed work.
Ezekiel names that work in a person: __“I will put my spirit within you, and cause you to walk in my statutes, and ye shall keep my judgments, and do them”__ (Ezekiel 36:27).

Anointing oil marks an office; lamp oil burns into light.
The king's appointment cannot be poured backward into the virgins' lamps and made their definition merely because both substances began at an olive.
The question in the parable remains what the oil in a lamp does, where it is stored, why it cannot be lent, and what the wise must do to obtain it.

[discrete]
=== The Anointed One

The recovered word has been spoken in every church service.
_Mashiach_ comes from _mashach_; Messiah means _Anointed One_.
Greek carries the title across as _Christos_, Christ.
Andrew says it without a dictionary: __“We have found the Messias, which is, being interpreted, the Christ”__ (John 1:41).

To call Jesus _Christ_ is to confess that God appointed Him — the King, Priest, and Prophet in whom every lesser anointing meets — and furnished Him for the work.
The title does not mean “the One who is oil,” nor does the verb mean “to give the Spirit.”
It names God's choice, claim, and commission.

*To anoint is to mark a person or thing as God's own and appoint it to a stated office or work.*
Oil may carry the visible mark; the Spirit may carry the power; the work declares what the appointment is for.
Keep those 3 in their places and the religious fog lifts: sign, power, and office, joined without being confused.

The anointing gives oil its office.
The next chapter takes another worked food in hand: sym:sym-butter[Butter], milk labored until it stands solid.

sources.name: 47-butter.adoc
sources.content:
---
title: "Butter"
slug: butter
order: 47
permalink: /books/meat-bibles-symbolic-language/butter/
description: "Very few would connect butter to sound doctrine — yet Scripture does. Butter is the word churned solid: milk worked by labor into the discernment diet ('butter and honey shall he eat, that he may know to refuse the evil, and choose the good'), the remnant's food, the wash of the walking feet ('I washed my steps with butter'). Faithful hands carried butter to David in the wilderness while the betrayer's words stayed 'smoother than butter, but war was in his heart' — the true food and its counterfeit, in one story."
og_title: "Butter — MEAT The Bible's Symbolic Language"
epigraphs:
  - quote: "Surely the churning of milk bringeth forth butter."
    ref: "Proverbs 30:33"
---
Butter begins at the churn: milk — the word received — worked by labor until it sets solid.
Very few would connect butter to sound doctrine and meat.
Scripture does, and in more places than the churn.

[discrete]
=== The Discernment Diet

Isaiah serves butter to the survivors:

[quote.scripture, Isaiah 7:22]
____
…for the abundance of sym:sym-milk[milk] that they shall give he shall eat sym:sym-butter[butter]: for butter and honey shall every one eat *that is left in the land*.
____

The remnant eats the worked word.
The outcome of that diet was named seven verses earlier — Immanuel eats butter and honey to __“know to refuse the evil, and choose the good”__ (Isaiah 7:15), the discernment link:/books/symbolic-language/introduction/[Hebrews assigns to the strong-meat eater] (Hebrews 5:14).footnote:fn41diet[Derived in the link:/books/symbolic-language/introduction/[Introduction].]

[discrete]
=== Washed Steps

Job, remembering his best days, packs four symbols into one sentence:

[quote.scripture, Job 29:6]
____
When I washed my sym:sym-way[steps] with sym:sym-butter[butter], and the sym:sym-rock[rock] poured me out rivers of sym:sym-oil[oil];
____

The steps are the walk — the sym:sym-way[way] a man's feet keep; and Job washed his in butter: a walk cleansed by the worked word.
Beside it, the sym:sym-rock[rock] — the covenant — pours out rivers of sym:sym-oil[oil], the pressed and proven works.
No literal dairy explains the sentence; the symbols read it in one breath.

[discrete]
=== Butter in the Wilderness

When David fled Absalom, provision met him in the wilderness:

[quote.scripture, 2 Samuel 17:28-29]
____
…wheat, and barley, and flour… and honey, and *butter*, and sheep, and cheese of kine, for David, and for the people that were with him, to eat: for they said, The people is *hungry, and weary, and thirsty*, in the wilderness.
____

The anointed king, hungering and thirsting in the wilderness, is fed butter by faithful hands.
The counterfeit belongs to the very same story.
Psalm 55 is David's psalm of the betraying counselor in that crisis, and it names his speech:

[quote.scripture, Psalm 55:21]
____
The words of his mouth were smoother than sym:sym-butter[butter], but *war was in his heart*: his words were softer than sym:sym-oil[oil], yet were they drawn sym:sym-sword[swords].
____

Counterfeit butter and counterfeit oil in a single verse — speech worked smooth to imitate sound doctrine, with drawn swords beneath.
The third symbol is *swords*, and the sword is the word — __“the sword of the Spirit, which is the *word of God*”__ (Ephesians 6:17).
All three terms of the psalm's ledger are word-symbols — butter, oil, sword.

A symbol's sense can turn with its bearer, and here every term is the deceiver's version; but the structure of the analogy holds, and its holding is itself a witness: even the counterfeit prices itself in the true currency.
In one crisis Scripture sets both dishes on the table: true butter carried to the fugitive king, and butter-smooth counsel hunting him.

[discrete]
=== A Lordly Dish

Jael's hospitality escalates through the whole dairy:

[quote.scripture, Judges 5:25]
____
He asked water, and she gave him sym:sym-milk[milk]; she brought forth *butter* in a lordly dish.
____

Asked for water, she serves milk and sets out butter — and the enemy of Israel, fed the richest the tent held, lies down and is finished.
Whether the asked-for water carries the living-water register is a question this book leaves open; the escalation itself — water, milk, butter — runs the symbol's whole ladder in one verse.

The churn stands, then, as more than a figure of growth.
Butter is the word worked solid: the discernment diet, the remnant's food, the wash of the walking feet — and the LORD himself accepted it at Abraham's table (Genesis 18:8) and listed it in His own provision (Deuteronomy 32:14).
The final test is whether what was set before you was churned — or merely smoothed.
And the meat on the same table has its counterfeit too — the flesh that presents clean and is not — and it is the next chapter.

sources.name: 48-the-other-white-meat.adoc
sources.content:
---
title: "The Other White Meat"
slug: the-other-white-meat
order: 48
permalink: /books/meat-bibles-symbolic-language/the-other-white-meat/
description: "The law defines the swine by a mismatch: the only beast in the lists that passes the outward test (the parted hoof) and fails the inward one (no cud). It wears the sign of the clean and lacks the work — the whitewashed tomb in beast form, the outward Jew of Romans 2:28, the synagogue of Satan that says and is not. From the boar at the vine to the pearls under trampling feet, from the Gadarene herd to the washed sow, one structure at every depth: the appearance of clean without the word worked inwardly — the counterfeit meat."
og_title: "The Other White Meat — MEAT The Bible's Symbolic Language"
epigraphs:
  - quote: "And the swine, though he divide the hoof, and be clovenfooted, yet he cheweth not the cud; he is unclean to you."
    ref: "Leviticus 11:7"
---
For a generation the pork industry sold its product under one slogan: *the other white meat* — pork marketed as if it were poultry, clean-looking flesh for the health-conscious table.
The slogan was better theology than its writers knew.
The law's swine is exactly that: the meat that *presents* clean and is not — and this book, whose title is sym:sym-meat[MEAT], owes its readers the counterfeit before the vocabulary closes.

Start where the law starts.
Leviticus sorts the beasts by two tests: the parted hoof — the outward test, the walk anyone can see — and the chewed cud, the inward one: food brought back up and worked again.
The camel, the coney, and the hare all fail the same way, cud without hoof.
Then comes the one beast in either list that fails the other way:

[quote.scripture, Deuteronomy 14:8]
____
And the swine, *because* it divideth the hoof, yet cheweth not the cud, it is unclean unto you: ye shall not eat of their flesh, nor touch their dead carcase.
____

Moses' _because_ is the definition: the visible sign is not merely insufficient — worn without the substance, it is the ground of the indictment.
The swine appears to walk the walk — the hoof is the look of obedience, not the life of it — and never chews the word.
The cud is this book's own mechanic in animal form: sym:sym-milk[milk] is the word received, meat is the will done, and between them stands rumination — the word brought back up and chewed again, __“in his law doth he meditate day and night”__ (Psalm 1:2).

The clean beast receives and re-works; the swine swallows once, swallows anything, and never brings it back.
That is why it cannot tell pearls from slop: what has no second chewing has no taste — and the law says so in its own vocabulary, for the __“jewel of gold in a swine's snout”__ hangs on __“a fair woman which is without *discretion*”__ (Proverbs 11:22), and the word under _discretion_ is *ta'am* — **taste**, the very word of __“O *taste* and see that the LORD is good”__ (Psalm 34:8).
Job states the equation the snout fails: __“Doth not the ear try words? and the mouth *taste* his meat?”__ (Job 12:11).

The New Testament has a one-word name for the hoof-without-cud structure.
__“Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, *hypocrites*! For you are like *whitewashed tombs* which indeed appear beautiful outwardly, but inside are full of dead men's bones and all uncleanness”__ (Matthew 23:27 NKJV) — the same outward/inward split as the parted hoof.
Paul writes the beast's definition into covenant standing itself: __“he is not a Jew, which is one *outwardly*… But he is a Jew, which is one *inwardly*; and circumcision is that of the heart”__ (Romans 2:28-29).
The swine is the outward-only covenant member, cast in flesh and forbidden at the table.

[discrete]
=== The Boar at the Vine

Asaph shows the beast at work against the covenant.
God __“brought a vine out of Egypt”__ and planted it (Psalm 80:8); the hedges broke, and __“the *boar out of the wood* doth waste it”__ (Psalm 80:13).
The boar is _chazir_, the swine; the wood is the forest — and the sym:sym-tree[Trees] chapter has already surveyed that forest: the towering trees are the gentile powers.
The boar out of the wood is the unclean nation out of the gentile forest, gnawing the vine of Israel.
Its verb is _karsam_, __“doth waste”__ — it stands nowhere else in the Hebrew Bible, and it is about to reappear.

[discrete]
=== Pearls Under Feet

The Pearls of Wisdom chapter opened this verse; here stands the beast that dictated it:

[quote.scripture, Matthew 7:6]
____
Give not that which is *holy* unto the sym:sym-dog[dogs], neither cast ye your *pearls* before *swine*, lest they *trample them under their feet*, and turn again and rend you.
____

The Hebrew Matthewfootnote:fn46hg[The Hebrew Matthew cited throughout this book is the Shem Tov text, preserved complete in Ibn Shaprut's _Even Bochan_ (c. 1385). The full text, alongside the book's other Hebrew witnesses, is at https://TimeTested.Bible[TimeTested.Bible].] tightens both halves.
__“That which is holy”__ is written there as *holy flesh* — _basar qodesh_, the sacrificial meat of Haggai 2:12, carried in the covenant hem — so the withheld thing is MEAT, holy meat.
And __“lest they trample”__ reads __“lest they *chew* them”__ — that verb, _karsam_, stands exactly *once* in the whole Hebrew Bible, at the boar in Asaph's vine.
A translator working backward from the Greek would have reached for the everyday word for trampling; this text reaches past it for the rarest verb in the language — the boar's own.

One beast, one mouth, vine or pearls: the Hebrew Matthew does not construct the connection, it carries it.
The consonants even close the scene: the verse ends _ve-yachzeru_ — __“and they *turn* to tear you”__ — _chazar_, the return-verb, written on the swine's own letters.
The _chazir_ chazars; the beast does what its name says.
Peter will need that pun shortly.

[discrete]
=== The Herd and the Tombs

In the country of the Gadarenes the symbol walks.
Isaiah had marked where the swine-eaters dwell, seven centuries before:

[quote.scripture, Isaiah 65:4]
____
Which *remain among the graves*, and lodge in the monuments, which *eat swine's flesh*, and broth of abominable things is in their vessels;
____

Now hear Mark set the scene:

[quote.scripture, "Mark 5:3, 5, 11"]
____
Who had his *dwelling among the tombs*… And always, night and day, he was in the sym:sym-mountain[mountains], and in the tombs, crying, and cutting himself with stones… Now there was there nigh unto the sym:sym-mountain[mountains] a great herd of *swine* feeding.
____

Graves, mountains, swine: the prophecy staged as an exorcism.
The mountains are not scenery: a sym:sym-mountain[mountain] is a kingdom, and the herd feeds hard against the kingdoms — the unclean nation grazing on the powers of the age — until it is driven off them into the sea of the peoples.
The unclean spirits' own plea names their preferred house — out of the man, into the swine — and granted it, the herd __“ran violently down a steep place into the sym:sym-sea[sea]… and were choked in the sea”__ (Mark 5:13): Legion, a Roman army word, drowned like Pharaoh's host, as the link:/books/symbolic-language/sea-and-waters/[Sea & Waters] chapter read it.
The city then begged Jesus to leave — the economy of the unclean preferred its herd to the healed man — and the man himself, clothed and in his right mind, was sent: __“Go home to thy friends, and tell them how great things the Lord hath done for thee”__ (Mark 5:19) — pulled out of Isaiah's tombs and mountains, and planted in gentile ground as its first herald.

[discrete]
=== The Far Country's Trough

The prodigal lived it from the other side.
In the far country the younger son __“joined himself to a citizen of that country; and he sent him into his fields to feed swine. And he would fain have filled his belly with the husks that the swine did eat: and *no man gave unto him*”__ (Luke 15:15-16).
The lost house in exile, bonded to the unclean nation, tending its appetites, envying its slop — and discovering that the far country feeds its swine and not its servants.
His coming to himself is a bread-count — __“how many hired servants of my father's have sym:sym-bread[bread] enough and to spare”__ (Luke 15:17) — and his restoration is a robe and a table: __“Bring forth the best robe… bring hither the fatted calf… and let us eat”__ (Luke 15:22-23).
Feeding swine is what exile *is*; the feast is what return looks like.
Between the trough where no man gave and the table where the Father gives stands the whole gospel — and the swine-field is the one station with no giver in it.

[discrete]
=== The Sow That Was Washed

Peter closes the case on the beast, and he closes it on teachers:

[quote.scripture, 2 Peter 2:22]
____
But it is happened unto them according to the true proverb, The sym:sym-dog[dog] is turned to his own vomit again; and the *sow that was washed* to her wallowing in the mire.
____

The chapter is doctrinal end to end — it opens on __“false teachers… who privily shall bring in damnable heresies”__ (2 Peter 2:1) and calls them __“wells without water”__ (2 Peter 2:17) — and it ends on the pun the Hebrew Matthew wrote into the swine verse: both halves of the proverb turn on *returning*, and the _chazir_ is the returner.
The washing was real; the nature was not changed by it.
The sow's appetite survived her bath, because a bath is not a birth: __“by one Spirit are we all baptized *into one body*”__ (1 Corinthians 12:13) — washed *and* incorporated.
Washed only, she goes back under the feet that trample — into the mire, the trodden street-clay, the one place Ezekiel's healing river passes by: __“the miry places thereof… shall not be healed”__ (Ezekiel 47:11).

[discrete]
=== The Swine Inside the Gates

The Old Testament's last swine verses aim inward — not at Rome, but at covenant men wearing the beast's structure.
Isaiah's indictment builds across two chapters: they sacrifice in gardens, burn incense on altars of brick, __“remain among the graves… which eat *swine's flesh*, and broth of abominable things is in their vessels”__ — and then the boast that gives the beast away: __“which say, Stand by thyself, come not near to me; for *I am holier than thou*”__ (Isaiah 65:3-5).
The swine-eater claims *extra* holiness — hoof without cud, worn as a crown.
In the next chapter the offerings themselves invert: __“he that killeth an ox is as if he slew a man… he that offereth an oblation, as if he offered *swine's blood*”__ (Isaiah 66:3) — worship from the self-willed is the unclean offering, whatever is on the altar.
The sequence ends at the LORD's coming:

[quote.scripture, Isaiah 66:17]
____
They that *sanctify themselves*, and purify themselves in the sym:sym-garden[gardens] behind one sym:sym-tree[tree] in the midst, eating *swine's flesh*, and the abomination, and the mouse, shall be *consumed together*, saith the LORD.
____

The gardens are not horticulture: a sym:sym-garden[garden] is a planted stand of nation-sym:sym-tree[trees], as the link:/books/symbolic-language/trees/[Trees] chapter surveyed — so these seek their sanctification among the nations, behind one tree in the midst, with a deliberate menu of the forbidden on their lips (the mouse stands on the same Leviticus list as the swine).
Self-sanctified, gentile-grown, and judged at the coming: the food law stands in Scripture's final vision, and the man who eats the counterfeit meat has made himself its emblem.

Now set Isaiah's swine-eaters beside a phrase of Revelation.
Twice the risen Lord speaks of __“them which *say they are Jews, and are not*, but are the *synagogue of Satan*”__ (Revelation 2:9; 3:9) — the assembly that claims the sym:sym-name[name] without the sym:sym-truth[truth] of it; and __“thy law is the truth”__ (Psalm 119:142): the name worn, the law missing.
That is the swine's structure stated of a whole assembly: the outward sign worn, the inward work absent — Romans 2:28-29's outward Jew, gathered into a body.
Isaiah had already drawn them: __“Your brethren that hated you, that *cast you out for my name's sake*, said, *Let the LORD be glorified*”__ (Isaiah 66:5) — persecution dressed in praise, from inside the family, in the very chapter where the swine's flesh is eaten by the self-sanctified.
The parted hoof can incorporate; it can fill a room and call itself an assembly.
What it cannot do is chew the cud — and by that test, not by the nameplate, the two assemblies are told apart.

Under the flesh-as-teaching register this book keeps meeting, one more floor opens.
The consonants of _basar_, flesh, are the consonants of the herald's tidings — the root of _besorah_, the sym:sym-gospel[gospel]-word, as the link:/books/symbolic-language/gospel/[Gospel] chapter found.
To eat swine's flesh, at that depth, is to receive the swine's *tidings* — __“another gospel: which is not another”__ (Galatians 1:6-7) — the counterfeit good-news of the nation that never chews what it swallows.
The other white meat is the other gospel.

[discrete]
=== Peter's Sheet, and the Boundary

One vision guards this symbol from both abuses.
When God opened the door to the nations He showed Peter a sheet of __“all manner of fourfooted beasts”__ with the command, __“Rise, Peter; kill, and eat”__ — and Peter gives the vision's own interpretation, twice: __“God hath shewed me that I should not call *any man* common or unclean”__ (Acts 10:28).
The sym:sym-beast[beasts] are men; the vision is God taking nations into covenant — the link:/books/symbolic-language/trees/[Trees] chapter walked it through.
It changes what the nations are, not what dinner is: years later Peter still writes of the washed sow, because the beast that stays a beast stays unclean.
A man may stop being pictured by the swine — the Gadarene was; the prodigal was — and the sheet declares that no nation is beyond the cleansing.
But the picture itself never becomes food.

[discrete]
=== Living the Similitude

Now weigh what the whole case makes of the command itself.
God says of the prophets, __“I have multiplied visions, and used *similitudes*, by the ministry of the prophets”__ (Hosea 12:10) — and the Signs & Similitudes chapter showed what that ministry cost: Hosea's marriage was the similitude, Ezekiel's siege-brick was the similitude; the prophets did not merely speak the pictures, they *lived* them, by obedience.
It went as far as the oven.
Ezekiel was commanded to bake his siege-bread over human dung (Ezekiel 4:12), and the similitude was decoded on the spot:

[quote.scripture, Ezekiel 4:13]
____
Even thus shall the children of Israel eat their *defiled* sym:sym-bread[bread] among the Gentiles, whither I will drive them.
____

His protest is the measure of the man: __“Ah Lord GOD! behold, my soul hath *not been polluted*: for from my youth up even till now have I not eaten of that which dieth of itself, or is torn in pieces; neither came there *abominable flesh* into my mouth”__ (Ezekiel 4:14).
A prophet cast in a similitude of defiled food pleads his clean diet as his whole credential — and God changes the sign, not the man: __“I have given thee cow's dung for man's dung”__ (Ezekiel 4:15).
The food law casts every covenant household in the same theater.
The man who eats the clean and refuses the swine enacts, three meals a day, the picture the law drew: take in what walks and ruminates — the word received and worked — and take nothing that only appears clean.
His table is a lived similitude, as Hosea's house was.
The theater is not the reason the command binds — it binds because God spoke it — but it is the reason revealed: obedience is a role in the play, and the prophets teach us to want the part.

You have now watched the beast from every side — at the vine, under the pearls, among the tombs, at the trough, in the mire, and inside the gates claiming the name.
Keep the command, and you fulfill the picture; explain the picture away and drop the command, and you have become the picture's subject — the parted hoof with nothing brought back up.
The command stands, the similitude stands on it, and the two assemblies stand before it: one brings the word back up and chews it toward doing; the other wears the hoof.
Taste is the whole difference — and the glossary ahead holds the vocabulary this book has assembled so that yours, by use, may be exercised to discern.
